r: Brut is a local-first, bring-your-own-key node canvas for orchestrating generative-AI providers: Google Gemini (images, Gemini Omni video), OpenAI, Anthropic (text), Kling, Seedance and Seedream (BytePlus), Black Forest Labs (FLUX) and Ideogram for generation; Magnific and Topaz for upscaling; OpenRouter, fal and Replicate as aggregator routes when you'd rather hold one key than six. Your keys. Your machine. Zero markup. Brut never sits between you and the provider — every generation call goes straight from your computer to the provider, billed to your own account at their price. A working archviz graph: stills in, a contact sheet of viewpoints, a correction pass, a 4K upscale, every step on your own keys

Most AI tools are a website that holds your key, runs the model on their servers, and marks up the price. Brut inverts that: Bring your own key (BYOK). You paste your provider keys once; they live in your OS keychain and are used only for direct calls from your machine. Local-first. Brut runs entirely on your computer. Graphs, outputs and projects live on your disk (or your NAS). Nothing routes through a server anyone pays for. Zero markup, ever. Calls go from your machine to Google/OpenAI/Kling/etc. at their price. Brut is never in the call path. Never pay twice. Every node remembers what it was given: if nothing changed, the last result is reused for free. Re-run a graph after a client note and only what actually changed costs money. If you work under NDA, this matters: your renders go only to the provider you pick, on your key — never to us.

Brut runs entirely on your machine. A small local engine holds your keys, talks to each provider directly and writes every output to your disk. There is no Brut server in between and no hosted version, by design.

Images — text-to-image, image-to-image, inpainting, composition, and multi-shot exploration (a whole contact sheet of viewpoints from one scene, with a deck of surprise cards so the takes never repeat). Corrections: Adjust lets you paint or click where the change goes, or draw arrows and notes on a render and attach a reference, and the model applies those changes one step at a time, the original kept outside each edit; Layers paints the original back wherever the model overreached, locally and for free. Compose by hand first — the Sketchpad: brush strokes and wired images as movable layers on one canvas, flattened locally into the image you generate from. Free. Video — animate stills into clips with Kling, Gemini Omni or Seedance, with an itemized cost quote before a cent is spent. Whole films — the Cinema Sessions: a crew of AI agents (scenarist, art director, DoP, script supervisor) that plan a sequence from your stills, which you then render as clips and edit together on your machine (the edit is free). Delivery resolution — upscale stills and clips to 4K/8K with Magnific or Topaz (or your own local Topaz Video AI, free). Ready-made workflows — a shipped bank of pre-wired chains for the recurring jobs (clay to photoreal, day to dusk, populate, weather, an editorial sheet, a hero still to a clip, and more): each drops as one card with knobs, on named models, from the home screen or the library. See Workflows. A studio companion — Marcel reads your canvas, narrates what happened, advises on models and looks, and can build graphs for you on request — on your own key, every call in the ledger.

Install & first run — get Brut running and sign in. Your first image — a three-node graph, start to finish. Nodes & graphs — how the canvas thinks. Marcel — the companion that lives beside the canvas.
Brut is a native Windows app: one installer, one window. No Python, no terminal, no browser tab.

Windows 10/11. A billing-enabled API key for at least one provider (see Providers). A free-tier key usually has zero image quota: an error 429 on your first image means billing isn't enabled, not that you hit a rate limit. That's it — the installer brings everything else.

Download Brut-Setup.exe from getbrut.app/download — log in with the email address your beta approval was sent to (that address is your access; your approval email links straight there). The sign-in email carries a link (press Continue on the page it opens) and an 8-digit code you can type on the page instead, handy when your company's mail system opens links before you do. Windows SmartScreen will warn about an unrecognized app — expected: the beta build isn't code-signed yet. Click More info → Run anyway. The installer runs per-user — no admin prompt — shows the beta license, and adds Start-menu and desktop shortcuts. Launch Brut from either. The window appears in a couple of seconds; the engine starts (and stops) with it. A tray icon in the notification area shows the engine's status and offers the engine log and Quit.
Install the desktop app › Where things live

Your work — projects, outputs, library, account state — lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut, as plain files on your disk. Your keys live in the OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager), never in a file. The engine log is at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut\logs\engine.log (previous launch kept as engine.log.1) — attach it when reporting a bug. Uninstalling never deletes %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut — your projects and keys survive uninstall and reinstall.

No auto-update in the beta: getbrut.app/download always serves the latest build — when we announce a new version, download it there and run it over the old version. Projects, keys and sign-in all carry over. Brut does check for you: at launch, while signed in, it compares your version with the latest installer and shows one line under the toolbar (Brut x.y.z is available, with a Download button) when you're behind. Up to date means nothing is shown.

Brut requires a free account (it's how we count seats during the beta — nothing about your prompts, images or keys is ever sent). On first launch you'll hit a sign-in screen: Continue with Google or GitHub, or Email — enter your address. The email carries a link (open it and Brut finishes signing you in) and an 8-digit code you can type into the same screen instead. Use the code when your company's mail system opens links before you do: it uses the one-time link up, the code still works. Sign-in is required, but it never bricks you: once you're in, a 30-day offline grace keeps you working through flights and outages, and if the sign-in server is ever unreachable a "continue for now" option appears. Right after your first sign-in, Brut shows the beta license once and asks you to accept it (again only if the license changes). Your seat is personal: please don't pass the installer around — someone else wants in? Ask them to register on getbrut.app.

Click the key icon on the left rail (or the setup wizard walks you through it on first run). For each provider, paste your key and Brut validates it on save. Keys are stored in your OS keychain — never in a graph, never sent anywhere but the provider. The setup wizard: paste a key, Validate, done. Keys go to the OS keychain, never to us
Add your provider keys › Your first project

On first launch the wizard also asks where your work lives: name your first project and choose its folder, a local folder or a share on your NAS. That step cannot be skipped — every graph, result and ledger row you make lands in a project, and the starter graph that follows lands in this one. Create more any time from File ▾ → New project…, and move a canvas between projects with File ▾ → Save project as… (see Projects & the ledger). See each provider's page for where to get a key and its billing quirks. The quickest start is Google Gemini: a Nano Banana 2 Lite render is about $0.03.

Brut opens on a home screen, not a bare canvas: the place the day starts from. Continue — the big card is your live canvas: which graph, which project, when it was last saved, and its latest results as the cover (hover it to flip through the last five). Continue (or Esc) puts you back on it. Beside it, What's new lists Brut's development and the models that joined the catalog, newest first, each entry linking to its docs or changelog page (the list scrolls); when a newer installer exists, the first entry says so with a download link. Recent graphs — every saved graph across all your projects, newest first, each carrying its project as a colored badge. Two rows show at a time; the pager at the gallery's lower right (arrows around a "1 / 3" counter) turns the pages. The cover is the graph's own most recent result; hover it and it flips through the last five results downstream (the dots let you pick one), so you see what that graph made, not one frame. A • next to a name means the canvas holds changes not yet saved to it (the card then shows the canvas' own results). Click a card and Brut switches project if needed and opens the graph; the usual "unsaved work" guard still asks. The select narrows to one project, the search box to a name. Workflows — New graph first (it asks for a name and saves the starter graph under it, so you never land on unsaved work), then the workflows that ship with Brut and the ones you saved, as cards with their picture. A template starts a new graph; a composite drops onto your canvas as one card. Hover a cover that holds a pair and it shows what went in, then what came out. The chips filter by category, the label you give an item when you save it. Two rows show at a time; the pager at the lower right (arrows around a page counter) turns the pages. The last tile, Open the library, opens the full gallery. Brut opens on the home screen: Continue where you left off, recent graphs from every project, templates to start from The house icon on the left rail (just above Settings) and File ▾ → Home bring the screen back any time. The checkbox at its bottom, Show this screen at launch, turns the landing off; the house icon still works.

The window has two homes for controls. The top bar holds the workspace controls: the File ▾ menu, the project and graph selectors, the spend readout, ▶ Run, your account, and the engine status dot. The File menu reads label and keyboard shortcut, nothing more (hover an item for a word on what it does). Project actions sit on Ctrl+Shift: Ctrl+Shift+N new project, Ctrl+Shift+S save project as, Ctrl+Shift+O open project. Graph actions sit on Ctrl+Alt: Ctrl+Alt+N new graph, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S save as, Ctrl+Alt+I import a graph file; and Ctrl+S saves the graph, as always. The project selector lists the ten projects you opened most recently; the rest sit under N more… (see Projects & the ledger). ▶ Run is a two-step button: it first reveals, replaying every cached, pinned and free step for $0 and marking the nodes whose inputs changed with a needs a run badge (they keep their last result on the face); if anything would bill, one dialog itemizes it with the estimate, and you choose Generate or Keep cached only. The ▶ on a node runs that node and its upstream straight away, as before. The left rail is your tools: add a node, undo/redo, tidy, the Library, Marcel, the home screen, keys, feedback, and the theme toggle. Hover any rail icon for an instant tooltip with its name, its keyboard shortcut, and one line on what it does — and the » pin at the rail's bottom expands it to show labels next to every icon (on by default; collapse it once the icons feel familiar). The rail on the left holds every tool and panel; the top bar keeps only the workspace controls The rail's + opens the node browser: every node grouped by category — Inputs, Text, Images, Video, Cinema team, Utilities — plus your saved Library composites. Hovering a row shows what the node does, what flows in and out of it, and whether it costs money ($), is free, or is free with a paid option inside (free · $: the Sketchpad draws and flattens for free, only its generation layers bill a model). Click a row to place it at the canvas center, or drag it to drop it exactly where you want. (Pressing Tab over the canvas still opens the quick palette at your cursor — the fast path once you know the names.)

Right after the setup wizard, Brut walks you through the interface once — a short spotlight tour of the canvas, the node families, projects, running & caching, the spend ledger, Marcel, and where your keys live. Skip it any time with Esc, and relaunch it whenever you like from File ▾ → Functionality tour.

The Marcel button on the left rail (the pulse icon) opens the studio timeline — a chronological feed of what's happening: plans, runs, results and errors, plus your chat with Marcel, Brut's built-in companion. The timeline is saved with the project, so reopening it (even after a restart, or on another machine via a NAS share) shows the continuous history. A Raw events / Chat only toggle in its header hides the technical lines when you just want the highlights.
Found a bug? Tell us from inside the app

The green speech-bubble button on the left rail opens Send feedback — a bug, an idea, anything. Reports go straight to the team, tied to your account email so we can reply. Diagnostics (Brut's version, OS, recent error messages) are opt-in, and the modal shows exactly what will be sent before you send it — never your graphs, images, prompts or keys. Details in Privacy. When you quit the desktop app after a session that ran something, Brut asks for a one-line note on how it went ("Before you go"). It's the same feedback form with a session summary on top; Quit without sending is always one click, and nothing is sent unless you press Send & quit.

If the engine dies mid-session, the desktop app tells you — a dialog with the last lines of engine output and a button to the full log — instead of a frozen window. If the app shows an "engine offline" banner, relaunch Brut. And if launch fails with "Port 8723 is taken", some other program on your machine is using Brut's port — close it and relaunch.
Let's make one image end to end. This takes about a minute and costs roughly $0.03 on Gemini's cheapest image model.
The fastest path: the starter graph

The setup wizard offers a starter graph on its last step, right after it has you create your first project — a ready-wired Prompt → Refine → Text→Image → Preview chain on Nano Banana 2 Lite. Click Add starter graph, then hit ▶ Run in the toolbar. Done. (Re-open the wizard any time from File ▾ → Setup wizard….) Add the starter graph, press Run, watch the image land with its cost on the badge If you'd rather build it by hand, here's the same thing in three nodes.

Add a Prompt node. Press Tab over the canvas (or + Node) and pick Prompt. Type a description: A sunlit modern villa at golden hour, floor-to-ceiling glass, a calm reflecting pool, photographic Add a Text→Image node. Drag from the Prompt node's output onto empty canvas — the add menu opens filtered to compatible nodes; pick Text → Image. It wires up automatically. In the node, choose provider Gemini and model Nano Banana 2 Lite. Add a Preview node the same way, wired from the Text→Image output. Run. Click ▶ Run (or the ▶ on the Text→Image node to run just it). ▶ Run never generates blindly: it first replays everything that is already cached (free), then asks once, with the estimate, before anything is generated. On a fresh graph that is one dialog: Generate calls Gemini with your key, downloads the image to your project's outputs folder, and shows it inline. The node badge reports the cost. Drag from an output onto empty canvas: the menu opens filtered to what fits, and the pick arrives wired That's the whole loop: prompt → generate → preview.

Brut made one call to Gemini on your key and saved the image in your project's outputs folder. The node remembered the result together with what produced it. Run again and it's free — nothing changed, so nothing is re-billed. Change the prompt and only that node re-pays. See Never pay twice. The generation was recorded in your project ledger — click the 🕘 on the node to see its history and re-pin any past result. The 🕘 on any paid node: every past result, and one click pins it back as the output, free

429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED on the first call → your Gemini key isn't billing-enabled (the free tier has zero image quota). Enable billing in Google AI Studio. See Google Gemini. A ⚠ "Add your … key" button on the node → that provider isn't configured; click it to jump to the wizard. An image edit comes back with no image (the error mentions OTHER) → Gemini refused it without saying why, usually because of an input image (a real person's name in facade lettering, a face, a logo) rather than the prompt. Remove or crop the offending image.
Refine your prompts with the Prompt Helper. Image generation — editing, inpainting, composing. Multi-Shot — a contact sheet of viewpoints from one scene.

Brut ships with a small bank of ready-made workflows: chains of nodes already wired, with their prompts and models set, for the jobs that come back every week. You find them in two places: the Workflows row of the home screen, and the Library gallery (the book icon on the left rail, or File ▾ → Browse library…), on the From Brut shelf. The cards below match exactly what drops on your canvas.

A composite drops as one closed card with a few knobs on its face: a brief, a mode, a shot count, the model of a stage. Wire your image into its inlet, set the knobs, press Run. Open the card (⤢) when you want to see or edit the nodes inside. A template drops onto your canvas too, as a group of live nodes named after it. Nothing is hidden; edit anything. Every image stage is set to a named model at a named size, so a workflow gives the same kind of result on every seat. Video and upscale stages ship unset: the provider choice, and its price, are yours. The card tells you when a stage still needs a pick. Try with sample, on the workflows that ship with one, copies a sample picture into your project and drops the workflow already wired to it, with the shipped result on the card (captioned sample result) so you see what it does before paying for a run. Nothing runs until you press Run; a real run replaces the sample result. A card glows while a stage inside it renders, like any node, and its title bar carries 🕘 (every past take of a stage) and ↻ (a fresh take of a stage); a card with several stages asks which one. Cards whose result is a clip rest on the still they take and play the clip on hover. Once a card has a result, its Next chips offer the workflows that usually follow: one click drops the next card beside it, wired to the result. A dropped card is frozen at the version you dropped: it never changes under you. When Brut ships a newer version of that workflow, the card shows a small vN in the library chip; drop the workflow again to get the new recipe. Your own saved composites and templates sit on the Yours shelf, as the same kind of cards. The Never pay twice rule holds inside a workflow: a changed knob re-renders the stage it writes to, everything else is reused for free.

Any chain you have tuned can become a workflow of your own. Select its nodes, Collapse to composite, and press 💾 Save to library on the card; the save dialog asks for a category from the pick list (Architecture, Characters, Cinema, Text, or one you type) and keeps the card's result as the cover. ⚙ Add knob on the card exposes an inner field on its face. A whole graph saves as a template from File ▾ → Save graph as template…. The details, ports, knobs and versions, are in Library & composites.

Brut is a node canvas. You build a graph — nodes connected by wires — and run it. Nodes are shots and decisions, not low-level settings: a node is "generate an image," "animate this clip," "plan the film," not a low-level knob.

Add a node — the + on the left rail opens the node browser: every node by category (in workflow order), with a hover card showing what it does, what flows in and out, and whether it costs money. Click places it at the canvas center; drag drops it where you let go. Or press Tab over the canvas for the quick palette at your cursor — type to filter, ↑/↓ + Enter to place. With nothing typed the list is alphabetical (so is the list a dragged wire offers); typing ranks the matches. Pan — middle-drag. Box-select — left-drag: anything the rectangle touches is selected, nodes and wires (a box drawn over a bundle of wires alone picks them up, wires light up as the box sweeps over them and when you hover them; Delete then removes everything selected). Zoom — scroll wheel, anywhere on the canvas, including over a board or contact sheet whose tiles all fit. Only a grid that actually overflows takes the wheel for itself, to scroll its tiles; text areas do the same. A grid or text box that overflows shows its scrollbar while your pointer is over its node, or while you are typing in it; at rest it simply clips. That is what keeps panning and zooming smooth on a canvas of a hundred nodes: every live scrolling box inside the canvas costs the browser work on every frame, so there is none until you need one. Left-drag selects, middle-drag pans, the wheel zooms, Tab opens the node menu at the cursor Menus inside nodes — a model, aspect or quality menu on a node opens as a list drawn at screen size, so it reads the same at every zoom; greyed entries show their reason on hover, arrow keys and typing move through it, Enter picks and Esc closes. A native drop-down inside the canvas costs the browser a layout on every pan or zoom step; this one does not. Wire — drag from an output port to an input port. Drop a wire on empty canvas and the add menu opens, filtered to compatible nodes — pick one and it's placed and wired. Three gestures work on wires you already have, all explained under Ports and wires: double-click a wire to splice a node into it, Alt-click a wire to split it with a dot and send it to more nodes, Alt-click a pin to move all its wires to another pin. Wire style — the three wire buttons on the left rail (curved, straight, stepped) set how every wire in the graph is drawn. One style per graph: it's saved in the graph file and Ctrl+Z undoes a switch. Old graphs open curved, exactly as before. Snap to grid — the magnet on the left rail. On, a dragged node lands on the canvas dots (the dots are the grid); off, nodes go exactly where you drop them. It's a preference of this computer, not of the graph, and it stays as you left it. Magnet off, a node stops between dots; magnet on, it lands on them and lines up with its neighbor Move children: the toggle under the magnet. On, dragging a node drags everything upstream of it (its inputs, their inputs, through composite ports and reroute dots), the way a linked hierarchy follows its parent in a 3D package; off, a drag moves only what you hold. What a node feeds never rides along. Nodes already in your selection move once, never twice. A preference of this computer, like the magnet. Opening a graph fits it to the window: from the home, the graph switcher or a file, the canvas lands zoomed on the whole graph, never on where the last viewport happened to be. Undo, autosave and Marcel's additions leave your view alone. Its pictures are there at once, too: the small copies the canvas shows are made the moment a file lands in the project (a generation, a tool's result, an upload), not the first time you look at them, so a big graph opens as fast on a fresh machine or a shared project folder as on the one that made it. Pull a wire off — an input pin holding one wire: press it and drag, and you pick that wire up instead of starting a new one. Drop it on another pin to move it there, on empty canvas to remove it (Ctrl+Z puts it back), on a pin that refuses it and it snaps back. A click without a drag changes nothing. Inlets holding several wires (a board's stills) keep the usual new-wire drag, and Alt on a pin is still the bulk rewire. Wire menu — right-click a wire: Color (Auto follows the node the wire leaves, None keeps it plain, or one of the six hues — applied to every selected wire when the clicked one is part of a selection), Add reroute here (the Alt-click split), Insert node… (the double-click splice), Delete wire. Node menu — right-click a node: Color, Run, Duplicate, Group, Collapse to composite, Delete. With several nodes selected, Duplicate and Delete act on all of them, and Group / Collapse light up. Text fields and image previews keep their own menus. Node color — pick one of six hues (the same ones group frames use) from the node menu. The whole node takes the color (body, outline and title — readable zoomed far out), and so does every wire leaving it — the fastest way to read a dense graph. Right-click one node of a selection and the color lands on all of them. Reroute dots pass the color along; a wire can also be given its own color from the wire menu; a hovered or selected wire still shows the accent. Run — ▶ Run executes the whole graph; the ▶ on a node runs just that node and everything it depends on. Copy, paste, duplicate — Ctrl+C copies the selected nodes, Ctrl+V pastes fresh copies, Ctrl+D duplicates in one step. Copies keep their incoming wires: a duplicated node arrives already fed by the same upstream nodes as the original (outgoing wires are not duplicated — that would double-feed whatever the original feeds). Ctrl+V pastes at your cursor — point where you want the copies and paste; a multi-node selection keeps its arrangement, and a copy pasted inside a group frame's area joins that group (exactly like dropping it there). Ctrl+D still lands the duplicate just beside the original. Paste an image — Ctrl+V with an image on the OS clipboard (Photoshop Ctrl+A+Ctrl+C, a render buffer's Copy button, a browser image) drops a ready-filled Image In node at your cursor. If you copied both, whichever you copied last wins the shortcut. Tidy: the grid button on the left rail auto-arranges the graph as a table that follows the wiring: columns are the pipeline stages, and a Prompt, the Multi-Shot it feeds and that Multi-Shot's Shot Board share one row with their tops aligned. Tidying again changes nothing. It's one undo step: Ctrl+Z puts everything back. Hierarchy: a Prompt or an Image In sits in the column just before the node it feeds; a shared input that feeds several rows (one frame feeding five renders, each with its own prompt) sits level with the middle of them; variants of one prompt sit side by side. A set of inputs feeding the same node (say, eight Image Ins feeding one board) wraps into a compact grid, a 3×3 contact sheet rather than a tower. Many short chains: independent chains (pipelines not wired to each other) stack top-down in the order they were and never interleave. When many short chains would make one tall column, say five pairs of a Prompt and a Text → Image or ten loose Image Ins, Tidy lays them side by side in rows instead, in the same order, each keeping its own shape. Sticky notes: a note parked beside a node (touching it, or within a short gap) stays with that node and keeps its room. A note above a node makes the whole row start lower, a note beside it makes the column wider, and a title wider than its node spans the row without widening anything. A note far from every node rides along with the nearest one and is set down clear of the nodes if it would land on or right next to one. Pen strokes ride along too and never make room. Selection: with two or more nodes selected, only those are tidied, in place: the block keeps the selection's top-left corner and nothing outside it moves (select a group frame to tidy its inside). If that arrangement would land on a node outside the selection, Tidy tries a plainer one that stays clear of it. If no plainer one fits, it keeps the full arrangement. Node ids — every node's title bar shows its id in small type (multi_shot-21). That's the name Marcel and the ledger use when they refer to a node — click the id to copy it.

Every node exposes typed ports. Wires carry one of three things: images, text (prompts and plans), or video. Ports are labeled by role — a Compose node has scene and reference image inlets. Brut only lets you connect compatible types, and picks the right inlet automatically when you drag-to-connect. Some nodes expose per-tile output plugs — a Shot Board tile has its own handle so you can route one chosen shot downstream, a Clip Board tile has one per clip.
Ports and wires › Splice a node into a wire

Double-click a wire (or right-click it → Insert node…): the add menu opens, filtered to the nodes that fit between the two ends. Pick one and it lands on the wire, wired in and out — an Upscale between a generator and its Preview, a Conform in front of a board, without redrawing anything. Double-click a wire, pick a node: it lands on the wire, wired in and out
Ports and wires › Split a wire with a reroute dot

Alt-click a wire and a small dot drops on it at that point: the wire now runs through the dot, and the dot is a branch point. Send the same output to more nodes — drag a new wire off the dot to any compatible input. Drop it on empty canvas and the add menu opens, filtered to what the wire carries; the node you pick arrives already wired. One output feeds as many nodes as you like, and you branch from where you are instead of going back to the source node. Route the wire around things — drag the dot (Substance style). Add more dots for more bends. Right-click a wire → Add reroute here does the same. A dot has one inlet and as many outlets as you drag off it, and it carries the color of its wire along. It's purely cosmetic: it changes nothing about how the graph runs or what it costs, so nothing downstream re-runs or re-pays, and Marcel doesn't see it. Delete a dot and the wire heals: its input reconnects to every wire that left it, nothing is left dangling. Alt-click a wire: a dot drops on it; drag a new wire off the dot and the same output feeds a second node
Ports and wires › Move wires between pins (Alt-click a pin)

To re-plumb a graph without redrawing it, Alt-click a pin. Every pin on the canvas starts pulsing: a rewire is armed on that pin (the Activity panel says so). Then click the destination pin (Alt no longer needed): Same kind (an output, then another output; or an input, then another input): every wire on the first pin moves to the second, and their other ends stay where they are. Five nodes fed by one Prompt? Alt-click its output, click the output of a new Prompt, and all five are fed by the new one. An input, then an output: whatever fed that input now comes from that output — "feed this from there instead". An output, then an input: the wires leaving that output are pulled onto that single input. Click the armed pin again, press Esc or click empty canvas to cancel. Two wires that would end up on the same two pins merge into one. The Activity panel logs what moved, and Ctrl+Z undoes it like any other edit. Alt-click a Prompt's output, click another Prompt's output: every wire moves across in one go

Run starts each node as soon as its inputs are ready, so independent branches run at the same time. A node whose inputs haven't changed answers from its last result, for free. See Never pay twice. Two runs can happen at once, and nothing is ever paid twice. Run: independent branches execute at the same time, unchanged nodes answer from cache instantly

Family Nodes Inputs Prompt, Image In Text Refine, Text → Text, Text Board, Join text Images Text → Image, Image → Image, Adjust, Layers, Sketchpad, Compose, Upscale Image Exploration Multi-Shot, Shot Board Cinema team Reference Board, Director (plan + proof sheet), Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor, Storyboard, Film Shots Video Image → Video, Clip Board, Extract frame, Upscale Video, Sequence Utilities Conform, Preview, Compare, History 3D Scene, Camera Each family has its own page under Nodes in the sidebar. Sticky notes, emoji stamps, the pen and text labels aren't nodes — they're annotation tools in the rail's Organize section, also one right-click away via the ring menu (all documented on the utility page).

Brut saves your canvas into the project a moment after every change, and it remembers which named graph it is: relaunch the app, or reopen the project from another machine on a NAS share, and you land exactly where you left off, name in the selector and all. Named saves are still explicit (File ▾ → Save, Ctrl+S); a • next to the graph name means the canvas has changes not yet saved to it, and opening another graph over unsaved work asks first instead of silently replacing it, saying how many nodes are not saved under which name. Undo/redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z) covers structure and parameters — never generation results, which are the ledger's job, so undoing a parameter edit keeps your past results. A new graph is named when you create it. File ▾ → New graph and the home's New graph both ask for a name (unique in the project) and save the fresh canvas under it at once, so your work never lives on an unnamed canvas by accident. Importing a graph file does the same, with the file's name suggested. Earlier versions. Every graph keeps its last five saves: each Ctrl+S shelves the version it overwrites. The autosave is covered too: when another graph replaces a canvas you had not saved under a name (an open, a new graph, an import), the replaced canvas is shelved, the last five of them. File ▾ → Restore an earlier version… lists them all, newest first, with the graph, the number of nodes and the time; pick one and it lands on the canvas under its name, marked unsaved until you Ctrl+S. A restore is one undo step: Ctrl+Z brings back the canvas you restored over, exactly as it was, and Ctrl+Shift+Z applies the restore again. Restoring is itself a replacement, so the canvas you restore over is shelved the same way. The shelves live in the project folder (graphs/.history/) and travel with it. Delete a node by mistake, Ctrl+Z brings it back with its results intact

A project is a first-class container: it owns its outputs, its saved graphs, and its ledger. Everything you make lives inside the active project on disk. Switch projects from the toolbar's project selector; the whole workspace swaps. Started building in the wrong project? File ▾ → Save project as… takes the current canvas into a brand-new project of its own — name it, pick its folder, and everything moves with it: every image and clip the canvas references moves into the new project's outputs/ (same subfolders). A file that another graph in the old project also uses stays there as a copy, so nothing else breaks; the ledger rows of the carried nodes move too, so 🕘 history and spend show up in the new project, and the files those past takes reference come along; if the canvas was a saved graph, its file moves with it and keeps its name; the graph is rewritten to the new locations and stays warm: unchanged nodes replay for free on the next Run instead of paying again, and a real edit still runs again, as it should. The old project is left with a fresh canvas. History that belongs to another saved graph stays in the old project. The log line under the action says how many files and rows moved and how many stayed as shared copies. Wait for a running generation to finish first — the action refuses while something is generating. To find any result on disk, right-click its preview → Reveal in Explorer. Create a project (File ▾ → New project…) and choose where it lives: anywhere, including a NAS share. NAS-rooted projects store their data in the folder you chose. A second computer can Open project… on the same folder and work in it too: that's how a studio shares live work. The default project keeps its files where they always were, so nothing you already made ever moves. The project list stays short. The project switcher in the top bar lists the ten projects you opened most recently, newest first, with the one you are in always among them. Hover a row and a ✕ appears: it takes that project off the list and nothing else changes, its folder, files and settings all stay. N more… at the bottom shows every other project, the removed ones greyed with a ↺ to put them back; picking any project there opens it, which puts it back on the list too. The home screen's recent graphs show every project as before, so a graph you worked on last month is still one click away even when its project left the list. File ▾ → Forget “project”… goes one step further for a project rooted at its own folder: Brut forgets it on this computer (its budget and naming settings with it) while the folder and every file stay on disk; Open project… on that folder brings it back. File holds the actions; the two switchers beside it only switch, project and graph Projects can be exported whole (outputs + graphs + ledger) to an empty folder — the copy is itself openable — or packed into a single .brutpack file.

Every generation (finished, failed or cancelled) is recorded in the project's ledger with its node, model, prompt, files and cost. Text and planning calls are recorded and priced too (Text → Text, Refine, the Multi-Shot planner, the Director and the cinema crew). Marcel's own calls are counted separately. No spend is invisible. The ledger powers three things: Per-node history & re-pin. Click the 🕘 on any generation node to see everything it ever produced on this graph, and pin a past result as the active output. See Never pay twice. Spend. The toolbar readout aggregates the ledger into a running total, broken down by provider — and clicking it opens the full ledger: totals for generations and for Marcel's own calls and every row newest-first with its model, status, and estimated cost. Budgets. File ▾ → Project budget… sets a spend ceiling for the project. The readout shows $spent / $budget and tints as you approach it (amber past 80%, red past 100%), and every paid confirmation dialog adds a budget line near the cap. Budgets are soft by default — they inform, you still hold the OK. Tick hard cap and paid confirmations refuse instead until you raise or clear the budget. Comparisons use the ledger's estimates; leave the amount empty to remove the budget. Click the spend readout: the ledger panel, per provider and per node, with the budget cap on top If Brut closes while a video is still rendering at the provider, it picks the job back up on the next launch and records it once, at the right price. Paid work is never lost.

<project>/ outputs/ your images and clips graphs/ your saved graphs (.history/ holds their last five versions) ledger/ history and spend project.json lets another computer open the project Keys are never here — they live in your OS keychain.

Every file Brut writes into outputs/ is named so the folder reads on its own, without opening anything: <project>_<graph>_<node>_<provider>_<model>_<date>_<job>.<ext> tournesol_facade-study_t2i-12_openai_GI25F_260923_a3f91c2e.png tournesol_facade-study_film-3-c02_kling_K30_260923_0c77e4b1.mp4 tournesol_facade-study_sb-2-kf-s3_gemini_NB2_260923_5d10aa07.png project and graph are the names you gave them, shortened to a slug (untitled while the canvas is not saved as a graph). node is the node's id with its kind abbreviated (t2i Text → Image, i2i Image → Image, i2v Image → Video, ms Multi-Shot, up Upscale Image, sb Storyboard, film Film Shots, dir Director …) and, for the nodes that make several files, which one: ms-4-s07 is Multi-Shot 4's shot 7, film-3-c02 is Film Shots 3's clip 2, sb-2-kf-s3 the keyframe of card s3 on Storyboard 2 (-end for a generated end frame), dir-1-proof a proof sheet. provider is who made it: the provider that actually served the call (a job run through OpenRouter says openrouter), or the free tool on your machine for its own results (conform, layers, sketch, sequence, and tvai for Topaz Video AI on your machine). model is the model's short code, in capitals so it stands out, for model tracking at a glance. A job run through OpenRouter still names the model you picked; the provider segment says who served it. Free tools have no model, so the segment is simply absent. Code Model Code Model NBP Nano Banana Pro K40 K30 K30O K30T Kling 4.0 · 3.0 · 3.0 Omni · 3.0 Turbo NB21 NB2 Nano Banana 2.1 · Nano Banana 2 K26 K25T KO1 Kling 2.6 · 2.5 Turbo · o1 NB2L Nano Banana 2 Lite K21 K21M K20M K16 K15 K10 the older Kling tiers (files made before Kling's API stopped serving them) NB Nano Banana (original) IG45 IG45P IG45BG IG4T Ideogram 4.5 · Precise Edit · Replace Background · 4.0 Transparent GI2 GPT Image 2 OMNI Gemini Omni Flash GI25F GPT Image 2.5 Flare SD25 SD20 Seedance 2.5 · 2.0 GI25SB GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst SD20F SD20M Seedance 2.0 Fast · Mini GI26F GI26SB GPT Image 2.6 Flare · Sunburst SR5P SR5F SR5L Seedream 5.0 Pro · Flash · Lite MGC MGP2 Magnific Creative · Precision V2 TS2 THF2 TCGI TLR2 Gigapixel Standard 2 · High Fidelity 2 · Art & CGI · Low Resolution 2 TVP4 TVR TVG Topaz video Proteus 4 · Rhea · Gaia CG (cloud and local alike) TRD TSMX TRC3 Topaz Redefine · Standard MAX · Recover 3 FX3 FX3K FXO FLUX 3 Image · Klein · FLUX Outpaint TW35 TW3 Topaz Wonder 3.5 · Wonder 3 date is the day it was written, yymmdd. job is the first eight characters of the ledger's job id: the traceability key. It is what makes every name unique (two graphs called the same thing collide on nothing), and it is how a file finds its row: right-click any picture → Find in ledger shows the run that made it — model, node, graph, prompt, parameters, cost, date — and opens the node's 🕘 history on that row when the node is on the canvas and the take was made on this graph (a node with the same id on another graph is another node: the button says which graph made the take). It works for files with the older random names too, as long as a ledger row lists them. Files you bring in (outputs/inputs/) keep your own filename: tournesol_facade-study_facade-photo_in_260923_ab12cd34.jpg (paste for a clipboard image; the same picture dropped twice on the same day is kept once). Exports keep their readable stems in outputs/exports/. Files made before this convention keep their old names for good: renaming them would break the graphs that use them. Path length. A full name is 55 to 75 characters. Windows caps a whole path at 260 characters unless long paths are enabled, so a project rooted very deep on a server has less room for the name than for the folders. Brut never fails on that: when the full path would not fit, the name drops the project and graph segments, then the node, and keeps the traceable tail (date_job), which is shorter than the old random names ever were. A shallow project root on the server stays the comfortable choice. Your own pattern. File ▾ → Output file names… sets a per-project pattern from the tokens {project} {graph} {node} {provider} {model} {model_id} {date} {time} {job} ({model} is the short code above, {model_id} the full model id; {job} is required; the default is {project}_{graph}_{node}_{provider}_{model}_{date}_{job}). The dialog shows what a file would be called; an invalid pattern is refused with the reason. It is set on each computer: on a shared NAS project each machine names its own files.

The cache is a feature with a euro sign on it. Every node remembers exactly what it was given; unchanged inputs mean the cached output is reused and nothing is billed. This is what makes iterating on a graph affordable.

When a node runs, Brut checks whether anything that affects the result changed since its last successful run: the prompt, the model, the parameters, the input images, the mask. If nothing did and the node still holds that output, the node is skipped: status cached, cost $0. Change any input and that node, and only that node, re-pays. A revision round that touches three shots costs you three shots, not the whole graph. Change one prompt in a four-node graph and Run: only that node bills, the rest answer from cache Moving a graph is not a change. A project that moves (Save project as…, a .brutpack opened on another machine, a NAS share under a different drive letter) keeps its cache: a move stays free. Re-run a finished graph and everything shows cached. That's the point: your outputs are already on disk, and replaying them is free.

Everything that would change the result: the prompt text and any negative prompt, the provider and model, the parameters (aspect ratio, resolution, audio, duration…), the incoming images, and for an Adjust step, its mask or its marks (an Adjust step keeps the take you picked whatever you change on it: the change goes into its next take, made with ↻). What doesn't count: cosmetic things like node position or size. Moving a node never re-pays.

Sometimes you want a specific past result to stay, even as you tinker upstream. Click the 🕘 history button on a generation node to open its ledger history — every result that node ever produced on this graph — and 📌 pin one. A node with the same id in another graph of the project is another node: tick Every graph in this project in the panel to see those takes too, each badged with the graph that made it. A pinned node emits that exact output on every run, free, until you unpin. Pins beat both the cache and a fresh generation. Hover a row's thumbnail for a quick preview; click it for the lightbox, where ←/→ walks the node's whole history at screen size. Pin any past result from the node's history; it stays the output, free, until you unpin Multi-Shot tiles pin individually, so you can lock the three keepers from a contact sheet and keep re-rolling the rest.
Re-roll — a fresh take on purpose

The cache answers ▶ for free, which is right until you want another take of the same prompt. Generation nodes (Text → Image, Image → Image, Compose, Adjust, Image → Video) carry a ↻ re-roll button in their title bar: it forces one fresh generation with the inputs unchanged (this node bills again; everything upstream still replays from cache). The take it replaces is not lost: it stays in the node's 🕘 history, pinnable like any past result. A pinned node can't be re-rolled (the pin would win): unpin first, the button says so.

Some nodes never touch a provider at all and run entirely on your machine: Conform with its crop and pad methods (its extend method paints the missing part with a paid model), Sequence (video assembly), Layers, Compare, Preview, and the Sketchpad's drawing and flattening. They cost nothing and aren't metered.

The toolbar shows a running spend estimate; hover it for a per-provider breakdown. Every generation, finished, failed or cancelled, is recorded in the project's ledger, with full context (node, model, cost) — so you can always answer "what did this cost, and who received the money?"
Reuse is first-class in Brut. A pipeline you've perfected shouldn't be rebuilt by hand on the next job — collapse it, save it, drop it in anywhere.

Select two or more nodes and press Ctrl+G (or Group in the floating selection bar, or the rail's Organize section) to wrap them in a labeled frame. A group is purely visual — it moves as a unit and keeps things tidy. ✕ on the frame ungroups. Select a group to style its identity: six frame colors (dashed line + background wash) and a label size up to genuinely gigantic — big enough to read the group's name zoomed all the way out. Groups also adopt: drop a node inside a group's area (or add one there from the Tab menu) and it joins the group automatically — drag it out and it leaves. No re-grouping ceremony. Ctrl+G frames a selection; rename it, color it, and a node dropped inside joins the group

A composite is a subgraph collapsed into a single node (select nodes → 📦 Collapse to composite). Cut wires become labeled ports, and a result that is wired to nothing, or only to a Preview, Compare or History inside, becomes an output port too, so the closed card shows it and you can wire it on; the nodes inside keep their past results, pins and history. Open / Close — ⤢ opens a composite into a live frame you can edit inside, then ⇱ packs it back up, exactly where it was, with the same ports (new outside wires you made while it was open become new ports). Only nodes that are members of the frame close into it — a node you add or drag inside joins automatically; a node that merely overlaps the frame's area stays out. Run — ▶ on a composite runs its whole inside plus everything upstream. Preview — a closed composite shows the images its output ports currently carry, one thumbnail per result captioned with the port name, read live from the nodes inside: it is there before any run, survives Open / Close, and updates as inner nodes finish. 🔍 pages through them like any node result; right-click reveals the file. Explode — 💥 permanently dissolves it back into loose nodes. Knobs — a closed card can show a few of its inner fields on its own face: a prompt variant as a select, a brief as a text box, a shot count, or the model of a generation stage (it lists the models your keys can reach). ⚙ Add knob on the card exposes one field: pick the field, name the knob, choose the control; for a menu, write one choice per line as name | text. Or, with Drive every node of the same kind ticked, the same field on every inner node of that kind at once (one Model knob over four picture stages, one text knob over three prompts); × on a knob removes it. A knob writes straight into the node inside, so it costs exactly what typing on that node would: an edit is one undo step, a changed prompt or model re-renders that stage only, everything else keeps its result. A select whose inner text was edited by hand shows (custom) rather than pretending. A knob can drive several stages at once (the Character Lab's Model and Size knobs set all three picture stages); when the stages inside were changed by hand and differ, the knob says so and the next pick realigns them. A copied card (Ctrl+D, or Ctrl+C then Ctrl+V) is as independent as a fresh drop: its knobs set its own stages, never the card it was copied from. Opening a graph saved by an earlier version may put a line about such a card in the Activity panel: pick its model again on the card and every stage follows. Knobs survive Open / Close and travel with the composite into the library; Marcel sets them by name. The ports survive a close the same way: opening a card and closing it again brings back exactly the inlets and outlets it had, plus a port for any wire you connected from outside while it was open; nothing else is added. A card's inlets feed the nodes inside it on the face as well as on a run: the Stills → Film card generates its keyframes and its proof sheet while closed, from the stills wired into its inlet. Knob controls. A select (a menu of whole values, a prompt variant per entry), a text box, a number, a model menu (the models your keys can reach) and a tick list (several toggle chips plus a free line that takes anything you type, commas between items, like the Character Lab's Accessories). On the shipped cards, a text knob left empty leaves that choice to the model. A clip stage's Duration, Resolution, Ratio and Audio knobs follow the video model picked on the card, and grey out in place when that model has no such setting (an Omni clip has no audio switch, Seedance 2.5 follows its start frame); an image stage's Size and Quality knobs do the same (Quality lights up on the OpenAI models, which take one). A Prompt style knob greys the refiners written for another video model than the one picked; a pick that no longer fits stays, with a warning line, never swapped behind your back. Some select knobs on the shipped cards draw (a small 🎲 beside them): they start on a random pick each time the card is dropped, 🎲 Draw again on the card draws them all again while the other knobs stay as you set them, and the 🎲 beside one knob draws that knob alone. Pick any value yourself to keep it; a copy of a card (Ctrl+D) keeps its picks. Dropped from the library — a card dropped from the library remembers where it came from. Its meta line shows the version it was dropped at, and a small chip says when the library holds a newer one; nothing is rewritten under you, drop the workflow again to get the new recipe. If a stage inside is set to a model this computer cannot reach, the card itself shows the ⚠ button that opens Settings on that provider (the node that needs it is hidden inside). And once the card has a result, a workflow that ships with a suggested follow-up offers it as a chip under the picture: one click drops the next workflow beside the card, wired to its result. Collapse a selection into one card with labeled ports; Open it in place to edit, Close packs it back Composites are how any tuned chain — say, your Director with its house style plus its Storyboard — becomes one droppable node.

The library opens as a gallery: the book icon on the left rail, or File ▾ → Browse library…. Every workflow is a card with its picture. From Brut holds the workflows that ship with the app, by category then name; Yours holds the composites and templates you saved, newest first. Every shipped workflow, with its knobs, its pinned models and what it takes in, is listed on the Workflows page. Each shelf shows two rows at a time and turns pages with the arrows at its lower right, like the home screen's recent graphs. Presets sit below, grouped by what they are. The picture is the result the item made when it was saved. When the item also kept its input, hover the cover: it shows the before first, then the after. An item with no picture yet draws the glyphs of the nodes it contains. The chips say what it is (composite or template), what a run costs on your keys at list prices ($? when a stage has no model picked or no measured price, never a guess), how many knobs its card exposes, and which key it still needs on this computer. Add to canvas drops a composite where you were looking as one card, or a template as a group of live nodes named after it. Try with sample, on workflows that ship with one, copies the sample image into your project, drops the workflow already wired to it and shows the shipped result on the card until you run it. Nothing runs until you press Run. The From Brut shelf ends on a More to come tile: the bank grows with the releases. The chips at the top filter by category (the label you give an item when you save it: Characters, Cinema, Architecture…) and by kind; the search box matches names, descriptions and categories. Esc closes. The same cards sit on the home screen's Workflows row. Composites, whole-graph templates and presets can be saved to a global library — deliberately cross-project, so the same shelf appears on every project. Save a composite — 💾 Save to library on the composite node. Same name = a new version (everything is versioned; any past version is retrievable). The save dialog asks for a category from a pick list (Architecture, Characters, Cinema, Text, plus any you already used; the library's filter chips are made of them), or a new one typed beside it, and takes the result the card shows at that moment as the item's cover; with no result yet, the item gets a glyph until a later save brings one. If an image is wired into the card when you save, it is kept as the before picture, and the gallery shows the pair. Save a graph as a template — File ▾ → Save graph as template…. Same here: a category, and the canvas's last result as the cover. The graph's first Image In file becomes the before picture. Save a preset — 💾 on the node that owns the settings: the Prompt node and Multi-Shot notes save prompt presets (reusable brief texts), the Upscale Image node saves upscaling presets (model + dials). Browse — the gallery above, or find saved composites right in the Tab add-node menu under Library. Each drop is an independent copy: changing one never changes another. Presets are listed under Yours, grouped by what they are: Prompts (texts you load on a Prompt node or in the Multi-Shot notes) and Upscale settings (model and dials you load on the Upscale Image node), with chips to show one kind at a time. They are applied from their node, and deleted in the gallery. Tab, Library, Character Lab: a saved composite drops in with fresh ids, ready to wire Library items carry an optional category (a shelf label you pick on save) and hold only the recipe (prompts, models and wiring). No images, no past results, no keys are ever written into a library item, so they're safe to share. Some items ship with Brut: the whole bank on the Workflows page, such as the Stills → Film card (the cinema pipeline as one composite: the Director's dials, the film aspect and the three models as knobs; open it to judge the proof sheet and the keyframes) and the Character Lab composite: design a character from its rollouts (sex, age, ethnicity, features, hair color, haircut, facial hair, style, clothes from casual to bohemian chic or at home, colors, a tick list of accessories), or wire a character image and clothing references in, and it produces one 16:9 character sheet: a bust, then the full body from the front, the left side, the back and the right side, five panels separated by thin lines on a light grey background under soft studio light. That one picture is the person's reference wherever they appear next. The ethnicity, the features (the face and the build), the hair, the haircut and the palette start on a random pick on every drop, so two cards with the same other choices give two different people; 🎲 Draw again gives another one on the same card. The sheet stage comes preset to GPT Image 2.5 Flare at 4K, xhigh quality: it keeps a detail worn on one side (a watch, an earring) on that side in every view, which GPT Image 2 and the Nano Banana models tend to mirror. The Model knob changes it, Size and Quality follow the model picked. For Seedance, register the sheet with a Seedance assets node, or pick a Seedream 5.0 model with nothing wired into character: a sheet made from text that way is accepted as it is (the measured rule). A Character Lab card dropped before the sheet version keeps its design, expression grid and turnaround, and shows that a newer version is in the library. Built-ins can't be deleted; saving your own item under the same name shadows the shipped one.
A composite is a node — a reusable building block you drop into an existing graph. A template is a whole graph — a starting point for a job, dropped onto your canvas as a group of live nodes.

Your references, in one place, beside the canvas: film frames, photographs, the renders you were proud of, the people and places a project keeps coming back to. Elements reads folders on your disk as they are and shows them as a panel; tiles drag straight onto the canvas. Open it from the rail (the pictures icon, above Library). It slides in on the right, left of Marcel, as wide as you drag it; the slider at the bottom right (between the two zoom glyphs) sets the size of the tiles, the bar between the two sections of the list drags up or down to give one of them more room, and the line between the list and the tiles drags sideways to widen the list (double-click resets either). The list keeps its width whatever a folder is called; long names are cut short.
Two levels: your elements, your folders

The list on the left has two sections. Elements, on top, is what the canvas can name: Cast (a person or character: their character sheet, their face, a turnaround), Sets (places), Props (objects or products that must stay themselves), Styles (looks), and Saved (pictures you saved from the canvas with no type yet). Each category shows blocks, one card per element with its first picture, its name and how many pictures it holds. Click a block to select it (its name, type and descriptor are editable in the drawer), click it again to open it and see its pictures. Drag a block onto the canvas and the whole element lands as one Image In. Folders, below, is the file explorer: every folder you added to the vault, with the folders inside it as collections and shelves, unfolded with the chevrons like any file explorer (a click on a name opens it and shows it; the chevron only folds or unfolds, and what you unfolded stays that way while you browse the elements above). Your folders are read as they are: Movies/, Office/, Mood/, whatever you keep. A film works best as one folder per film, named <Title> (<Year>) - <Director>, with an info.txt beside the frames holding a few key: value lines (title, year, director, dop, kind, moods, a look: paragraph): the panel reads the folder name and the file, so the credits, the moods and the look you typed once filter the vault forever.
Folders: add, remove, where Brut saves

The 📁 button (and Add a folder… on a right-click in the list) adds a folder of references to the vault: your references share, a project's folder, any number of them. The files stay where they are, nothing is moved, and each folder keeps its own small index inside it, so a shared folder brings its index along. Take out of Elements on a folder's right-click removes it from the list; its files and its index stay on disk. What Brut adds goes into one of these folders, under Brut/: a picture you save from the canvas lands in Brut/Saved/, a character in Brut/Cast/, a place in Brut/Sets/, an object in Brut/Props/, a look in Brut/Styles/. That folder is marked with a dot in the list and named in the panel's head; Keep Brut's elements here on a right-click moves the choice to another folder. A studio that points this at its share shares its elements; a solo seat keeps them beside its library. The same picture saved twice is one element, whatever it was called. ⟳ reads the folders again: new and changed pictures come in, deleted ones leave. Dropping files into a folder from Explorer is the normal way to fill it; the first read of a thousand frames takes a few seconds (every picture gets its palette), later reads are instant. Each picture gets a palette at reading time, free and local: the hue chips in the filter bar find "the blue frames", "the pink ones", by the nearest swatch. The filter bar (search, the type chips, Seedance-approved, a hue) narrows whatever the list shows; ✕ clear drops the chips and keeps your place in the list.

A fresh vault can start with a few elements made of pictures Brut ships: some sets and a character. Add Brut's starter elements… on the list's right-click (or the button on the empty-vault card) asks first, then copies them into the folder Brut saves into and opens the Sets category; adding them twice adds nothing twice. Never film frames, never anyone's client work.
Importing: from the web, from a video

Two more ways to fill a folder without Explorer. Both run in the background: a line under the filter bar shows the progress with a Cancel (what is already written stays), and the Activity panel gets one line when it ends. Import from the web… (the ⇩ button in the panel's head, or the list's right-click) takes web addresses, one per line: A film-grab.com gallery becomes one film folder named <Title> (<Year>) - <Director> with every frame in gallery order and an info.txt holding the credits the page states (director, cinematographer, production and costume design, year, aspect ratio, country, genre), plus empty look:, moods: and references_for: lines for you. The frames land under Movies/ unless you name another collection. A film-grab director, cinematographer, year or tag page brings every film it lists, across its pages; the films already in the vault are skipped. Any picture address is downloaded into a named set (Web/<the name you give>/), each picture keeping its address as its source. Any other page is read for the pictures it shows: they land as a set named after the page (or after the name you give, for one page alone), icons and thumbnails left out. Brut reads only the pages you paste, never the pages they link to. A page that builds itself in the browser or sits behind a sign-in shows no pictures to Brut: it is listed as a failure at the end, with the reason, and the import goes on with the next address. A film already in the vault is left alone; tick rewrite the credits the page states to refresh the credit lines of its info.txt from the page while every line you typed yourself (the look, the moods, anything else) stays as it is. Frames to Elements… on a clip's right-click, or Frames from a video file… on the list's right-click for a video anywhere on your disk, takes stills out of a video into a set of the vault: after every cut (one frame per shot; the threshold says how different two frames must be, 0.35 to start, higher keeps only the sharper cuts), every N seconds, or at the times you name. A clip of a project or of the vault plays in the dialog: scrub, + Add this time, as many times as you want. The dialog says how many frames the run would take; a run over the cap (300 to start) stops before writing anything and says what to change. The frames are JPEGs named after the set, each one's source being the video and its time; the folder's info.txt names the video. The video stays where it is, never copied in. Film frames are copyrighted material for private study: they stay on your disk and never enter Brut.

Any picture is a reference you can drag. A typed element is a block the canvas can name. Select one or several pictures (Ctrl-click adds, Shift-click ranges), click Make an element…, give it a type, a name and one line about it in your words ("a woman of 35, short grey hair, navy coat"). The pictures keep their own names; the element's name is on the block and on each picture's second line. The drawer edits all of it later; Untype returns the pictures to plain references. An element lives in one folder of the vault: pictures from two folders are saved to Elements first, then made into one element. Typing is never required. It is what makes an element addressable: an Image In titled after it, and that one line riding into every generation the element's pictures feed (below). Describe… in the drawer writes the line for you: a vision call on your own text-model key (Gemini 3.8 Flash by default, a fraction of a cent, in the ledger) reads up to six of the element's pictures and proposes one line and a few tags (the category, the dominant colors, the era, moods as mood:word). You edit, then Keep: the line goes on the element, the tags on its pictures as proposed tags (your own tags stay yours), and the panel's search finds them. Cancel writes nothing. Promote to style… in the same drawer turns an element into a named look in your style library, the one Marcel cites and writes prompt language for: a name, a shelf (archviz, photography, cinema, trend), the look in a sentence or two and its prompt language, both prefilled from the element's line, references if you have them. Free, local; the element stays in the vault, the style joins the looks Marcel knows.

Drag a tile, a selection or a block onto the canvas. An element lands as one Image In holding all its pictures, titled after it and wearing its type; a single picture lands as an Image In titled after it; several loose pictures land together in one plain Image In. Onto an existing Image In, the pictures append. A look is the exception: it lands as an Image → Image node (below). Add to canvas in the drawer does the same at the center of the view. Elements… on an Image In, + Elements on a Reference Board, and Pick from Elements… on a Seedance assets node open the same picker: tick, Use. On the board the picks arrive as an Image In wired in. Right-click any picture on the canvas → Save to Elements…: pick a shelf (or a type, which makes an element on the spot), a name, a line, and a copy goes into the vault.

A look is a Style element that carries what it does to a picture: a family (time of day, weather, season, atmosphere, finish), the words it sends and the model it was made on. Its picture is a menu picture, the look shown on one sample scene so the list reads at a glance; it is never sent with a request. Brut's looks. Thirty-four of them: times of day from dawn to night, weathers from clear to light snow, seasons from early spring to deep winter, atmospheres (calm, dramatic clouds, storm light, a warm evening…) and finishes (filmic, editorial, matte, high key, moody…). Add Brut's looks… on the list's right-click, on the card an empty vault shows, or on the card in Styles while no look is there yet, asks first, then copies them into Brut/Styles/ of the folder Brut saves into. Adding them again adds nothing twice and never undoes an edit of yours. In Styles the looks sit under their family, each card with its picture and its family; your plain styles follow. Drop one on a picture. Drag a look onto any picture on the canvas: an Image In's picture, a node's result, a Reference Board tile, a Shot Board tile. Brut adds an Image → Image node wired from the plug that picture comes from, with a Prompt holding the look's words, on the look's model when your keys reach it, else on the first image model they reach (the Activity line says which). A model that can keep the picture's size gets Same as the picture. Nothing runs: ▶ on the node renders it, and ▶ Run prices it first like any node that has not run. A picture with no plug of its own (a tile of a Multi-Shot sheet, one of an Image In's several pictures, a hidden Reference Board tile, the frame of a muted Storyboard card) first gets an Image In of its own. The new nodes land beside the picture, clear of every node already there and with room left for the result each one will show once it has run, even when you drop several looks in a row. On a Preview or a Compare, the node is wired from the node that picture comes from, so a new take flows on. Dropped on empty canvas, the look lands as the node alone, waiting for a picture. A second look dropped on the first look's node chains a second node from it, even before the first has run (its face shows only the picture it takes in; the second waits for the first's result). A clip, or a video node, takes no look: take a frame of the clip first. Edit a look. Its drawer shows the family, the words (edit them, leave the field: saved) and the model it runs on, with the fallback named when that model is out of reach. A look is a starting point: change the words to make it yours. Your own looks. Right-click a picture you generated → Save to Elements… → tick Save as a look and pick a family: the look keeps the prompt and the model of the run that made that picture, read from the ledger, and the picture becomes its menu picture. A picture Brut did not make (an import, a paste) has no run to keep; the dialog says so and saves nothing. Cost and limits. Adding looks and dropping them is free; the render costs what the model costs, shown before anything runs (Brut's looks were made on Nano Banana 2.1, about three cents a picture at 1K). The model redraws the whole frame, so fine details can move; when the rest must stay exactly as it was, Reconcile with input lays the original back where nothing was asked to change.

A generation node fed by an element's Image In (Image → Image, Adjust, Compose, Image → Video) adds one sentence to the prompt it sends, naming the pictures that element occupies among the pictures sent and its line: Images 2 to 3 show Maria (cast): a woman of 35, short grey hair. The model then knows what each reference is for, which is the whole point of a typed element. The face shows a ✦ line naming the elements the prompt names; untick it to send the pictures without a word (the node alone, nothing else changes). A line edited in the panel reaches every Image In made from that element, and the next run carries it: that is a new prompt, so the node renders again. Numbering follows the pictures as the node sends them: on Image → Image the wired pictures in order; on Adjust the picture, then the references; on Compose the scene first, then the references; on Image → Video the start frame, the end frame, then the references. An element whose line is empty is still named with its type. How many references a model reads was measured on one scene (2026-10-19: fourteen distinct objects, each a reference, one prompt asking for all of them on a table; the pictures looked at by hand): Seedream 5.0 Pro and Flash kept all 10 of their 10, FLUX 3 all 10 of 10, Nano Banana 2.1 all 14 of 14 (smaller, reordered), Ideogram 4.5 all 5 of 5, GPT Image 2.5 Flare 12 of 14 (the vase and the clock gone, every object drawn smaller). Up to each model's cap, a reference is not lost for being the ninth. Image → Image and Compose warn on the face when more pictures are wired than the model takes per request.
Describe the library, then search by meaning

The search box matches words: every word you type must appear in a title, a line, a tag, a credit, a folder name, or a picture's description (below). The ≈ by meaning chip beside it ranks instead by what the pictures show: "a snowy night drive" finds the frame of a car's headlights on a snowy forest road at night, whatever the file is called. For that, each picture is described once. The line under the panel's count offers Describe the library… with the number of pictures and the price before anything is spent: Gemini 3.8 Flash looks at a small copy of each picture on your Gemini key and writes what it shows (a few sentences, then subjects, setting, time of day, light, weather, colors, mood, shot). About $0.0009 a picture, so a library of a thousand pictures costs under a dollar and takes a few minutes in the background, with a progress line and Cancel; every call is in the ledger. The description is stored in the folder's index, travels with the folder, and is written again only if the file itself changes. It shows in the drawer under What it shows, its tags (time of day, weather, shot, moods) join the panel's tags in their own list, and the word search reads it too. After that first run, pictures you add are described as they arrive: drop frames into one of your folders, import a page, save a render to Elements, and a few seconds later they are described. Pictures added while Brut was closed are described when it starts. More than a thousand new pictures at once wait for a click instead. The switch Describe new pictures as they arrive, at the end of the count line, turns this off and on again. A meaning search then compares your words with the stored descriptions. A query you have not asked before is first rewritten into the kind of description the library stores and kept for good, a few seconds and a fraction of a cent once; asked again, it answers at once and for free. Every picture whose description stands out from the rest comes back, best first, with no fixed number. Without a Gemini key the line says so; with only an OpenAI key, descriptions made earlier (they travel with the folder) can still be searched.

Marcel reads the vault: its folders with their counts, the typed elements by name with their lines, the tags in use. Ask him what you have ("a rainy neon street?", "every cast element", "something in that blue") and he searches it the way the panel does, by words, type, tag, hue, Seedance approval or meaning, and answers with what he found, each picture's description included. Ask him to use a picture or an element and he puts it on the canvas exactly as a drag would: one Image In per element, titled after it, its line riding into the generations it feeds. He never invents a path; what he places comes from his search. The other way works too: point him at a render on the canvas ("make a style element of this one and describe it") and he saves it into the vault's Brut folder as a typed element with a name and a line written from what the picture shows, or turns vault pictures he found into an element, or rewrites an element's line. The panel and the element's Image Ins follow at once. The vault also hosts Marcel's notebook, a Notebook folder inside your primary Elements folder: your own taste as short markdown notes (a look, a subject, a client, something to avoid, a habit), written only when you agree to keep one, read back by Marcel before he cites them, editable in any text editor, with a README.md index Obsidian reads as a vault. The 🧠 Memory window in Marcel's panel says where the folder is and what it holds. Nothing in the notebook or the vault leaves your machine on its own: a search runs locally, and only what Marcel then says about it travels to your text model, like any chat message.

Pictures Seedance accepts the people in (the ones registered in your BytePlus asset library through a Seedance assets node, or by hand in the console) carry a ✓ in the vault and a Seedance-approved filter; the pictures you registered are kept in Brut/Cast/, and every asset of your BytePlus account is brought in the first time you pick from a Seedance assets node. An approved element keeps its approval wherever it goes: dropped on the canvas, its Image In says so, and a Seedance pick downstream accepts it in every role. The approval follows the picture's content, so a copy under another name is the same asset.
A folder shared by several machines

A folder on a studio share can be added to Elements on several machines. They all read the same index inside it, so what one machine does there (descriptions, tags, notes, elements and their lines) the others see, and a library described once is never described or paid for again on another machine. Each folder has one describer: the machine whose Gemini key pays for its descriptions. The first machine to describe a folder becomes it. The other machines leave that folder's new pictures to it; their count line says so ("12 new pictures in References wait for OFFICE-PC (seen 3 days ago)") with a Describe them here button, priced, for when that machine is away. Right-click a folder to see who describes it, and Describe this folder from this machine to take it over: its new pictures are then described on this machine's key. Describe new pictures as they arrive on each machine covers the folders that machine describes. Never twice at once. While a machine describes, Brut leaves a small file in the folder naming it, so another machine that clicks at the same moment waits; the file goes when the work ends, and one left by a machine that went away is ignored after a few minutes. A moment without the network loses nothing. A folder Brut cannot read during a pass keeps its pictures and everything they carry; a picture moved or renamed keeps its description, tags, notes and element. A shared graph keeps its elements. An Image In made from an element stays tied to that element on every machine, even when the machines list their folders in another order. The folder Brut saves into (the dot) is each machine's choice. Point it at the share and that machine's saved elements and Marcel's notebook go there too, shared with everyone who uses it; keep it on the machine's own disk to keep them personal.

A picture of your own folders is hidden from the vault with Hide, never touched on disk. The red Delete file… deletes the selected pictures from disk, after a confirm, wherever they sit (an imported page brings every picture it shows; the ones you do not want go this way). A picture Brut copied in (under Brut/) has only the red button.

Everything. The folders, their indexes (one small database file inside each), the palettes, the descriptions. The one thing Elements fetches from the web is what you paste into Import from the web…, read straight from those sites by your machine, one page deep. Describing the library, Describe… and the meaning search call Gemini (or OpenAI) on your own key, after your click, as described above; nothing reaches us.

Every studio has that colleague who's seen everything — knows which film your lighting reference is from, which tool does the job cheapest, and what you tried last Tuesday. In Brut, that colleague is Marcel (named after Marcel Breuer — Bauhaus, brutalism, the Brut lineage).
