His panel is open when the app starts, showing the conversation view (the Raw events toggle adds every technical event); the Marcel button on the left rail (the pulse icon) hides and shows it. The panel is two things at once:

A chronological diary of everything that happens in the project — runs, results, planner reasoning, errors, and your conversations. It's saved with the project (a file inside the project folder), so it survives restarts and travels with a NAS share or a folder export. On a shared project, everyone writes to the same diary, and entries are tagged with who was signed in. A run finishes and Marcel remarks on it in the timeline; the rail badge counts what you haven't read The Raw events / Chat only toggle switches between every technical event and just the conversation. When the panel is closed, anything Marcel says on his own — a remark, a suggestion, a failure diagnosis — badges the Marcel button on the rail, so ambient commentary never lands invisibly. A long diary stays comfortable: the panel opens at the newest message and follows the conversation as it streams; scroll up to read history and it stops following (a ⤓ Latest button brings you back). Only the newest stretch renders by default — ⋯ Show earlier unfolds the rest in place. And the 🔎 search at the top of the panel searches the whole diary — every chat, plan, and failure back to the project's first day, not just what's on screen — with dated results.

Type at the bottom of the panel and Marcel answers — streamed live, in whatever language you write. Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line, and the box grows with your message. The whole panel resizes too — drag its left edge to make Marcel as wide as you like (double-click the edge to reset). He knows Brut inside out: every model in the catalog with its real price, every node and how its ports wire, and the whole of this documentation. Ask him things like: "Which model should I use for a photoreal archviz still, and what does it cost?" "What's the cheapest way to get a 5-second clip?" "How do I route one shot from a Multi-Shot into Image → Video?" He recommends only from the catalog — if a price isn't known, he says so instead of guessing, so "which model for this job?" gets a grounded answer, not a vibe.

Marcel is a seasoned artistic director, not just a manual. Ask him for direction and he answers with concrete, citable references — named photographers, films, DPs, architects, eras — never "make it more cinematic." He carries a style library: a curated set of named looks across photography (Stoller, Shulman, Binet…), archviz conventions (the MIR mood, the clay model, the dusk money shot…), cinema (Deakins nights, Villeneuve scale, Kubrick symmetry…) and current trends — each with a description, ready-to-use prompt language, and which models render it well. Ask "give me three directions for this facade" and he'll cite them by name, with the prompt fragments to try. It's yours to shape: ask Marcel to add or change a look, rewrite one, drop what you disagree with, add the studio's own. Show him your work. Four ways, all landing on the same message: Name the node. Write a node's id in your message, as its title bar shows it (storyboard-101, image_input-96, director-12), and its current stills go along: a render's result, a Reference Board's pool in board order, a Multi-Shot's curated set, every card frame of a Storyboard, a Director's proof sheet. Before you send, a line under the composer says what Marcel will also see ("👁 Marcel will also see storyboard-101 (8 card frames)"), and the message ends with a short bracketed line telling him which image is which. A named node brings at most 16 stills on its own; the line says when it cut. Right-click any picture → Send to chat. The image joins your next message and Marcel's panel opens on it. It works on every preview: outputs, imports, board tiles, the magnifier. The 📎 button lists every still on your canvas, newest first: the most recent result sits on top and the order holds still while you work. Storyboards list their generated keyframes, a Director its proof sheet. From outside Brut: From disk… at the top of the 📎 list, or paste an image into the message box, or drop a file (or a picture dragged out of a node) onto the panel. The file is imported into the project like any image you bring in; no node is needed. Ask "what would you change about the light?" — Marcel actually looks at it. A few practical notes: Attach a still with 📎, ask about the look, the answer streams in with real references Images are downscaled to ≤2048px for the conversation (provider request limits — your originals are untouched, and generation always uses full resolution). Attachments ride only the message you send them with. Later turns re-send text alone, so an image-heavy conversation doesn't re-bill the pixels on every reply. Naming the same node again sends its stills again. An image-heavy turn costs more than a text turn — the exact number lands in the ledger per call, like everything else. A message carries up to 50 stills, and at most 18 MB of them, whatever the brain (that is Brut's own cap, set under every provider's request limit). A bigger set goes over two messages; remember that each message re-sends only its own images. Marcel looks at stills; videos can't be attached (yet). Send to chat shows greyed on a clip for that reason. He only sees what rides the message: if he says he can't see something, name the node or attach it. His replies are formatted. Bold, lists, headings and quote blocks render as such in the chat, so a prompt you copy out of a reply comes out as clean text, ready to paste into a node.
Marcel acts — building and running the graph

Marcel doesn't just advise; ask him to do it and he works on your actual canvas: "Give me a 6-shot dusk study of this render." He'll place the nodes, wire them, set the prompts and parameters, and offer to run it — you watch each step land on the canvas as he narrates. His toolkit is the same as yours: add, wire, rewire, edit, delete nodes, drop in a saved library composite (yes, the whole Cinema Team) and set its knobs by name, read any node's output, search the project diary, and run nodes. He also reads the names your pictures answer to (the ones on each Image In, and the legend on every node that takes pictures), writes them as @name in the prompts he sets, and can name a picture for you when you ask. Ask for a graph and Marcel builds it, wired and tidy, the actions folded into one card; a paid run still asks you first In the chat, his actions fold into a compact "🤖 N actions on the canvas" block between his messages — expand it to see every step, or ignore it and just read the conversation. When he names a node (multi_shot-21), that id is visible in the node's own title bar — click it there to copy it. And the layout isn't his problem (or yours): whatever he builds is auto-arranged into tidy columns that follow the wiring, placed where you're working — beside the nodes it connects to, or centered on your current view when it stands alone, always nudged clear of your own nodes, which are never touched. The same layout is available for any graph via the ⌗ Tidy button on the rail — the whole graph, or just the nodes you have selected (Ctrl+Z undoes it, like everything). Three rules keep this comfortable: One Ctrl+Z undoes the whole turn. Everything Marcel does in one reply — however many nodes and wires — collapses into a single undo step. Don't like the construction? One keystroke removes it all (and undoing a delete brings a node back with its results). Paid work always asks first. Free actions (building, wiring, editing) apply immediately. But before anything would bill one of your keys, you get an itemized confirm — which nodes, which models, the catalog price per step — and nothing is generated until you click. Declining costs nothing and Marcel takes it in stride. Film Shots keeps its own per-clip confirm on top. What ran is what's ledgered. Marcel's runs work exactly like yours — unchanged steps replay free, same history, same ledger rows. He can also save a style: when a look you've been chasing together deserves a name, he'll offer to add it to the style library — only with your go-ahead, and only citing models that exist in the catalog. Saved looks are kept in your library folder beside your own workflows, so an update never removes them. He knows your Elements. Marcel sees what your Elements vault holds: its folders, your typed elements by name with their lines, the tags in use. Ask "do we have a rainy neon street somewhere?" and he searches the vault (by words, by type, by tag, by a hue, by what Seedance accepts, and by meaning when the words find nothing or you ask for "something like", on your embedding key) and answers with the pictures he found. Ask him to use one and he puts it on the canvas the way a drag does: a whole element lands as one Image In titled after it, its line riding into the generations it feeds; a few pictures land as one Image In. He never guesses a file path: what he places comes from the search. He can also make an element: show him a render on the canvas, ask for "a style element from this one" and he saves it into the vault with a type, a name and a line he writes from what the picture shows (or changes an existing element's line when you ask). The panel shows it at once. He keeps a notebook with you. When something about your taste comes up in a conversation and you agree to keep it, Marcel writes a short note into your notebook: a look you keep reaching for, a subject, a client's habits, something to avoid, a way you work. He reads the notebook back before citing it, and a note he proposed but you never ruled on is marked as such. The notebook is yours to open and edit (see Memory below).

Marcel can also speak unprompted — and how much is entirely your call. The slider at the top of the panel has four levels; each one adds exactly one behavior to the previous, so you always know what you've turned on (and what it can cost): Level What Marcel does Off Nothing. The timeline stays a passive journal; Marcel never calls a model on his own — not even the quiet taste passes. Reactive Answers when spoken to, and diagnoses failures: when a run errors, one short remark names the likely cause and the fix to try first. He knows Brut's classic traps on sight — Gemini quietly refusing a picture (usually because of an input image), an error on your first call that means billing isn't switched on, replies cut short. Narrator + run commentary (a sentence or two when a run that actually generated something finishes — free replays stay silent, and re-running an already-generated graph is exactly that) and a recap when you open a project: where things stood, what finished or failed while you were away, what's still running. If nothing happened since the last recap, he doesn't spend the call at all. Partner + unsolicited 💡 suggestions — an artistic direction, a model swap (always with real catalog prices), a next step — appearing as small cards in the timeline. Off, Reactive, Narrator, Partner: each level adds exactly one behavior The setting is per-account, so your level doesn't change a colleague's. Ambient remarks run on the cheap narrator lane, so a remark costs a fraction of a cent on Haiku or Gemini Flash. Every one of them is a ledgered call you can verify, like everything else. And when there's genuinely nothing worth saying, Marcel says nothing — silence is a designed outcome, not a failure.

Marcel keeps two plain-text memory documents, both stored on your disk and both yours to read and edit (the 🧠 Memory button in the panel): A taste profile — tied to your account and shared across every project. What you make, references you love, looks you avoid, the palette and light you keep reaching for. It's private, never synced anywhere, and hand-edits are respected on Marcel's very next reply. Project notes — a small memory for this project: what it is, decisions made, where it's heading. It travels with the project (a NAS share or a folder export), so the studio's context follows the work. The notebook — your own taste as short notes, one markdown file each, in a Notebook folder inside your Elements vault. Five kinds: a look, a subject, a client, something to avoid, a habit. Marcel writes a note only when you agree to keep it, in your words where he has them; each note says when it was written, which models it applies to and which pictures show it. The folder is plain text: edit a note in any editor, and Obsidian opens the Elements folder as a vault with the notebook's index (README.md) linking every note. The 🧠 Memory window says where the folder is and what it holds. A look that has settled becomes a style (the library Marcel cites and writes prompt language for): the Elements panel's Promote to style… does that from an element, or ask Marcel. He also proposes notes from your pictures. The quiet pass that runs when you leave a project looks at the pictures you kept and the ones you rejected on the same node (pins, ✓ and ✗ ticks), sends them to the cheap text model on your key with one question, what the kept ones share and what the rejected ones have, and proposes at most two notes per pass as 📓 cards in the timeline: a look ("You keep the pale, even light and drop the hot orange") or something to avoid. Keep writes the card into your notebook as a note with the kept pictures as its examples, edited wording and all; Discard drops it. Each set of pictures is looked at once, nothing lands unreviewed, and the taste profile is not touched by these cards. Off on the Assist slider = no pass at all. He builds the profile as you work. In quiet moments — when you switch projects — Marcel runs a cheap pass over your recent prompts, re-rolls, and rejections and proposes a note or two: "Noticed you keep re-rolling golden-hour skies → prefers cool, overcast light." Each proposal appears in the timeline as a card you rule on — Keep (folds it into your profile, and you can Edit the wording first) or Discard. Nothing is locked in without your say-so; until you rule, it's treated as a working hypothesis. Inference cards: Keep, Discard or Edit what Marcel thinks he learned The taste interview. The first time Marcel can run (once you've added a text key), he offers a short, entirely optional interview — what you make, references you love, pet peeves, preferred vibe. You don't have to describe your taste from a blank page: two rows of chips (drawn to golden-hour warmth, clinical minimalism, brutalist mass… / allergic to sterile renders, HDR crunch, plastic skin…) write editable sentences straight into your answers, so you react instead of invent — and every word stays yours to rewrite before anything is sent. Then, instead of filing your answers raw, Marcel can distill them: one call on his brain lane reads what you wrote and proposes back a structured profile in his own words — palette, light, mood, composition, references, hard NOs — "here's what I think you like — correct me." The proposal appears in an editable box; fix anything that's off, then Accept to make it your taste profile (or Redo for another read, or go back and answer more). Prefer no model call at all? Save without distilling files your raw answers exactly as before. The distillation is ledgered like every Marcel call — a few cents on a flagship model. The interview is never one-shot: relaunch it any time from Marcel's memory (🧠 → Redo the taste interview) or ⚙ Settings → Marcel. Re-running pre-selects the chips that match your current profile, and nothing is overwritten until you accept the new proposal — the rest of your profile (learned notes, hand edits) stays untouched.

Marcel runs on your own text-model key, like everything else in Brut — there is no Brut server in the conversation. Add a Gemini, OpenAI or Anthropic key and chat works; without one, the panel remains a fully working journal and the composer shows a quiet add a key link. One OpenRouter key also works. If you hold no native text key but have an OpenRouter key, Marcel's lanes route through it — chat, ambient narration, acting, everything — visibly (the composer shows ⇄ runs via OpenRouter), at pass-through token rates, so long conversations stay as cheap as on a direct key. A native key added later takes over automatically. Two model lanes, both pickable in ⚙ Settings → Marcel: Brain — the model behind chat and advice. Auto picks your best configured model (Claude Sonnet 5.5 when an Anthropic key exists, Gemini 3.8 Flash when your Google key is the only one). Every model in the picker shows its price today (in / out, per million tokens; an introductory rate shows as such until its end date, then the row moves to the later rate by itself) and, once picked, one line on why you'd choose it. Google's flagship, Gemini 4 Argon, is in the list for the hardest work; it is never picked for you. Narrator — the cheap lane behind everything ambient: failure diagnoses, run commentary, session recaps, and the quiet taste passes. Auto picks Claude Haiku 5.5 or Gemini Flash, whichever key exists. Both lanes carry a Reasoning dial and a Thinking switch under their pickers, for full control over speed and cost on each lane. Reasoning sets how hard the model thinks before answering: deeper costs more. It works on the GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 models and on Claude Sonnet 5.5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 4.8 / Opus 5 / Opus 5.5; on a model without it the row shows not supported rather than hiding. On a direct OpenAI key the brain lane's Reasoning is fixed at none, so that Marcel can act on the canvas (the row says so; the narrator lane keeps its dial). GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol can advise but can't act on a direct OpenAI key for now; through OpenRouter they can. The Thinking switch is for Claude: off is faster and cheaper when you don't need deep deliberation (on Sonnet 5.5, off means no thinking before acting). Opus 5.5 has no switch (its thinking is always on), so its cheap setting is a low Reasoning. Details on the OpenAI and Anthropic pages. Every call's ledger row records the settings it ran with. Settings, Marcel tab: brain, narrator and prompt cache, each with its model and dials

Every Marcel call is ledgered like a generation: provider, model, exact token counts reported by the provider, and a dollar estimate from the catalog's per-token prices. Click the spend readout in the toolbar to open the full ledger — per-lane totals up top, then every call newest-first, Marcel's rows tagged with what kind of turn they were. Real numbers from a measured full-day session (your ledger will show yours): Ambient remarks (failure diagnoses, run commentary, recaps, taste passes) run on the cheap narrator lane and cost well under a cent each — measured ≈0.1¢ for a diagnosis, ≈0.7¢ for a recap on Claude Haiku 4.5; Haiku 5.5, the lane's default, bills a tenth of that rate. Chat carries everything Marcel knows, about Brut and about you, so it costs more than a remark. On a flagship model that would cost about 19¢ per message, so Marcel keeps the conversation's setup ready (on Claude models): the first message of a session costs more, and the ones after it cost cents, scaling mostly with how long his reply is. The ledger shows what each call cost, so the saving is something you can check, not a promise. By default the setup stays ready for 1 hour, even while you work on the canvas between chats: chat, render for twenty minutes, chat again, and the second message is still cheap. The first message of a session costs about 36¢ on Sonnet at list, then the following ones cost cents. If you chat in one rapid uninterrupted stretch, switch ⚙ Settings → Marcel → Prompt cache to 5 minutes: the first message costs less (about 23¢), but any pause longer than that starts over. Studio events that land between messages (runs finishing, errors) add only a small amount, never the whole setup again. Cheap-lane chat (Gemini Flash, GPT-5.4 Mini) stays in the 1–2¢ range per turn. On a Gemini brain, Google keeps a long setup it has just seen on its own and bills it at a tenth of the input rate (a twentieth on Gemini 4 Argon); the ledger counts it that way. Brut estimates at each provider's list price, and every ledger row prices from the tokens the provider actually reports. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Sonnet 5 both list at $2 / $10 per million tokens. When Marcel acts, one reply may take several model rounds (think → act → look at the result → continue). Each round is its own ledger row, so an acting turn costs a few text calls rather than one — still cents; the generations he triggers are the real spend, and those sit behind the confirm.

The conversation goes from your machine straight to your chosen text provider on your key, and the diary, your taste profile, and project notes never leave your disk — see Privacy. Your taste profile is per-account and private; it is never included in an export or synced anywhere. When exporting, a checkbox controls whether the journal travels: on by default for folder exports (backups), off by default for .brutpack handoffs. Project notes travel with the project either way.
Brut is local-first, so "collaboration" means moving work between machines — not syncing it through a cloud. Two mechanisms cover it: .brutpack files and NAS-rooted projects.

File ▾ → Export project as pack… writes a single .brutpack file containing everything: outputs, graphs and the generation ledger. Your past results come with it, so whoever opens it can run the graph again for free. File, Export as pack: one file carries graphs, outputs and ledger, warm caches included Import with File ▾ → Import pack… → it becomes a new project, ready to run. Importing always makes a new project and never touches your existing ones. Older .forgepack files open too. A .brutpack never contains keys — those stay in each machine's keychain.

Instead of passing files around, point a project at a shared folder on your NAS (File ▾ → New project…, then choose the NAS path as its root). The project's data lives there. Brut leaves a small file in that folder, so a second computer can open the same project with File ▾ → Open project…, and both machines work against the same outputs, graphs and ledger. This is how a studio collaborates: one project on the NAS, every computer opening it. A project opens correctly on any machine, whether its files sit on your C: drive or on a NAS share. On the new machine, unchanged nodes still replay for free. Change one and it runs again.

Export project to folder — a live copy into an empty folder; the copy is itself openable and shareable (great for a NAS). Export project as pack — the same content as one .brutpack archive. Both ask whether to include the Marcel studio journal (conversations + narration): on by default for a folder export (it's a backup), off by default for a pack (packs leave the studio). A checkbox lets you override either way.
The nodes that feed everything else: text and images going into the graph.

A freeform text node. Type a prompt; its output flows down text wires to any node that takes a prompt — Text→Image, Image→Image, the cinema agents, and so on. Prompts are the most-reused currency in a graph. Prompt presets — the select under the text box loads a saved prompt from the global library (all projects), 💾 saves the current text as one, and ✕ deletes the loaded preset. A brief you refined once — a Multi-Shot scenario, a house style clause, a recurring negative — becomes one click on any future graph. Hand-editing the text detaches the preset name; the text on the node is always the truth. All saved presets are also listed (and deletable) in File ▾ → Browse library…. The node is resizable — hover it and drag the ⌟ grip in its bottom-right corner (the text-box gesture, applied to the whole node): the text box fills the node, so a long brief gets a wide, tall box, and the size is saved with the graph. Type @ to name a picture. When the prompt feeds a node that takes pictures (Image → Image, Compose, Image → Video, Video → Video, Adjust), typing @ opens a small list of the pictures wired into it: a thumbnail, the name each one answers to, its role (start, end, reference, scene). Keep typing to filter, ↑/↓ to move, Enter to insert the name, Esc to close; a click inserts too. A prompt feeding two nodes lists both, headed by node. You pick a picture by sight; Brut writes its name and, at run time, tells the model which picture that is (see Image In for where names come from). On a Prompt node wired to nothing yet, @ opens a one-line hint saying so.

An AI prompt-rewriter. Wire a Prompt (or any text) into Refine, choose a preset, and it rewrites the text through a text model — sharpening a vague idea into a precise, photorealistic prompt without changing your intent. Several text wires into its prompt inlet are all read, in wire order (one per line), so six short Prompt nodes can compose one brief; the same holds for Text → Text. Generation nodes keep taking the first text wire only: put a Join text in front of one to give it several. Pick a preset, run, and edit the result in place; hand edits flow downstream A name your text gives a picture (@woman, see Image In) comes out of Refine exactly as it went in, whatever the preset: the node the refined prompt feeds is the one that resolves it, and a video preset's own @Image wording never replaces a name you wrote. The Model select picks the writer: the default is Gemini 3.8 Flash (the newest Flash, a fraction of a cent per refine; it thinks for a couple of seconds first), and any planning model in your catalog is one click away — Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite if you want the fastest, GPT-5.6 and Claude models too, with a Reasoning dial when the model has one; a "⇄" marks a model reached through another service such as OpenRouter. Changing the model re-runs the refine. Twenty-one presets ship with Brut, including: Enhance prompt — the general-purpose sharpener. Screenshot → photoreal, Cinematic relight, Camera language, Scene dressing, and more. Character turnaround sheet and Character expressions — wire a character image in and get an image-editing prompt for a 4-view orthographic turnaround, or a grid of facial expressions, both keeping the character exactly as the image shows them. (Character Lab cards dropped before its sheet version run these two.) Character sheet — from attribute lines (sex, age, style, clothes…) or a short description of a person, and from a character image when you wire one, writes the prompt for one 16:9 character sheet: a bust, then the full body from the front, the left side, the back and the right side, five panels separated by thin lines on light grey under soft studio light. It names on which side of the body anything worn on one side sits (a watch, an earring). Render it at 16:9. It is the recipe the Character Lab library composite runs. Scenario maker — writes a brief for a Multi-Shot Custom scenario (chain Prompt → Refine → Multi-Shot notes). Kling video prompt, Seedance 2.5 video prompt, Gemini Omni video prompt — the video-prompt writers, one per model, each writing in the form that model follows best. All three stay faithful to what you wrote: nothing is added that you didn't ask for (no invented gestures, props, dialogue or music), and the camera energy you state (dynamic, fast, slow) wins over the house's steady-camera default. Give them the facts you care about — the swap, the move with its direction and end framing, the action, the duration — and tell them in the notes which pipeline stage you're at. Seedance 2.0 video prompt — the same, written for Seedance 2.0. Refine shot — plan-aware: feed a shot plan in and it edits one shot. Seedance 2.5 shot plan / Seedance 2.0 shot plan — plan-aware: feed the Script Supervisor's whole plan in and every clip prompt is rewritten for that Seedance generation with ambient sound to match the scene, while the shots, their stills, keyframe prompts and frames stay untouched. Splice it between the Supervisor and a Storyboard to run the same film on Seedance — a second Storyboard fed this way keeps its keyframes, so a Kling-vs-Seedance A/B never re-bills the frames. Use the notes to direct the soundscape ("birdsong on the terrace, fireplace crackle at dusk"). Some presets are multimodal — wire an image in and the model sees it. Refine's output is editable text: hand-tweak it and your edits flow downstream; change an input or roll again and it regenerates over them. Like Prompt, the node is resizable — drag the ⌟ grip in its bottom-right corner; the result box (the notes box, before a result exists) fills the node, and the size is saved with the graph.

A free-form LLM call — a ChatGPT/Claude turn as a graph node. Pick any text model from your providers (Gemini, GPT or Claude — your keys, like everywhere in Brut), optionally give it a role in the System field ("you are a harsh photography critic"), type a message, run. Wired text is prepended to your message — chain Prompt → Text→Text, or feed one node's answer into the next. A chain of Text→Text nodes is a conversation materialized on the canvas: every turn editable, kept, and re-runnable. Wired images are seen — connect renders or photos and ask "what's wrong with this composition?", "describe this scene for a video prompt", "compare these two options". Images are downscaled for the model's request cap; nothing is uploaded anywhere but to your chosen provider. The answer is editable text — hand-tweak it and your edits flow downstream on the next run; 🎲 Re-ask requests a fresh answer. On models with a reasoning dial — GPT-5.6 Sol / Terra / Luna and GPT-6 Sol / Luna (none → xhigh, details) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 4.8 / Opus 5 / Opus 5.5 (low → max, details) — a Reasoning select appears: how deeply the model reasons before answering. Changing it is a new answer, like any input change. The node is resizable at two levels: the System and Message blocks each have their own grip (drag it to give one block more lines; the heights are saved with the graph and never shrink below three and four lines), and the ⌟ corner grip resizes the whole node, which can never crush the blocks below their minimums; extra height goes to the answer box. Unlike Refine (which rewrites prompts through fixed presets), Text→Text is open-ended: analysis, critique, translation, naming, alt-text, brainstorming — anything a chat assistant does, with the result flowing down a text wire. One-shot by design: for an ongoing conversation with memory, talk to Marcel. Calls are token-priced (typically well under a cent) and land in the ledger like every paid call.

The Shot Board for text: wire one long text in — a Text → Text answer, an agent plan, any pasted script — and it splits into numbered, editable blocks, each with its own output plug (#3 routes straight into a Text→Image while #4 feeds an Image→Video). Free and local: no AI call, nothing billed. One script becomes numbered tiles, each with its own plug Split modes: Auto-detect tries blocks headed SHOT 1, SHOT 2… (the script format many studios use), then lists in code format, numbered lists, and finally blank-line paragraphs; or pick a mode explicitly, including a custom separator. Blocks are editable in place — tweaks flow out the plugs immediately on the next run. Changing the wired text or the split mode re-splits (edits belong to the old content and reset with it). ✕ hides a block from the combined bottom output (its number and plug stay stable); ↺ restores it. The board grows to fit its blocks — every tile (and its plug) stays visible, so wires always attach where you see them. Shrink it by hand if you prefer; it only re-grows when the content changes. The killer combo: a scripted Text → Text (your reel/script prompt in its System field, renders wired to its images inlet) → Text Board → per-shot prompts fanned out to your image and video nodes. One click from "one long ChatGPT answer" to a wired production board. (For the specific case of cinematic reels, the cinema crew's Cinematic Reel (flourish) brief now folds this whole flow into one node chain — the Text → Text front-end stays the flexible, roll-your-own route.)

Several texts into one, with no AI call: every text wired into its inlet, in the order of the wires, plus a text of your own, joined with the separator you pick. Image and video nodes read only the first text wired into them, so this is how a fixed house prompt and a brief, or a style line and a shot description, feed one Text → Image together. Separator: new line, blank line, space or comma. Your own text goes after the wired ones; tick own text first to put it before them. Each piece is trimmed at both ends and empty pieces are skipped. Nothing else in the text is changed. The Result under the fields is exactly the text the next node receives, updated as you type or as anything upstream changes, with its character count. There is no ▶: nothing needs to run. Free and local, nothing billed. With nothing wired and no text of its own, the result is empty and the next node says it has no prompt. Two prompts and a line of its own joined into one text for a Text → Image

Loads images into the graph. Add them by file picker, drag & drop, or paste — all append, so one Image In can hold several images. The footer line at the bottom left gives the first image's resolution (4000 × 2250, · ×3 when the node holds several). Each thumbnail's 🔍 (top right, where every node keeps it) opens the lightbox at screen resolution — ←/→ pages through the node's images, wheel-zoom loads the original pixels only when you actually zoom; ✕ at the top left removes that image from the node. Dropping image files anywhere on the canvas creates a ready-filled Image In node right where they land — and so does pressing Ctrl+V over the canvas with an image on the clipboard (copy from Photoshop, a render buffer, or any browser image; a new Image In appears at your cursor). To append a pasted image to an existing Image In instead, click that node first and then paste, or use its Paste button. On disk, a file you bring in lands in the project's outputs/inputs/ under a name that keeps yours recognizable — <project>_<graph>_<your-filename>_in_<date>_<code>.<ext>, paste for a clipboard image (see what a filename tells you). Results can be detached the same way: drag any image off a node — a generation preview, a Multi-Shot or Shot Board tile, a Reference Board still, a Storyboard card frame — and drop it on empty canvas to get a ready-filled Image In right there (drop it on an existing Image In to append instead). No re-upload, no copy: the new node points at the same project file, now frozen as a base for further exploration even if the source node later re-rolls or is deleted from the plan. From the Elements vault. Drag tiles from the Elements panel onto the canvas: an element (a person, a place, an object, a look you typed in the vault) lands as one Image In holding all its pictures, titled after it, with its type on a chip; loose pictures land together in one plain Image In; onto an existing Image In, they append. The Elements… button on the node opens the same vault as a picker. A picture Seedance accepts the people in (a registered BytePlus asset) says Seedance-approved on the node, wherever the file came from. Drop files from Explorer onto the canvas, or drag a result off any node: a ready-filled Image In either way Every picture has a name; say it in the prompt. Nobody types anything. A picture is named the moment it arrives, after what you already know it by: the file's own name for a picture you brought in (villa_cam03_clay.jpg answers to @villa-cam03-clay), the node that made it for a render (@i2i-7, the same code as in its file name), the element's name for a picture from Elements. Then, a second or two later, Brut names it by looking at it: a small copy of the picture goes once to Gemini Flash on your key, and the few words it answers (@concrete-house-dusk) replace the file's name on the card, in the legends and in the @ list; the file's name keeps working as a second name. It costs a fraction of a cent per picture, every call is in the ledger, and a picture is looked at once for good, wherever it is copied. The switch is on the Gemini card in ⚙ Settings (Name pictures by looking, on by default); off, or without a Gemini key, pictures keep their file names. Two pictures that would share a name, say three takes dragged off one node, are told apart in the order you added them: @i2i-7, @i2i-7-2, @i2i-7-3, each card showing its own. The field under each thumbnail shows the name greyed; type in it to give the picture a name of your own (Woman in red is @woman-in-red, accents may be typed or not), clear it to get the automatic one back. A pasted picture has no name until it has been looked at, or until you give it one. The node's own Name field names all of its pictures at once, so @woman and @man point at one picture each while @cast means both (the people of @cast sit by the window); a node dropped from Elements arrives named after the element. Write @name in the prompt of the node the picture feeds, by hand or through the Prompt node's @ list (type @, pick the picture by its thumbnail): Brut tells the model which picture you mean, whatever the order of the wires and whatever the model. The node it feeds shows a legend under its inlets with each wired picture, its name and its role, so you always see what the model will be told. A picture nothing names can still be pointed at by its place among the pictures a node receives, @picture3, and the legend says so. Two pictures given the same name: the second one is @woman-2, and the legend warns. A name that matches no wired picture stops the run before anything is sent or billed, and the message lists the names you can use. Naming changes nothing on its own: a node whose prompt writes no @ runs, and replays from cache, exactly as before. File vs. paste, for big renders: adding a file (picker or drag & drop) keeps its original bytes — a 12 MB JPEG stays a 12 MB JPEG. Pasting can't: the clipboard carries decoded pixels, not your file, so Brut stores them losslessly as PNG (never a silent re-compression) — a 20-megapixel render lands around 38 MB that way. Same pixels, bigger container. Paste is perfect for screenshots and quick grabs; for production renders, prefer the file — smaller payloads and the exact encoding you delivered. Image In is the entry point for image-to-image work, composition, inpainting, and the stills that ground the cinema crew. For the crew, your stills are the project's identity anchors, not a shot list — the film can hold more shots than you have stills: invented compositions generate their start frames from these anchors, so every frame stays your building.

Loads clips into the graph: footage from your phone, a playblast from your 3D software, a clip made elsewhere. Add them with Choose… or by dragging files onto the node; both append. Dropping video files anywhere on the canvas creates a ready-filled Video In where they land. The clip plays on the node, and a line per clip reads its size, length and frame rate (1076 × 1926 · 4.0 s · 24 fps), with its ✕. Video In feeds Video → Video, and any node that takes a clip (Upscale Video, Extract frame, the Sequence).
→ Image generation — turn these into pictures.
The core image nodes. All of them take a prompt (and, where relevant, images) and produce an image on a provider of your choice.

Generate an image from a prompt. Pick a provider and model, set the aspect ratio and (on Gemini) the resolution, wire a prompt in, run. This is the starting point of most graphs — see Your first image. A ratio a model does not render at the chosen size is greyed in place with the reason (Ideogram 4.5 has no 21:9 at 1K: pick 2K). Providers: Gemini (Nano Banana family), OpenAI (GPT Image 2, plus the GPT Image 2.5 and 2.6 pairs, Flare and Sunburst; both pairs unlock two extra quality steps, xhigh and max, on the quality select, and the 2.6 pair adds a Complexity select: how much the model plans before it draws) and Seedream (BytePlus's Seedream 5.0 Pro, Flash and Lite, on the Seedance key: 1K / 1.5K / 2K, Lite 2K / 3K / 4K, from $0.018 per image; you get exactly the size you pick). Every image node's footer shows its result's resolution (2048 × 1152, · ×4 on a batch) at the bottom left, on the output pin's row, the real pixel size of the file, not the preview's. Every image node's title bar has ▶ (run this node and what it needs; unchanged inputs replay the last result, free), 🕘 (history: every past result, pin one) and ↻ re-roll (a fresh take with the same inputs: bills again, the current take stays in history). See Never pay twice.

Edit or transform an existing image with a prompt. Wire an Image In (or any upstream image) into the image inlet and a prompt into prompt. Good for variations, retouching, and style changes. A picture wired into reference is the look to follow (see A reference: the look to follow), and several pictures can each get their own render (see Each picture its own render). Several pictures can be wired into image, in wire order (connect the picture to edit first). What the model does with them differs by family. Nano Banana and GPT Image treat the first wire as the picture being edited and the next ones as references the prompt can name as image 2, image 3: a clay frame first and a portrait second, with the small figure is the man of image 2, renders the frame in that man's likeness (measured on Nano Banana 2.1). Seedream blends several pictures into a new composition (its maker's own term: multi-image blending): no picture is the base and the framing follows the richest one, so the same wiring came back as the portrait reshaped to the frame's aspect, on Pro and on Flash alike. To put a subject at a place in a picture on Seedream, use a marks step on an Adjust node: a box on the place, with the portrait as the mark's reference, puts the subject there. With nothing wired into image, the node renders the prompt as text-to-image on the same model (when the model offers it) and says so in the activity log; an aspect of auto then falls back to the model's own default aspect, since there is no input to follow. Which picture is which. Under the inlets, the node lists every wired picture: its thumbnail, the @name it answers to and its role, in the order the request carries them. Write those names in the prompt (the small figure is @man, match the light of @villa-cam03), by hand or through the Prompt node's @ list: Brut tells the model which picture you mean, on every model. Names come from the Image In (a picture is named after its file or the node that made it until you type a name); a picture nothing names reads unnamed · @picture2, and @picture2 works too. The same legend sits on Adjust, Compose and the video nodes. When the rest of the picture must stay exactly as it was, 🗇 Reconcile with input under the result lays the edit back over the input and keeps only what changed: see Reconcile with input. A look dropped on a picture. Drag a look from the Elements panel (dusk, fog, golden autumn, a filmic finish…) onto any picture on the canvas: Brut adds an Image → Image node wired from that picture, with a Prompt holding the look's words, on the look's model when your keys reach it. Nothing runs until you press ▶, and ▶ Run prices it first. Drop a second look on that new node, run or not, to chain another change after it. Size on Seedream: Same as the picture. On the Seedream models the Size menu of this node, of Adjust and of Compose opens with Same as the picture, and it is the default when you switch the node to Seedream: the edit comes back at the input's own pixel dimensions (on Compose, the scene's), so nothing has to be scaled or cropped when it is laid over the original in a Layers or Compare node. (The model still redraws the frame: the result can sit a few pixels off, see Keep the original outside the edit.) The model's range decides how far that holds: Pro and Flash render 0.9 to 4.6 MP, Lite 3.7 to 16.8 MP; a picture below the range comes back at the model's smallest size, one above it at its largest, with the proportions kept. Pick a size from the menu to resample on purpose. See Seedream. Gemini gotcha: Gemini sometimes sends back no picture and no reason: that is a silent refusal (shown as OTHER or IMAGE_OTHER), usually triggered by an input image (a real person's name in facade lettering, a face, a logo), not the prompt. It happens again every time, so Brut doesn't retry it. Fix by removing or cropping the offending image. A picture that comes from an element of your vault is named in the prompt with the element's line (a ✦ line on the face says which; untick to send the pictures bare), and the face warns when more pictures are wired than the model takes per request.
Image → Image › A reference: the look to follow

The reference inlet takes the look you want: a render you already like, a photo, a material sample. The render takes its materials, colors, light and atmosphere from it, while the view, the framing and every form stay those of the picture on image. The legend under the inlets lists it as a reference. A reference alone, with nothing on image, has nothing to render: the node stops with one line and sends nothing. With nothing on reference, the node works exactly as it always did. On the Clay → Photoreal and Clay to Client Set cards, the step that writes the prompt reads the reference too: the materials, the planting, the light and the sky in the prompt are described from the reference picture, never invented from the clay, and a Materials or Vegetation knob left empty (or reading as on the reference) is answered from it. Both cards render on FLUX 3 Image: on a tower seen from two cameras with a reference photo wired, it was the one model that held each capture's view and took the reference's materials, where the others redrew the view or invented materials; the Model knob takes any other.
Image → Image › Each picture its own render

Wire several pictures into image (the clay of each camera of a Scene, several viewport grabs of one project) and tick Each picture its own render: the node makes one render per picture, in wire order, instead of one render of the first picture with the others riding along. The box is greyed, saying why, until two pictures are wired; once ticked it can always be unticked. One look for the set. With nothing on reference, the first render sets the look of the rest (Look of the rest: the first render): the first picture renders first, then every other picture keeps its own view and takes the first render's materials, colors, light and sky, so the building is not reinvented from one view to the next. If the first render fails, the others do not start (they would have no look to follow). Pick none, each on its own to render every picture independently. With a picture on reference, that picture sets the look of every render, the first included, and the face says so. The renders of one set come back at one size when their pictures share a shape. Names in the prompt. The prompt is written once for the whole set. An @name of a reference reaches every render; an @name of one of the pictures reaches that picture's render only, and the legend says so. The tiles. One tile per picture, each at its picture's own shape (the framing of every camera is what you check): the picture itself, dimmed, until its render lands, then the render (🔍 to magnify, drag it out to detach it). A render that failed turns its tile red, and its plug carries nothing until it renders; hover it for the provider's words. ↻ on a tile renders that picture again and keeps the others; on the first tile, while it sets the look, the others render again with the new look, and the price is asked first. Pin a render from 🕘 and it pins that picture alone: every row of the history names the picture it was rendered from (picture 2, say), and the pinned tile wears a 📌 and keeps that render on every run, free, until you unpin. Pin as many pictures as you like, each from any run or model. A pinned first picture is the look of the others, so they render again with it. Click the pin on the tile to unpin, or ↻ on it: it asks to unpin first. Unplug a pinned picture and its pin goes with its tile. The plugs. Each tile has its own plug on its edge: wire one render into a clip, an upscale or another card, and only that render goes. The main plug carries every render, in the order of the pictures. Unplug a picture whose tile's plug is wired, and its tile stays, saying the plug carries nothing, so you can see and delete that wire. Untick the box and the tiles' plugs go, with the wires on them. A pinned picture's plug carries its pinned render, and the main plug carries the set with the pins in place. No prompt, no render. A node with pictures and no prompt stops with one line and sends nothing, a reference wired or not. On a card such as Clay → Photoreal, if the step that writes the prompt fails, the renders do not go out either. Never pay twice: each picture keeps its own result. Change the prompt and every picture renders again; wire a new camera and only that one renders (with the first render as its look, unchanged); a render that failed is the only one retried on the next run, the others stay. A new first render (a re-roll, a new prompt) gives the others a new look, so they render again too. Cost: one image per picture, priced like any single render on that model (three cameras = three renders). ▶ Run prices the renders before anything is sent. While a node above still writes the prompt, the quote reads up to N renders (some may replay free); while a node above still has to make the pictures, the set waits for it, without a price. ▶ or ↻ on the node asks once before rendering; Keep cached only sends nothing. The node's history (🕘) holds every render.

One node for every correction of a picture. Paint or click where the change goes and say what goes there, or point at things with arrows and notes. Each fix is a step, each step keeps its takes, and outside each edit the picture stays the original. Inpaint and Annotate & Correct nodes in older graphs open as Adjust nodes with one step: their mask or their marks become that step, their last result its picked take (it stays the step's result; a change you make to the step goes into its next take, with ↻). If the old node was changed after that result was made (a mask painted again, a note edited, another model picked) and saved without running, the step runs once, as the old node would have. An aspect picked on the old node is dropped: an Adjust step keeps the picture's own shape. Wire a picture into image (run upstream once so it has one). Click ✏ Start editing. The editor opens full screen on the picture, with a first step ready. Mark the change (a mask or marks, below), write what should happen, click Generate. Keep going: + on a step starts the next fix on that step's picked take. The editor. Four fixed zones: nothing in it moves or resizes when you switch views, steps or kinds, hover a take or generate. Left: one column of tools for the selected step (the mask tools or the mark tools, in the same place, each with its key), with the keyboard button at its bottom: it shows every shortcut of the editor, and so does ?. In the middle, under a one-line bar (the active tool's settings on the left; Clear, 100 %, Fit and the picture's size and zoom on the right): the picture the step works on, with what you drew on it, or, with Picked take, the step's result drawn in exactly the same place, so the two compare in place. Show the mask (or Show the marks) lays what you drew over the result. On a mask step the mask stays editable while the result shows: see Editing the mask after a take. On a marks step nothing on the result can be drawn or changed: the tools and the marks' cards stay where they are, greyed, and Picture is one click away. The wheel zooms at the cursor and middle-drag or Space + drag (the pointer on the picture) pans, on the picture and on the result alike; 0 fits. Right: the steps, then the selected step (Picture or Picked take, Mask or Marks, its prompt, its marks, its model) and, always in view at the bottom, Keep the original outside the edit, Generate with the price, and Save. Bottom: the selected step's takes. A step is a Mask or a Marks step: pick which in its panel (once it has a take, add a new step for the other kind). Save keeps what you drew without generating; so does everything else that takes the picture away (closing the editor with Esc, picking a take, clicking another step, a new take of the step before): what you drew is kept with the picture it was drawn on. Every key the editor uses stays in the editor, whatever it shows: Delete, Ctrl+Z or Ctrl+D never touch the canvas behind it. ? shows every shortcut.

The first row of the steps list is the picture itself: the picture wired into the node, with its thumbnail and its name (the name you gave it, else its own). It has no takes and nothing is drawn on it: click it to see the picture alone, and + on it starts a step on the original picture. The first steps hang from it, so two steps made on the picture read as a fork like any other. A step is one request on one picture: the node's picture for the first step, the picked take of the step before it for the next ones. Each Generate adds a take to the step and picks it. The take you picked is what the steps after it start from: a new take picks itself, and a click on another take in the bottom strip picks that one, so the next steps start from it instead. Nothing else moves a pick: editing the step, adding a step after it or generating one never switches it to another take. Hover a take to see it as the model made it, in the editor's picture, at the same place and size, the line above the picture naming that take (a take of another shape fills the frame the way it is laid back, its edges cropped, never stretched). Clicking a step that has a picked take shows that take; Picture is one click away to draw again. ↻ on a step (or on the node's title bar, for the step it shows) makes one more take of that step. The button names its price first, and a step before it that still needs a run runs with it. Generating a step that has steps after it makes the node show that step: the steps after it keep their takes and nothing else is billed. Click one of them and generate it to carry the new take on (it runs again, on the new picture). + on any step adds a step on its picked take. On a step that already has one after it, that is a branch: a second way to continue from the same picture. Click a step to work on it; its branch becomes the one the node shows. The steps list is drawn as a tree: steps made one after the other go straight down in one column, however many there are. Only where a step (or the picture itself) has two or more steps made on it does the list indent: a line comes down and forks, and each of those steps starts a branch one level in, its own chain then straight down again. The lines of the branch the node shows are drawn in the accent color. Deeper forks indent less and less, so the list never scrolls sideways. A chevron shows only where there is something to fold. Where the list forks (a step, or the picture, with two or more steps made on it), a chevron sits on the fork and folds every branch under it into one line, 3 steps folded; a click on the chevron or on that line opens them again. The first row of a branch with more rows after it carries a chevron too, which folds the rest of that branch. A branch of one row has none. Folding only tidies the list: nothing is hidden from the node, nothing runs, nothing changes, and Ctrl+Z does not count it. When the step you work on is inside a fold, wherever you picked it from, the fold opens again; while it stays folded, the folded row is outlined with a dashed line. Pick another take of a step and the steps after it run again on the next run (their picture changed), and only those. Pick a take back and a step after it that was already made on that picture comes back as it was, free. The node's output is the picked take of the last step of the branch shown. 🕘 on a step (or on the node, for the step it shows) lists every take that step ever made, from your history; Use this take makes one the step's picked take again, free, with the original kept outside the edit when the step keeps it. On a node opened from an older Inpaint or Annotate & Correct node, the old node's results are listed there too. ✕ on a step removes it and every step made on it, after asking. Their takes stay in the history. To set a branch aside without losing it, hide it: the eye on a step is open while the step is shown, and a click on it folds the step and every step made on it into one muted row (hidden · 3 steps · eye to show) with a closed eye. Nothing is deleted, its takes stay, and a click on the closed eye shows them again. A hidden step never runs and is never the one the node shows: when the node showed it, the node shows the nearest step before it. The only branch left shown can't be hidden.
Adjust › A mask: where the change goes

On a mask step, mark the area that should change, then write what goes there ("a green velvet sofa"). The tools: Brush (B) and Eraser (E): the brush circle under the pointer shows the real size; [ / ] resize it. Soft feathers the edge of both, from 0 (a hard edge, the default) to 100, the way Photoshop's hardness does: the circle is where a soft brush paints at half strength, the paint fades smoothly past it, and a dashed ring shows how far (at 100, twice the circle, with only the very center fully painted). Alt+right-drag sets both, as on the Sketchpad: left and right for the size, up and down for the softness, with the numbers beside the circle. Shift+click draws a straight stroke from the end of the last one. Hold Alt as you start a stroke and the brush erases instead (the brush circle turns dashed), without switching to the eraser. On a tablet, pressure drives the size (a lighter touch, a thinner stroke) and the softness (a lighter touch, a softer edge; full pressure paints at the Soft setting), each with its own box, so either works alone. After each stroke the bar shows what Brut received, for example pen · 78 %; a tablet showing mouse · no pressure sends mouse events: turn Windows Ink on in its settings. The softness and the two boxes are remembered on this machine. On the cut (Edit the cut) a soft edge blends the take into the original; a model that takes the mask itself reads a soft edge as painted out to its middle. Lasso (L): drag around an area; it fills when you let go. Hold Alt to cut an area out. Polygon (P): click each corner, for straight edges (a window frame, a roof line, a wall). Close it by clicking the first corner again (a dashed ring shows where), with a double-click, or with Enter; it fills when it closes. Backspace drops the last corner, Esc cancels the polygon (it does not close the editor). Hold Alt as you close it to cut the area out. Each polygon is one Ctrl+Z. Rectangle (R): drag a box; it fills when you let go, exactly the pixels inside it. Hold Alt to cut the box out, Shift for a square. Each box is one Ctrl+Z. Wand (W): click an object and all of it is selected, a slat panel, a railing, a window, a tree, the sky. Each click is one object: a left click adds it to the mask, so three clicks on three objects keep all three; a right click (or Alt + click) takes the object under it out. Shift + click refines the last object: one more point that takes (Shift + right-click: one that leaves), that object worked out again with it. The bar counts the objects and how much of the picture the mask covers. Every click is one Ctrl+Z, even right after typing in the prompt or choosing in a menu. A Ctrl+Z while a click is still being worked out (Selecting…) cancels that click: nothing lands, and the next Ctrl+Z takes back the object before it. A click takes: how much one click selects. Detail is the smallest piece under the click (a cushion, a handle), Part a part of the object, Whole object (the default) the largest. Your choice is for the next click: an object already taken stays exactly as it is, so switching sizes never changes what you have selected. A Shift + click refine uses the size shown when you make it. The wand only offers a size when it is confident about it: where the largest choice would spill onto the wall behind or onto the next object, Whole object gives the largest clean one instead, so two sizes can give the same selection. On an object made of many parts (a glazed door, a window of many panes), Whole object usually takes it all; if a click still takes one part, click the next part too, or Shift + click to grow that object. Every object comes out clean: specks that do not touch it are left out and small holes inside it are filled; real openings (a facade's windows) stay open. Grow: widens or narrows the next object, from −64 to +128 px (a shadow, a soft edge). While you drag the slider, the last object grows or shrinks on the picture so you see the result, and it takes the new value when you let go. Dragging within 1 px of zero snaps to 0; the arrow keys step one pixel at a time (so a small value such as 2 px stays reachable); a double-click on the slider or on its value puts it back to 0 px. Color (F): click to fill the area of similar color; tolerance sets how close a color must be. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo, Clear empties the mask (undoable). The wheel zooms at the cursor, middle-drag or Space + drag pans, 0 fits, 100 % shows one picture pixel per screen pixel. The wand runs on your machine, not at a provider: the first time you pick it, Brut downloads its model once (about 156 MB) and keeps it. After that a picture takes about a second to read (a fraction of a second on a graphics card) and every click answers at once. It is free, and the picture never leaves your machine for it. The wand reads the picture first: as soon as you pick it, the line under the picture says Reading the picture… and the pointer shows that it is waiting. You do not have to wait with it: a click made meanwhile is kept, waits its turn, and lands as soon as the read is done, three clicks as three objects, in the order you made them. The line counts the clicks waiting. If you move on to another picture during the read, the clicks made on the one before are dropped, and that picture's read never blocks the new one. If the read fails, the clicks made during it are not used and the reason shows under the picture; the next click tries the read again. Generate, Save and closing the editor wait for a click that is still being worked out, so a step never generates on the mask from before it; a click that fails stops Generate, and the reason shows under the picture. You can keep painting while a click is worked out: the object joins the mask as it is when the answer comes, and Clear drops a click still on its way, including the clicks waiting for the read. When Brut stops answering on your machine (it was closed, or it crashed), the line under the picture says The engine is not answering within a few seconds. Your drawing stays in the editor. Save and the wand work again once Brut answers. Closing the editor still asks before it drops a drawing you have not saved. Paint the whole object you want changed, with its shadow or reflection and a small margin: a thin stroke on one edge leaves the model to guess the rest. Editing the mask after a take The mask stays editable once a step has takes, in both views. With Picked take showing, any mask tool (the wand included) draws on the same mask as in Picture, and the mask shows over the take as you draw: a laid-back take and the original share the picture's frame, so the mask lands where you draw it. When the take shown is the model's own file (with Keep the original outside the edit off), the first stroke switches to Picture, then draws. Once saved, the edited mask goes into the step's next take: the picked take stays the step's result, and the steps after it keep starting from it, until you make one with ↻ New take (the button shows its price). The takes stay in the strip as the step's history. To change which part of a take shows rather than where the next take is asked, see Edit the cut.
Adjust › Marks: point and say what changes

On a marks step, point at things and say what changes, the way clients already brief on a picture. The tools (keys 1 to 7, A for the arrow): an arrow (point at the exact object), a box or a circle (hold Alt to draw from the center), a freehand lasso, a click-placed polygon (close on the first corner, with a double-click or with Enter; Backspace drops a corner, Esc cancels), a numbered point, and Select to move a mark (drag its number; on an arrow the number moves the tail, the tip re-aims it, the shaft moves the whole arrow) or a corner of a lasso or polygon; Delete removes the selected mark. Give each mark a note ("change this chair to a deep red", "remove this lamp") and, optionally: a color chip: the color wheel, the RAL Classic swatch grid (216 colors with search; screen colors approximate the physical chips), or the eyedropper to take a color straight from the picture; a reference picture: drop or browse a picture onto the mark's card, "replace THIS with the object shown". Formats a provider does not take (AVIF from a web page, for instance) are converted. Each mark's card (its note, its color, its reference) sits in the panel on the right, under the prompt; select a mark on the picture and its card comes into view. The marks are the prompt: the step's own text is optional ("keep the late-afternoon light") and applies to every mark. Ctrl+Z takes the last change to the marks back. Each model gets your marks in the form it reads best, and the result comes back with no marker in it. A marks step runs on the models that follow marks: Nano Banana 2.1 (the node's default), Nano Banana 2 and Pro, GPT Image, Seedream 5.0 Pro and Flash, and Ideogram 4.5 Precise Edit. The other models stay in the step's model menu, greyed with the reason (reads no marks). On our five-mark test room Nano Banana 2.1 put every edit where its mark was drawn; the original Nano Banana applied only some edits and left markers in the result, which is why it reads no marks here. Nano Banana Pro is the strongest with many marks; GPT Image is best with a handful at a time. GPT Image 2.5 and 2.6 read your marks natively, as OpenAI built them to: in our tests each edit landed where its mark was drawn with no trace of the mark left, a mark's reference picture was followed more closely than before, and one picture less is billed per run. The marks belong to the picture, not to the model: switch the step to another model and the same marks run again, with nothing to redraw. On Ideogram 4.5 Precise Edit the step runs one pass per mark, in order, each on the result of the one before: five marks are five passes at the price shown.

On Seedream 5.0 Pro and Flash a marks step places each edit where you marked it. On a test interior with five marks, one of each kind (recolor the sofa to a RAL green, remove the coffee table, hang a painting at a point on the wall, lay a rug inside a circle, fill a shelf outlined with a lasso), then with a reference armchair placed in a box: Seedream 5.0 Flash Seedream 5.0 Pro Nano Banana 2 The five edits all five, each at its mark all five, each at its mark all five, but the painting on another wall and the rug three times the circle Size of the result 2048 × 1143, the input's own 2048 × 1143, the input's own 2752 × 1536 Sofa color vs the RAL asked (#114232) #264933 #164335 #344d41 Cost and time $0.018, 21 s $0.045, 41 s $0.10, 16 s One scene is not a ranking, and Nano Banana Pro was not in that run. What it does show: on Seedream an edit lands where you marked it, the result comes back at the picture's own dimensions, and a correction step on Flash costs under two cents. Size: Same as the picture. On Seedream the Size menu opens with it, and it is the default: a 1376 × 768 picture comes back 1376 × 768. It holds for pictures between 0.9 and 4.6 MP; a smaller one comes back at 1K, a larger one at 2K, the model's limits. Pick 1K, 1.5K or 2K to resample: the picture's proportions are kept. No 4K on a marks step. Seedream 5.0 Pro and Flash render up to 4.6 MP (2K); only Lite goes to 3K and 4K, and Lite reads no marks. For a 4K result, correct at the picture's size and finish with an Upscale Image node. A mark that touches several things: name the one you mean in the note ("the lamp on the left"). A reference picture on a mark is one more input: on Pro each input after the first adds $0.003; on Flash inputs are free. Up to 9 reference pictures. Through an OpenRouter key the step reaches the same models, at OpenRouter's sizes (1K / 2K).
Adjust › Keep the original outside the edit

A model redraws the whole picture, even with a mask or marks: outside the edit the picture comes back close to the original, not identical (fine texture redrawn, a few pixels of shift, small tone changes). This is true of every provider; OpenAI's own guide says it of its masks: "Masking with GPT Image is entirely prompt-based." So each step, by default, keeps the original outside the edit: when a take lands, Brut lines it up with the picture the step worked on and keeps the model's result only where it changed near your mask or your marks; everywhere else the picture is the original's own pixels. It is local, free and takes a few seconds. With the switch on, nothing outside the area you asked for ever reaches the output. Two masks, two words: the mask is where you ask for the change, before the run; the cut is which part of the take shows over the original, afterwards. Brut makes the cut for you, and you can paint it yourself: see Edit the cut. What it can undo, and what it cannot. It undoes a small move of the whole frame (the model's few pixels of shift and stretch), read on the part of the picture that should not have changed, so a large change inside your mask (a lake in place of the garden) does not get in its way. It cannot undo a reframe: when the model moved the picture (another framing, a zoom, a restyle), no small move puts it back. When your mask leaves little of the picture outside it (a bare sky, a thin border), the move is read on the whole picture instead, and a take with a large change can then be refused. When it is refused, the step keeps the original. Two cases, each said on the picture itself, under the bar, with the way out: The model moved the picture: the original could not be laid back. The step hands the original on, unchanged. ↻ for another take, or untick Keep the original outside the edit to use this take as the model made it. The model changed nothing where you asked; the change elsewhere is not used. The step hands the original on: a change the model made outside your mask or marks never reaches the output. ↻ for another take, or untick the switch to use it as made. On a mask step whose model is only shown a picture of the mask, the line also suggests GPT Image 2.5 Flare on your OpenAI key, which takes the mask itself (below). A soft change (a new tone, a warmer light) can read as nothing: Edit the cut on that take opens on your painted mask and keeps the change inside it. The take itself is kept: the strip shows what the model made, marked not used, and a hover shows it in the picture. The Activity keeps a line too. A graph saved before this behavior keeps its takes: one that was not laid back is tried again once, free. Which models receive the mask itself. GPT Image on your OpenAI key and Ideogram get your mask with the request, as a mask; the other models (Nano Banana, FLUX, Seedream, and the others reached through fal.ai) are shown a picture of it, as a guide. GPT Image through fal.ai or OpenRouter takes no mask: a mask step on it stops and says so. On every model the mask steers the change rather than fencing it in (GPT Image still redraws the frame), which is why the original is laid back; a model that only sees a guide is more likely to put the change somewhere else, and that take is then refused as above. The take as the model made it is always kept: hover the take in the strip to see it. Turn the switch off on a step whose model is meant to change everything (a restyle, a new light): the take as the model made it flows on at once, with no new generation. Turn it back on and the laid-back picture comes back (a take made with the switch off is laid back then, free). The steps after it run again on the next run, since their picture changed. When an edit removes something, its soft shadow on the wall or the floor goes with it: the original is not laid back over the place the shadow was. A replaced object can come out a little larger than the area you painted (a new sofa drawn taller than the old one): a change that touches your mask is kept whole, even where it runs past it. When it runs too far, erase the spill with Edit the cut. Something that did not change can stand in front of the edit: a tree trunk across a wall you recolored, a mullion, a post. When a mark points at one side, the edit on both sides of it is kept as one, and the trunk itself stays the original's. With a mask, paint across the trunk: a change your paint touches is kept, and a separate one just past it stays the original's. A change far from your mask or your marks is still left out, and so are changes scattered across the picture (foliage or gravel redrawn here and there): they are never carried along from one to the next. On Ideogram 4.5 a mask is a real mask (Ideogram paints inside it and keeps the rest, and the result is the picture's own size), and Ideogram 4.5 Precise Edit copies every pixel its edit did not touch: the lay-back then has little to do. Compare before and after With Picked take showing, press Compare in the bar above the picture, next to Edit the cut. A handle appears on the picture: on its left, the picture the step worked on; on its right, the take. Drag it across to see exactly what changed, and that nothing else did. The handle stays where you put it while you zoom and pan: zoom into a detail, then slide the handle over it. A double-click on the handle puts it back in the middle. Hover a take in the strip while Compare is on: that take is compared against the same picture. It is the slider of the Compare node, inside the editor. It is a view only: it changes nothing in the step, costs nothing, and stays on from one step to the next until you press Compare again. It is greyed in the Picture view (there is no take to compare yet) and while you edit the cut. Edit the cut The cut Brut makes is right most of the time. When it is not (the take's new sofa spills past the slab, a tone change you wanted was left out), you decide which part of the take shows. With Picked take showing, press Edit the cut in the bar above the picture. The picture under the tools is then the live result: the original, with the take wherever the cut is. Paint where the take should show; erase where the original should come back. Every mask tool works on the cut: the brush and the eraser (Alt + brush erases; Soft feathers the edge, so the take fades into the original), the lasso, the polygon, the rectangle and the color fill, Alt taking an area out. The result updates at the end of each stroke. The wand reads the take, not the original: a click picks the model's new object whole (the new sofa, and nothing around it); a right-click takes an object out. Show the cut tints it, like the mask. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y step through what you did since you opened it. Done (or Esc, another step, another take, Save, closing the editor) keeps the cut: the take is laid back again through it, free, on your machine, and its thumbnail in the strip carries a small ✎. The line over the picture then says the cut edited by hand. Reset to the automatic cut puts back the cut Brut made, at any moment: what you painted since you opened the cut is dropped (Ctrl+Z brings it back), and a cut kept earlier goes too. You stay in the cut to paint again. It is greyed only while the cut is the automatic one and nothing is painted. The cut belongs to its take: every take has its own, and a new take gets its own automatic cut. Editing the cut never touches the step's mask, so the next take is asked for the same area. The steps made after it read needs a run, since the picture they start from changed (Reset brings their takes back when nothing else changed). What you painted on those steps stays where it was. On a take refused because the model changed nothing where you asked, the cut opens on your painted mask: Done keeps the take's change inside it. A take refused because the model moved the picture has no cut (the button is greyed and says why), and so does a step with Keep the original outside the edit off: turning the switch off shows the take as made, turning it back on shows it through its cut again.

Every step runs on the node's model unless you pick its own in the editor. The node's Model, Size and Quality (and Complexity, on a model that has it) are the default for every step that did not pick its own; on a workflow card, its Model knob drives them all. In the editor, on the node's model the size is the node's: Size and Quality there set the node's own (the line under them says so) and every step on the node's model takes them; a step on a model of its own has its own size and quality. When the model runs through an aggregator key, the menus offer that route's own sizes (a setting the route lacks is greyed). While a marks step runs on the node's model, the node's menu greys the models that read no marks. Cost: one generation per step, at the model's price (a marks step on Ideogram 4.5 Precise Edit: one per mark). Picking a take, adding or removing a step, branching, laying the original back and the wand are free. Generate shows the price of what it runs before it runs (the step, and any step before it that still needs a run). ▶ on the node runs the steps that need it on the branch shown; Run on the whole graph lists them first, with the price, and asks. A step needs a run when it has no take on the picture it works on: a new step, or one whose step before it now hands on another take (you picked another one there). The step list says needs a run on those steps, and Generate counts them in its price. Rarely, Generate finds an older result no longer holds as you press it: nothing runs, and the button shows the new price. A step with a picked take keeps it whatever you change on it afterwards: its mask or marks, its prompt (typed or wired), its model, Size or Quality, a reference picture wired or removed, the Elements line of the node's picture, the name of a picture its prompt names with @. The change goes into the step's next take: ↻ New take in the editor (or ↻ on the node's title bar, for the step it shows) makes it, with its price on the button. ▶ on the node replays the picked takes, free. A wired prompt belongs to the last step while that step has no text of its own: its line reads from the wire, and its field shows the wired text. When you move on to another step, the step keeps the wired text as its own, and its take with it; from then on it follows its own text, not the wire. A changed wired text, like a step's own text, goes into that step's next take. A step's prompt and a mark's note may name the node's pictures with their @name (the legend under the inlets): @chair is the reference picture, and the name of the node's picture means the picture that step works on (the take of the step before it). A mask or marks belong to the picture they were drawn on.
