They still fit another take of the step before at the same size when both takes keep the original outside the edit (they then share the original's framing); on any other picture (the node's own picture changed, a take of another size, or a take as the model made it, which can sit a few pixels off) the step asks you to draw them again and sends nothing. The editor shows them only where they would be sent: the others stay on the step, hidden, until you draw on that picture, which replaces them. A step keeps the picture's own shape (on Gemini, the closest shape the model offers), whatever the reference pictures look like. Masks, marks and takes are not saved into library items (they belong to your pictures); the steps and their prompts are. If you reach Nano Banana through fal.ai or Replicate instead of your Google key, masks still steer the edit. Masks on GPT Image need your own OpenAI key. Reference pictures go through the same content filters as everything else: a photo of a real person can trigger a Gemini safety refusal; the node shows it. Swap the reference.

A generative edit redraws the whole picture. Even when the result has the same size as the input, everything in it has moved a little (a few pixels) and has been re-rendered in detail, with small tone shifts on top. On Image → Image and Compose, 🗇 Reconcile with input under the result gives you the picture you actually wanted: the original, pixel for pixel, with only the edits in it. (Adjust does this by itself at every step: see Keep the original outside the edit.) One click spawns a Layers node, already set up and composited: The original is the base. Everything the edit did not touch stays the original's own pixels. On Compose the original is the scene; the references are not part of the stack. The result sits on top, lined up with the original, so an edit meets its surroundings without a step. The layer's row says aligned. A mask shows only what changed: the new object, the opened door, with a little room for a shadow. On these two nodes nothing points at where the change goes, so every change shows, the model's stray differences included (a hedge re-rendered, a facade tinted); paint the mask black where you want the original back. Reconcile with input: the Layers node opens with the original as base, the result aligned on top and masked to the two edits; a brush stroke reveals a little more Then the Layers editor opens on that mask, an ordinary one: paint white to show more of the edit (a longer shadow, a reflection), black to give an area back to the original. ✓ Use this stack composites again, free. The node's own result is not changed. The aligned picture is a separate file that only the Layers node uses; anything else wired to the edit node keeps receiving the model's picture as it came. Free and local. No provider is called; it takes a few seconds. The picture comes out at the original's size. If the model returned another size (Nano Banana at 2K on a smaller input, say), the result is fitted to the original first. When the two pictures can't be lined up (they have little in common), the result stays as it is and Activity says so; when no change shows, the mask starts empty and you paint it. The button shows once the node has a result and an original wired in. An Image → Image node run with nothing wired (a text-to-image render) has nothing to reconcile with, so it shows none.

Photoshop-style compositing, local and free — the node never calls a provider. A layer that carries transparency (a cutout from Ideogram 4.0 Transparent, any PNG with alpha) shows the stack below through its transparent pixels, with or without a mask. Wire two or more images in (the bottom wire is the base), then open 🗇 Edit layers & masks. The layer tray speaks Photoshop: A layer has no mask until you add one — ＋ mask on its row (click = white, reveal-all; Alt+click = black, hide-all). The brush paints the mask: white reveals, black hides — the dual swatch shows both colors (active one outlined), X swaps, D goes back to white. Alt+Backspace (or Shift+Backspace) fills the whole mask with the selected color, Ctrl+Backspace with the other one — Photoshop's foreground / background pair. Brush opacity is per-stroke (1–100%): overlapping segments inside one stroke never build up. Set it with the slider or digit keys — 5 = 50%, 1 then 2 quickly = 12%, 0 = 100%. (This is the stroke's opacity; the layer's own is on its row, below.) Alt + right-drag adjusts the brush — horizontal = size, vertical = softness — with the cursor pinned in place while you drag (like Photoshop); [ and ] step the size. Size, softness and opacity all have sliders too, and the live brush cursor shows the soft edge as a dashed ring. Shift+click on the image draws a straight stroke from the last stroke's end; Alt+click picks the mask's level under the cursor (white or black) as the paint color. Each row: eye toggle (Alt+click = solo — hides the others; again restores), layer thumbnail, B&W mask chip — Shift+click (or Tab+click / right-click) the chip to disable the mask (red ✕, layer shows fully), Alt+click to view the mask full-frame, Ctrl+I inverts the selected mask — and the layer name (double-click to rename). Below: the layer's opacity (0–100 %: the layer shows through, so you can see what is underneath — the final composite applies it exactly the same way), feather, invert, remove mask. Drag rows to reorder; the tray under the stack duplicates (Ctrl+J), deletes (duplicates) and moves the selected layer. Undo inside the editor: Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z) and the ↶ ↷ buttons in the tools bar step through strokes, fills, masks added or removed, layer settings and order — one step per slider drag or row drag. The canvas' own undo never fires while the editor is open. ? opens the full shortcut table. Pen pressure (Wacom & co) scales the stroke width automatically. Wheel zooms (past ~1.5× the preview switches to full native resolution), middle-drag pans. Why it matters beyond convenience: generative edits keep "everything else unchanged" only approximately — the whole frame regenerates and untouched regions drift subtly. Layers clamps every unpainted region back to the source pixels. Stack the original under a generation, mask in just the part you wanted changed, and the deliverable is pixel-faithful everywhere else. Paint the original back wherever the model overreached, feathered, local and free Notes: A layer tagged aligned (the result layer of Reconcile with input) stays lined up with the base as long as that base is the bottom of the stack. The base defines the canvas. A layer of another size auto-fits: scaled to cover and center-cropped — never distorted (the editor labels it "auto-fit"). This is the common case: a 4K generation never exactly matches its source's dimensions. Masks stay strict: an outdated mask stops the run with a clear message, never applies misaligned. Masks remember which image they belong to. If an upstream node re-generates (new output), the run stops with a clear message instead of silently applying or dropping an outdated mask — reopen the editor to repaint. ✓ Use this stack composites right away: the node's face shows the result the moment the editor closes — there is no ▶ on a Layers node (nothing upstream is run or re-billed; a whole-graph ▶ Run still passes through it for free). The composite is kept like any node output, and re-runs are free anyway. Layers or Sketchpad? Layers reconciles finished images (masks between versions, after the generation). The Sketchpad makes an image by hand to generate from (draw, place, arrange, before the generation). The other way round: Decompose result… Once the node has a result, the button under it sends that flat picture to Seedream 5.0, which splits it into a base and up to 16 layers with transparency, landed as a new Sketchpad next to the node. It is the one paid action here (the price is shown first) and needs your own BytePlus key; without it the button is greyed and says why. The same action sits on every picture's right-click menu.

Blend a scene with one or more reference images. Wire the base image into scene, the sources you want to pull from into reference, and a prompt describing the blend. Compose is handy for dropping entourage, materials or mood from references into a render. The legend under the inlets lists the scene first, then each reference with the @name it answers to (put @armchair by the window); the names follow the Image In. Scene, reference and prompt in; the reference rendered into the scene, not pasted It is also the house tool for grade transfer: scene = your shot, reference = the image whose look you want, prompt = the built-in Grade match preset (in the Prompt node's Presets menu) — the palette, tones and mood carry over while the architecture stays untouched. This is the recommended finishing pass after a Multi-Shot exploration. The same pass can borrow the reference's camera too: the Grade & camera match preset asks for its "filmic point of view" as well, and the shot is reframed to the reference's way of seeing — angle, symmetry, distance — while the building stays yours. For example, a daytime pool shot became a frontal mirror composition in one call. When only part of the scene should take the blend, 🗇 Reconcile with input under the result stacks the scene under the result and masks the result to what changed; paint the mask to keep the rest of the scene exactly as it was (Reconcile with input). One model on this node works without a prompt: Ideogram 4.5 Replace Background rebuilds the scene's background as the setting shown in the reference photo, keeps the people in the scene and leaves out the people in the reference, and returns the scene at its own size. Wire the picture to scene and a photo of the new setting to reference; the node says it reads no prompt. $0.22 per picture. References that come from an element of your vault are named in the prompt (the scene first, then the references, each element with its line); the ✦ line on the face says which, untick to send them bare.

The menu always lists the current models, each with its default settings. Cheapest-to-richest on Gemini: Nano Banana 2 Lite ($0.03, text-to-image only: it can't edit) → Nano Banana 2.1 ($0.034 at 1K, up to 4K, edits and up to 14 references) → Nano Banana Pro (up to 4K). Nano Banana 2 is still on the menu, deprecated by Google with no shutdown date yet; Nano Banana 2.1 replaces it. For edits, the original Nano Banana (~$0.04) is still the cheapest and stays on the edit menus. On the BytePlus key, Seedream 5.0 undercuts all of them: Flash at $0.018 per image for exploration, Pro at $0.045 (2K $0.09) for photoreal keepers, Lite at $0.035 up to 4K. A text-to-image picture of people from any of the three (Pro, Flash or Lite, the whole picture) is accepted by Seedance as a start frame or reference; Seedream edits and crops are refused. On a Black Forest Labs key, FLUX 3 Image Klein is the cheapest of all ($0.009 at 1K, $0.014 at 2K) for many quick tries, and FLUX 3 Image the richer one that can look a real building or product up on the web before it draws. On an Ideogram key, Ideogram 4.5 is the pick for lettering and layout, Ideogram 4.5 Precise Edit for a correction that must leave the rest of the picture exactly as it was, and Ideogram 4.5 Replace Background (Compose, no prompt) to put a picture's subject in another setting. See Providers for the full list and billing notes.
→ Multi-Shot & boards — explore many viewpoints at once.

Compose before you generate. The Sketchpad is a simple painter on a fixed canvas: brush strokes, wired images placed as movable layers, generation layers that render your marks in place, one stack. It flattens locally, for free, into the raster the generators consume. In the node browser it wears a free · $ chip: drawing, placing and flattening cost nothing, the generation layers are the paid part, and only when you ask for one. Typical use: block massing or a silhouette over a site photo, place an object where it should go, scribble the shape of a change, then wire the result into Image→Image, Compose or Adjust and let the model render what you drew. One quick stroke on the lawn of the site photo, the spark, 'a group of people playing and listening to music': a generation layer renders them in place; the layer's mask painted white shows the whole group
images (in): any number of images. They do not flow through by themselves: they appear in the editor's tray, and you drop the ones you want in as layers. image (out): the flattened canvas as a PNG.

The first wired image sets the canvas size. With nothing wired, pick a preset on the node (1K or 2K in 1:1, 16:9, 9:16, 4:3, 3:4). Once a sketch exists the size is locked; ✕ start over on the node clears the sketch and unlocks the choice. The canvas select (top of the right column) is what the flattened image shows wherever nothing covers it: white or black paper, or transparent for a PNG with alpha. With a wired photo as the bottom layer you never see it; erase a hole in that photo, or start from a blank canvas, and you do.

The tools sit in a rail on the left of the canvas, Photoshop-style; the bar above the canvas shows only the active tool's properties. Hover a tool for its shortcuts. The right column starts with the canvas select and the canvas size. Color works like Photoshop: a foreground / background pair in the properties bar (the brush paints the foreground; click the back square or press X to swap, D resets to black over white), an HSB panel at the top of the right column (the field is hue across and brightness down at the current saturation; H, S and B sliders with numbers), and a recent colors strip that fills with every color you paint or pick, kept per device. Brushes: six tips sit next to the color pair when the brush or eraser is active, each with a stroke preview. Hard round (the default, pressure drives the width), soft round, pencil (thin and grainy, a light touch stays faint), marker (a flat chisel that turns with the stroke: thin one way, wide the other, one width regardless of pressure), hard square and soft square. Picking a tip sets the softness slider and the two pressure boxes (size, opacity) to the tip's defaults; all three stay yours to override, so a soft round can drive opacity, or a pencil can keep one width. A mouse always paints at full pressure. The eraser uses the same tip. Your last pick is remembered on this device. Brush (B) and eraser (E) paint on paint layers. Size, softness and per-stroke opacity have sliders (while you drag one, the brush circle shows at the center of the canvas so you see the change), Alt + right-drag adjusts the brush like in Photoshop (horizontal = size, vertical = softness), with a Diameter / Hardness / Opacity readout beside the circles (solid = size, dashed = softness extent). Softness behaves like Photoshop's hardness: the solid circle is where a soft tip paints at half strength, and the paint fades smoothly out to the dashed one (twice the size at 100 % softness); a soft stroke spaces its dabs a little wider, as Photoshop does, so its edge stays soft along the stroke. With a mouse the cursor stays pinned; with a pen hold Alt, press the barrel button and drag (tip first then barrel, or barrel first, both work), the pen simply follows and the Windows press-and-hold ring is harmless, [ ] change the size, digit keys set opacity (5 = 50 %, 1 then 2 quickly = 12 %, 0 = 100 %). Pen pressure (Wacom & co) scales the stroke width, smoothly through curves. After each stroke a small readout next to the pressure boxes says what arrived: pen · 78 % (pointer type and peak pressure) or mouse · no pressure. The second one means the tablet driver is sending mouse events, not pen events: enable Windows Ink for Brut in the tablet driver (Wacom: the app's Mapping tab) and pressure comes through. Shift+click draws a straight stroke from where the last stroke ended: click once for a dot, Shift+click elsewhere for the line. Eyedropper (I), or Alt held in any tool: press on the canvas to sample the composite, a swatch with the hex value rides the pointer, drag to hunt the exact pixel, release to pick it. Bucket fill (G): click a region to flood it with the current color at the stroke opacity. The tolerance slider widens what counts as the same color; sample all layers (default) reads the whole composite so you can fill inside the lines of a placed photo, unticked it reads the active layer alone. Transform (T, Ctrl+T, or V) shows handles on the selected layer: drag anywhere to move, drag a corner square to scale about the center (Shift+corner scales width and height independently), drag the stem handle above the top edge to rotate (Shift snaps to 15°). Works on paint layers too. Selections: the marquee (M) drags a rectangle, the ellipse (Shift+M cycles between the two) an ellipse, the lasso (L) a freehand shape, the polygonal lasso (P) a shape with straight sides, one click per corner. Shift at the start of a drag adds to the selection, Alt at the start subtracts, a plain drag replaces it, a plain click deselects. Pressed after the drag started, Shift constrains the marquee to a square or the ellipse to a circle and Alt grows the shape from the point you started at, like Photoshop. With the polygonal lasso, close the shape by clicking its first corner again (a dashed ring shows there, lit when the pointer is close enough), by double-clicking, or with Enter; hold Shift (add) or Alt (subtract) as you close it, not at the first click. While the shape is open, Backspace, Delete or Ctrl+Z takes the last corner back and Esc cancels it, without closing the editor; a click is always a corner, never a deselect. Zoom and pan freely between clicks. Ctrl+A selects everything, Ctrl+D nothing, Ctrl+Shift+I inverts. Ctrl+click a layer's thumbnail selects its painted pixels, like Photoshop (Ctrl+Shift+click adds them, Ctrl+Alt+click subtracts); Ctrl+click a mask chip selects the mask's white. Handy to recolor a shape: Ctrl+click the thumb, then Alt+Backspace. While a selection exists the brush, eraser and bucket only touch the inside. Ctrl+C copies the selected pixels of the active paint layer, Ctrl+X cuts them, Delete clears them, Ctrl+V pastes the copy as a new paint layer in place, with the Transform tool ready to move it. Selections live in the editor session only. Alt+Backspace fills with the foreground color, Ctrl+Backspace with the background color, like Photoshop: the active paint layer's pixels, or its mask when the mask chip is active (the color's grey level: white reveals, black hides). A selection confines the fill. One undo step. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo inside the editor (also the two arrows at the bottom of the rail): strokes, transforms, layer changes, background, and selections. Each selection change is a step of its own (a shape added or subtracted, a deselecting click, Ctrl+D, an inverse), in the same history as your strokes, so Ctrl+Z after a wrong lasso takes back that lasso and leaves the layers alone. A layer made into a selection comes off in one Ctrl+Z with its selection back. The stack resets when you close the editor. Layers (right): the layer opacity slider at the top acts on the selected layer. Below it, the stack, top first, the only part of the column that scrolls. Eye toggles visibility, Alt+eye solos a layer (Alt+eye again restores what was shown), + (or Ctrl+Shift+N) adds an empty paint layer right above the active one (inside its group if it has one; on top when nothing is selected), ↑ ↓ reorder, 🗑 deletes (a group takes its children along). Drag a row to move it in the stack: the row lifts and a blue line shows where it will land; nothing moves until you release, and names never change. The 🗑 removes every selected layer. Double-click a name to rename it; right-click a row for a color label (Photoshop's eleven, shown as a colored edge, purely for organization) plus hide, rename and group. Layer masks, on paint layers, image layers and groups, exactly like Photoshop: the mask button in the tray (or the row menu) adds one, white = shows (Alt on the button adds a hide-all mask). The mask chip appears right of the layer thumbnail. Click the layer (name or thumbnail) to paint its pixels, click the chip to paint its mask; the active element carries the blue outline. Ctrl+I inverts the mask, Shift+click the chip disables it, Alt+click the chip views it white on black. While the mask is the target the color panel switches to greys (a black-to-white ramp, hue and saturation dimmed, brightness is the level, five grey swatches): white reveals, black hides, a grey reveals partially (so D then X flip between the two), the eraser hides, the bucket follows the same rule, and pressure, softness and selections apply as usual. With the mask active, the 🗑 deletes the mask and leaves the layer; select the layer itself to delete the layer. A group's mask applies to everything inside it as one. Masks move with their layer and are stored as files like paint layers; the row menu also offers reveal all, hide all, disable and remove. Groups: Ctrl+click rows to select several, Ctrl+G (or the folder button in the tray) folds them into a group (one level of folders, like a sketch needs), Ctrl+Shift+G dissolves the selected group. The folder row hides or shows its children as one, folds with the chevron, and moves as a block. Dragging a layer onto a group's child puts it in the group, dragging it onto a top-level layer takes it out. Groups are organization only: the flattened image is the same with or without them. Under the stack, the wired images tray: click one to add it as a layer (it lands fitted and centered; add it twice for two copies). Wheel zooms (past 1.5× the preview switches to full native resolution), middle-drag pans. ? (or the keyboard button at the bottom of the rail) shows the full shortcut table inside the editor. ✓ Use this sketch saves the painted layers and merges the stack, and puts the result on the node: the image plug is live immediately. The node has no ▶ of its own: it is the door to the editor, and any run downstream re-uses the flatten for free until you edit again.

The one paid thing in the Sketchpad, and the reason the sketch exists: a generation layer turns your marks into a photoreal render, in place, without leaving the editor. Sketch the intent on a paint layer: where the thing goes, how big, roughly what shape, which colors. A forest, a sword, a piece of cloth can never be drawn in detail, and they do not have to be. Then press the ✦ button in the layer tray (next to +): with a paint layer selected it makes a generation layer that follows that layer; with anything else selected it makes a general one that follows every painted layer below it. (Also: Ctrl+Enter, or right-click a paint layer → ✦ Generate from this layer…) The new layer lands right above, its row shows ↳ and what it follows, and the properties bar becomes the layer's own, one row: ↳ follows: one paint layer, a previous generation (iterate on a take: "make the lake frozen" over the lake you just rendered), all paint below, or whole scene below (rework): no marks at all, the flattened picture under the layer is the subject and the prompt changes it as a whole ("turn this image to winter, same character, same clothes"), generation layers included. A rework is always the whole frame, has no follow setting, and shows entirely (paint a mask if you want to keep parts of the original). Change the choice any time; the prompt: what the marks stand for ("a weathered oak bench", "a pine forest at low sun"); scope: whole frame / local. Whole frame renders the entire canvas. Local renders only a region around your marks and puts the take back in its place. This is how a 5000 px document stays a 5000 px document: nothing ever regenerates it whole, and you can edit it region by region at full production resolution. Canvases above 2048 px on the long side start in local; pick a size tier at or above the region's long side and the take lands without upscaling. The region-outline button on the bar draws the last region dashed on the canvas (off by default), and the price dialog states its size and aspect before you pay; follow: loose / balanced / close, how strictly the marks bind. Balanced (the default) makes placement, size and extent binding and leaves the outline, materials and detail to the model. Close makes the silhouette follow the painted shape. Loose treats the marks as a suggestion of placement and size; the model bar: provider, image→image model (the default is GPT Image 2.5 Flare at high), size tier, quality, the ⇄ chip when the model runs through another service such as OpenRouter, and the price of one render; the magnet switch, Line the take up with the picture, on by default (see below); ✦ Generate. The price is asked first, every time. Nothing renders on its own. The line under the canvas says where the layer stands. The model renders what your marks stand for where they are: their size, roughly their shape and colors, at the strictness you chose, in the scene's light, perspective, scale and grain, with the shadows and reflections it would really cast. The marks themselves disappear from the render. The render comes back whole-frame: the model may change what your object implies anywhere in the picture (a forest at low sun casts long shadows across the whole image). What you see of it is decided by the layer's mask, which starts around your marks with a soft edge. So by default the untouched scene stays pixel-faithful, and you paint the mask white to reveal more of the take: the long shadow, the reflection on the floor, the disturbed sand. Reveal all if the model reworked the scene well as a whole. The mask never re-renders anything: the layer holds the whole render, painting is free. The row menu offers Re-seed the mask from the sketch when you have redrawn the guide. The take lands lined up with the picture. A model redraws the whole frame, and its take comes back a few pixels off the picture it was given: shifted, sometimes very slightly stretched. Brut measures that move and undoes it before the take lands, so the generation sits exactly on your sketch and no doubled edge shows where the mask fades. It moves pixels back into place and changes nothing the model made; your mask still decides what shows. It is local and free. The magnet button on the bar is the switch: on by default and remembered by the node; off, the takes land as the model returned them. Switching it also moves the selected layer's current take. Every layer keeps both versions: right-click its row → Use the raw take, or Line the take up with the picture to go back, free and instant, nothing rendered again. When the model moved or reframed the picture too much for a reliable match (a rework that changes the view, a canvas with nothing to match yet), the take stays as it came and the row says not lined up; a layer showing its raw take by choice says raw take. A take rendered before this switch existed can be lined up from the same menu, as long as its render is in the project ledger. Generate into a selection. Nothing needs to be drawn: make a selection (marquee, ellipse, lasso or polygonal lasso, or Ctrl+A) and press ✦ (or Ctrl+Enter). The new layer says ↳ into the selection: the selection becomes its mask (with a soft edge of a few pixels), the model works from the flattened scene below it, and the prompt says what goes there ("a red sports car", "a wet cobblestone patch"). The selection itself is consumed; the layer keeps its outline, which the region-outline button on the bar shows dashed on the canvas (off by default), and re-rolls, staleness and takes work as for any generation layer. Scope defaults to local, so the model works on what you selected; switch to whole frame when the prompt names the place itself. There is no follow dial: with no marks, placement is the selection. An ellipse selection on the lawn, the spark, 'add a pond with lush vegetation': the render lands inside the selection only 🕘 takes on the bar lists every render this layer ever made, from the project ledger. Use this take brings any of them back as the layer's raster, fitted into the region it was rendered for and lined up with the picture (when the switch is on), your mask kept, free; it shows as stale if the sketch or the prompt changed since. A re-roll is never destructive. The node face counts stale generation layers. The row says where the layer stands: not rendered, stale (the sketch below it, the prompt or the model changed since the take), done, rendering…, or failed with the provider's reason, followed by not lined up or raw take when the take does not sit lined up with the picture (hover the row for the reason). A stale layer keeps showing its last take until you generate again; a take that still matches is free (Generate does nothing new). ↻ next to Generate asks for a fresh take of the same sketch and prompt, paying again. Every render is a normal generation on the ledger, with the layer named on the row. A rendered layer behaves like an image layer: eye, opacity, a mask you can paint, Transform. Its take is stored on the node the moment it lands, so closing the editor with Cancel never loses a paid render; ✓ Use this sketch flattens the stack with the generation layers in place. While a layer renders, its row carries the same travelling light as a running node on the canvas. A new Sketchpad opens with the first wired image already placed as the bottom layer and an empty paint layer selected, so you can draw right away.
From a flat picture: Decompose into layers

A Sketchpad can also start from a finished image. Right-click any picture → Decompose into layers… sends it to Seedream 5.0 (Flash or Pro, on your own BytePlus key), which splits it into a base (the scene with the elements lifted out and the gaps filled in) and up to 16 layers with transparency. Brut lands them as a new Sketchpad beside the picture: the base at the bottom, at the canvas size; every layer above it in the model's stacking order, scaled into its place in the picture and named by the model ("sky", "pavilion", "foreground trees"). Hover a name for the model's description of it; the original on top, hidden: click its eye to compare the recomposed stack with what you started from, or mask it to paint the original back. They are ordinary image layers: move, scale and rotate them with Transform, hide them, give them masks, paint between them, add a generation layer over the stack, and Export PSD carries all of it to Photoshop. The node shows the recomposed picture straight away, and its image plug is live. The model lifts each element out whole (a tree that stood behind a hedge can come back with its full trunk): a layer mask hides what should stay behind. Find in ledger on the node's preview shows the paid run. It is one paid call, and the price is asked first: a form for the model, the size and (optionally) what to separate, then the price dialog with the ceiling. The models, the rates and the size rule are on the Seedream page. Without the BytePlus key the menu item stays greyed with the reason. Right-click a render, Decompose into layers: the price, then a Sketchpad with the pergola, the bench, the building and each tree as its own layer
Export PSD, for the old schoolers

Export PSD in the editor's footer, or right-click the node's preview → Export PSD…, writes a Photoshop file into the project's outputs/exports folder (no dialog; Explorer shows it). Every layer goes in, hidden ones included: paint, placed images and generation takes as raster layers at their placement (moves, scales and rotations baked), layer masks as Photoshop layer masks (feather and invert baked, since PSD has no such switches), groups as folders with their own masks, names, opacity, visibility and color labels. The merged image is the flatten you see on the node. Photoshop, Affinity, Krita and GIMP open it. The export is local and free.

Painting, layers and the flatten are local and free: no provider call, no ledger row. Only a generation layer's render is a paid call, always behind the price gate. Paint layers, masks and renders are stored as files in the project's outputs, so the graph stays small and a .brutpack or a project on a NAS carries the sketch along. Wired images enter as references to their file, not copies. If an upstream node regenerates, the layer keeps pointing at the file it was placed from; add the new image from the tray when you want it. Sketchpad or Layers? Sketchpad makes an image by hand (draw, place, arrange) to generate from. Layers reconciles finished images by painting clipping masks between versions. Use Sketchpad before the generation, Layers after it.

Where Brut stops being a one-image-at-a-time tool. Multi-Shot explores a scene from many angles at once; the boards are the surfaces where you review, curate and route the results. Every board shares one review gesture: hover a tile and click its 🔍 to open the lightbox — the image fitted to your screen, wheel-zoom into the pixels, and ←/→ (or the on-screen arrows) paging through the whole board like a classical gallery. Clicking the image itself does nothing (no accidental tabs while panning the canvas); the full-resolution files live in the project's output folder.

A POV/composition explorer. Wire your base image(s) into a Multi-Shot node, pick an exploration scenario and a shot count, and a planner (Gemini by default) writes N distinct shot prompts from your base images. Then N image-to-image jobs fill a contact sheet on a resizable node, several render at once. One scene, one scenario, Run: the contact sheet fills in as the shots land in parallel Scenarios: Editorial, Ballsy, Morning → Evening, Four Seasons, Dutch Masters, Product and Product · Lifestyle (below), the five Lifestyle scenarios (Lifestyle, Lifestyle · Home, Lifestyle · Hospitality, Lifestyle · Work, Lifestyle · Public: below), and a Custom scenario that takes its brief from the node's Notes field. (Older scenarios are retired: the climate ones, Cold North, Mediterranean and Desert, whose weather registers now live as V2 deck cards, and Clichés. A saved graph that used one keeps working and shows it as retired.) Notes live on the node — a text box right under the scenario picker steers the planner on any scenario, and for Custom it is the brief. Wired text (a Prompt or Refine node into the notes input) still works and both flow to the planner — wire when the text has a life of its own, type when it's a one-off. Pair Custom with the Scenario maker Refine preset for a strong brief. 💾 Save as preset appears under non-empty notes — it saves the text as a prompt preset in the global library, loadable from any Prompt node in any project. It works on any subject, not only buildings. The planner first reads what your pictures show (a building, an interior, a landscape, a product, a fashion or portrait shoot) and says so in the Activity panel. Every shot keeps that subject as it is, keeps the background at its true size and distance, and never adds buildings the pictures don't show. A building seen far off in one picture stays far off. On a fashion or portrait shoot the people are the subject of every frame. Nodes made before this rule keep the old one until you choose otherwise, so saved sheets stay as they are and nothing is planned again on its own. The old rule assumed a building and could put one into pictures that had none. Such a node shows a line, Newer planner rules, with a Use them button; its next run plans the shots again (the run tells you what that costs first). Switching a V1 node to V2 takes the new rules too. Multi-Shot explores points of view — the look comes after. For grade/style transfer, don't feed a look reference into the exploration (feeding a look into the exploration pulls every composition toward it and makes sheets repetitive). Instead, run the shots you keep through a Compose node: scene = the shot, reference = the look image, prompt = the built-in Grade match preset. You pay once per keeper instead of per exploration, and 1-to-1 transfer is far stronger. The shot list is kept between runs, so unchanged shots aren't re-planned or re-paid. 🎲 rolls a new shot list. Per-tile controls — ↻ re-rolls one tile (only that tile re-pays; during a run, ↻ on any tile queues it and the node runs once more right after, so several tiles can be re-rolled at once), ✓ / ✗ mark keepers and misses, 🕘 re-pins a past result for that specific tile. Curation flows downstream — ✓ shots flow out the main port (or all non-✗ if none are ticked), taking effect on the next run (free). The contact sheet uses a tidy, fixed column count from the shot count (≤4 → 2×2, ≤9 → 3-wide, else 4-wide), so it stays neat at any node size. The node's corner grip sets its width only: the height always follows the content — the Notes box (eight lines minimum, drag its own corner for more), the controls and the sheet's rows of squares — so the tiles are never squashed. The eye button beside New shot list folds the sheet away (the shots are kept, the node shrinks to its controls; the Shot Board is the place to review them large).

New Multi-Shot nodes plan with V2; a small V1/V2 rollout next to the title switches generations (graphs made before V2 keep V1). V2 keeps your sheets from repeating the same ideas job after job — the same prop, the same weather trick: The card deck. Every plan draws a hand of ingredients from the scenario's pools (a light register, a life event, a prop domain, …) for the set to use. The hand is shown as chips on the node before you ever run — visible surprise — and the little 🎲 beside the chips redraws it without starting a run. Pick your hand. Random is the default, but the ✎ beside the chips opens the picker: one row per pool, each set to random or a card of your choice. Pinned cards always ride the hand (shown as accent chips; wild cards are pickable at any dial level), the Surprise dial fills the remaining slots randomly, and 🎲 redraws only those. Pin everything — or pin on Classic, which draws nothing on its own — and the hand is fully yours. Picks belong to their scenario's deck, so switching scenario clears them. The Surprise dial. Classic (no cards: the scenario's brief alone) · Fresh (the default hand) · Crazy (a bigger hand including each pool's wild cards, plus a push toward the never-published). Avoid recent motifs (off by default). Brut remembers the distinctive ideas of your recent plans, per scenario and across all projects. Tick the box and new plans steer away from them — the direct cure for "the same idea on every job". The memory ages out, so retired classics eventually return. The Surprise dial deals cards, 🎲 redraws the random slots, ✎ pins the ones you want to keep V2 also makes the planner model selectable — the text model that writes the shot list (the node's Provider/Model picks stay the image model that renders them). The default is Gemini 3.8 Flash; different planners have different instincts, which is itself a variety lever, and models with a reasoning dial expose it here too. Nothing is rendered until the shot list is valid: a planner reply that can't be read stops the run with a clear message before any image is paid for. Planning calls cost cents.
Multi-Shot › Product: one object, many settings

Wire the pictures of one object (a chair, a lamp, a watch, a shelf, a bag, a device) and pick Product. The planner reads what the object is and plans a presentation set: a hero frame (the product whole, three-quarter, the light shaping it), a straight-on frame on a plain ground, close details of a material or a joint, the product in use at human scale, and at least two different settings it names concretely (a studio sweep, a living room, a terrace, a workshop bench, a shop display). The product stays exactly what your pictures show, at its true size; the setting changes from frame to frame, which is the point of the set. The planner never invents a side or a detail your pictures do not show: a frame that would need the hidden side keeps it turned away or out of frame. Several pictures of the product (the front, the back, a detail) give it more to work with. The Surprise dial deals cards here as on the other scenarios. The pools are the setting (a studio sweep, at home, outdoors, in the shop, on the maker's bench), the light (window light, hard sun, one soft source, a low warm lamp), the framing (hero three-quarter, straight on, macro detail, in use), the people (nobody, hands only, one person using it) and the register (catalogue, editorial, documentary). ✎ pins the ones you want. Product · Lifestyle: the product in a real place, used by real people. Pick it and the node grows a product inlet: wire the object's pictures there (one or several sides of it) and the pictures of the place on place (the base inlet, renamed). The planner reads both, proposes the one or two people who would really use this product in this place (the household of a home, a guest and a waiter at a hotel, a maker at a bench), and the run stops on Meet the cast like every lifestyle scenario. Each shot then shows the product in use or in place at its true size, handled or approached by someone from the cast: a hero frame with the product whole in the place, close frames of it in hands, a wide frame where it is small and the place tells the scale, a detail of its material beside something of the place. The product stays exactly as your pictures show it, the place as your pictures show it, and the people as their sheets show them. The photographer dial and the angle work as on the other lifestyle scenarios. A set with the product alone, in settings the planner names, is the plain Product scenario.
Multi-Shot › Lifestyle scenarios: people, cast first

Five scenarios where people are the subject, with the place: the set shows the place as it is lived. They plan on V2. Lifestyle: the general one. The planner decides who appears from what it reads: a few recurring people, the people passing through, or both. Lifestyle · Home: one household across the whole set, chosen to fit the place (a couple and a child in a family house, a retired couple in a single-storey villa, one young professional in a city flat). The developer's sale: a week of their life here. Lifestyle · Hospitality: the same few staff throughout, a different guest party in each frame. Arrival, breakfast, dinner service, turndown, the night shift, wherever the pictures show the place for it. Lifestyle · Work: an office, a studio, a campus, a workshop. A few recurring people (the team this place would really hold), colleagues, visitors and couriers passing through once, from the morning arrival to the end of the day. Lifestyle · Public: a plaza, a park, a school, a museum, a station, a shop. The public at its real density for the hour, every age this place would draw, and the few people who belong here (a guard, a vendor, a teacher) recurring where the place has them. The stock moments of a brochure (the golden-hour toast, laughter on the sofa, the child running on the lawn) are left out of every lifestyle set: a meal, a coffee, an arrival are welcome when this place gives them a reason. The Surprise dial picks the photographer. On these scenarios the dial deals no cards; it chooses who takes the pictures, and the cast stays the same whatever you pick: Classic: a precise, classical photographer. Calm, exact frames: the camera level, the verticals straight, natural light at its best hour, the people in their real number and placed with care. Elegant, no tricks. Fresh: an avant-garde photographer. The set follows an angle read from your pictures (the night porter's round, the life of the place seen from under the deck) as a thread, with unexpected vantages inside the views your pictures cover and light used as a subject. Crazy: a restless young photographer. A bolder angle and daring frames (down from a gallery a picture shows, flash at dusk, motion blur, hard crops), still real photographs: true scale, nothing surreal. On Fresh and Crazy the people stay recognizable in most frames; a back or a silhouette appears at most once in a set. Every photographer shoots a photo story. Whichever one you pick, the set is planned like a reportage, not an architecture shoot: every frame has a moment (something happening between people, or between a person and the place), a point of view often close to the people, a foreground that gives the frame depth, lenses with a photographic look, light with direction. The distances vary across the set, from a close frame to a wide one where the people are small. The people come in their real number: the planner writes how many are in each frame, as the hour and the program would really bring them (a restaurant at dinner service is mostly full, a station at the morning peak holds dozens), and an almost empty frame says why. A person far from the camera stays small, their face unread. Place pictures per shot. Every shot is sent with the character sheets of the people in it, then the pictures of the place. The planner ranks the place pictures for each shot (the one the shot stands in first), and the shot carries as many as the image model takes: some models take fewer pictures in a request than others (Ideogram 4.5 takes five in all, Seedream and FLUX 3 ten, Nano Banana 2.1 fourteen, GPT Image 2.5 sixteen), and a frame goes out with the closest ones when they do not all fit. The node's Place pictures per shot select sets a count of your own, all, the closest 3 or the closest 5: in our tests fewer pictures held a person better and let the building drift more, so measure on your set. The shot list in the Activity panel says which pictures each frame went with when the list was cut. Pictures at 4K max. A Multi-Shot node sends copies of its pictures resized to 4096 px on their long side when they are larger (a 5000 by 4000 render becomes 4096 by 3277); the originals stay on disk, in the ledger and in History, and a picture within the cap goes as it is. This lets every model take the same set (Seedream takes a request up to 64 MB; FLUX 3 takes a picture up to 16 megapixels and gets a 16-megapixel copy of a larger one), and the models we tried read a 4K copy like the original. Untick the box under the dial to send the originals; nodes made before this box keep sending their originals until it is ticked. The box applies to this node only: Adjust, Layers and Conform always work on the picture's own pixels. The frames stay on your pictures. Your pictures are the only truth the image model has about the place, so every frame is shot from a view they cover: the camera moves a few steps, up or down, changes its lens or its subject, and the people and the moment make the frame new. A side, a room or a view no picture shows is not asked for; at most one frame per set leaves the covered views, and then as a close frame where the place is a fragment around the people. Dusk and night frames are kept to two per set, each from a view a picture covers closely, so the place is relit rather than redrawn. With a single picture, every frame is that view at another distance, height or crop, with another moment in it: more pictures of the place give the set more views. In our tests every frame that held the building was shot from a view a picture covered, and every reinvented building came from a view no picture showed or from a dusk relight. ✎ still pins a card from the scenario's deck when you want one (a lazy Sunday, a winter afternoon). The angle. Once the cast is approved, the planner reads your pictures and the cast and proposes three angles for Fresh and three for Crazy (one short call, a few cents, made once for both). An angle comes from what is done at this place and by whom (the program, the roles, the routines, the features only this place has), never from a device laid over it (a shadow clock, a day told by the light). Brut draws one, so the set does not always start from the planner's first idea. On the run that proposes them, the run stops on Pick the angle: the three angles with their ideas, the drawn one marked; pick one, or ↻ Propose others for three new ones, then Plan the set on this angle. Stop ends the run there with nothing more spent; the proposals stay on the node, and the next run plans on the one the Angle line shows without asking. The angle is a thread through the set: it shapes about half the frames and leaves the others free, so a set still shows different people, situations and parts of the place. The Angle line on the node shows it with its idea written under it: pick another of the three from the list, 🎲 moves to the next one, ↻ asks for three new ones right away. With the cast approved and no angles yet, ↻ Propose angles reads them before any shot, so you can choose first. Switching the dial between Classic, Fresh and Crazy plans the shots again for the same people; no new casting, no new sheets. The angles are proposed again when the pictures, the notes or the cast change. How a lifestyle run goes. The planner reads the place first and proposes the cast: each person gets a role here ("the mother", "the night porter"), never a name, with their sex, age, build and what their role makes them wear. Brut then draws each recurring person's face, hair color, haircut and palette from the same lists as the Character Lab card, so two roles never come out as the same person: a household shares one heritage and its children take after a parent. Then the run stops on "Meet the cast" before any shot is planned: One card per person. Edit the role, the age, the build, the clothes; change the heritage, the face, the hair or the palette from their lists, or 🎲 Draw again for a new face, hair and palette (the role and age stay). ✕ drops someone, + Add a person adds one, and a person can be set to appears once: a passing guest stays a few words in their one shot, with no face to draw and no sheet (set them back to recurs to give them both). Make the sheets. Every recurring person needs a character sheet before the shots: one 16:9 picture of them (a bust and four full-body views) made with the Character Lab's own recipe and model (GPT Image 2.5 Flare at 4K, xhigh: about $0.18 a sheet). Click a sheet to see it large, then ←/→ through the whole cast. ↻ New take makes another take of the same person. From a file… or Elements… uses a picture you already have instead (a sheet from the Character Lab, a photo). The sheet's text is written by Gemini; when Gemini declines to describe a person (it does for some children), the scenario's planner writes that sheet instead, and the Activity panel says so. If both decline, the card says what to change: the clothes or the build, a new draw, or a picture of your own. Approve and the shots are planned for this cast (on Fresh and Crazy, after the angle); each shot is sent with the sheets of the people in it only, so the same people come back in every frame. Stop ends the run there: nothing is planned or spent. A run whose cast is unchanged goes on without asking; edit the cast and the next run asks again. Save to Elements. A person with a sheet has a Save to Elements button on their card, and the footer saves everyone at once: each becomes a cast element in your Elements vault (the sheet as its picture, the role as its name, the one-line description as its descriptor), marked ✓ in Elements on the card. Bring them back into another set from the Elements… button on a card, or wire them onto the cast inlet from the Elements panel. Saving changes nothing in the cast or its approval. The cast stays on the node: wiring other pictures or changing the notes changes the shots, not the people (the node says when the cast was made from other pictures). 🎲 beside the cast on the node casts again on the next run; 👥 Meet opens the cast at any time, outside a run. The people in each frame show as small labels on its tile. The cast inlet. Wire character sheets or photos into cast (a Character Lab output, an Image In, an Elements picture): those people join the cast as they are, and the planner casts the rest around them. In the Editorial Sheet workflow. The Editorial Sheet card carries the same scenarios on its Scenario knob: pick Lifestyle, Home, Hospitality, Work, Public or Product · Lifestyle and the closed card runs the whole flow. The run stops on Meet the cast exactly as on the node, and the card gains a line under its knobs: the cast with its sheets, 👥 Meet (the cast at any time, outside a run) and 🎲 (a new cast on the next run), the photographer the Surprise knob picked, and on Fresh and Crazy the Angle line with its list, 🎲 and ↻. Place pictures per shot and Pictures at 4K max are knobs on the card; the first is greyed on the editorial scenarios, where it means nothing. A cast inlet appears on the lifestyle scenarios and a product inlet on Product · Lifestyle, where the base inlet reads place; they take the same wires as the node's. The card ships with pictures at 4K max on, like a new node. Each shot on the card carries ↻ (a new take of that shot, the others kept) and 🕘 (its past takes) on hover; a Shot Board wired from sheet stays the review surface for ✓ and ✗. The planner. These scenarios plan on Claude Sonnet 5.5 at high reasoning when the node's Planner is left on its default (it read the places best in our tests; a casting call costs about two cents, a shot plan about five). A seat without access to it plans on the usual default and says so in the Activity panel. A pick of your own on the Planner select always wins. What it costs, measured. A first set of nine shots on Nano Banana Pro at 1K with three or four sheets came to about $1.80–2.00; planning again with the same cast, about $1.26. In our tests the household stayed the same people from frame to frame with sheets, and not with words alone; no sheet's grey background or pose leaked into a shot. A small detail on one side of the head (a single earring) does not carry into the shots, even from a correct sheet. Every shot carries every picture of the place, with the sheets of the people in it. In our tests the way the sheets are sent decided whether a person held: a waiter came out as himself in 4 takes of 6 after we changed it, against 1 of 6 before. Sending only the one or two place pictures a shot needed held him in 6 of 6, but the building drifted and the people grew too big for the place, so every picture rides. If a person still comes out as someone else, ↻ on that tile tries again with the same sheet.

The review surface for a Multi-Shot node. Wire the Multi-Shot shots output into a Shot Board and get a large captioned grid — the prompt under each image, ✓ / ✗ / ↻ act on the Multi-Shot node. Each tile has its own output plug so you can route one chosen shot into Compose or Image→Video. The board re-emits the curated pool from its bottom port. Tiles show each shot at its real aspect (a 9:16 batch is a column of portrait frames, never a 4:3 crop); the Multi-Shot node's own compact sheet stays square thumbnails — the board is where you judge the actual frame. Accept and reject on big tiles, then wire one shot out of its own plug into Image to Video

Makes the crew's stills pool visible. Every image you wire in becomes a numbered tile — and the tile number is the global still number the cinema agents refer to, which kills the invisible wire-order problem. The crew's stills pool made visible: the tile number is the still number the agents use ↑ / ↓ reorder (the plan refers to the stills by number, so reordering changes what a wire carries: what you see is what flows). ✕ hide a tile / ↺ restore it in place. Each tile has its own output plug, addressing one still by its board number. A name field under each tile shows the name a prompt downstream writes as @name (the picture's own name after its file, or the node that made it, until you type one; see Image In). Typing a name on a tile names the picture on the Image In that holds it; a render wired straight into the board is named on the board itself. Free and local — it's just a lens on the images you already have.

The cinema planning nodes: they read your stills and pass a plan document (a plan, passed along a text wire) toward Film Shots. Planning runs on the LLM you choose — Gemini, GPT or Claude — on your own key; on models with a reasoning dial (GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Sol / Luna, details; Claude Sonnet 5.5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 4.8 / Opus 5 / Opus 5.5, details) a Reasoning select appears — deeper thinking for harder plans, billed as part of the answer. For the end-to-end story, see the Cinema Sessions walkthrough. The chain is: stills → Director → Storyboard → Film Shots. (The original four-agent crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor — is legacy, kept at the bottom of this page.)
The Director — the whole crew in one node

One agent that plans the whole film: it analyzes your stills, writes the concept, the look and the executable shot plan, and wires straight into the Storyboard. The anchors it writes use the numbers you see on the Reference Board. The plan comes out varied: an arc across the film, framing, lens, camera height and movement changing shot to shot, and no still overused. Its dials: a Brief (what film) and a Style (what look) from the same libraries the crew uses, the shot count and runtime, a People dial (none / subtle / lively), and an Audio switch that has every clip carry a one-line ambient sound note (used only by video models that produce sound). The plan it writes also carries a concept paragraph: the film's emotional tone, arc, lighting mood and pacing, readable and editable in 📖 Review like everything else. Advanced dials — locked production choices. The Advanced disclosure exposes six craft dials: Camera (RED digital / ARRI / Sony Venice / Blackmagic / IMAX / 35mm / 16mm film), Lenses (clean primes / anamorphic / vintage / long-lens compression), Lighting, Composition, Emphasis and Movement (contemplative → kinetic). Each pick is binding and wins over the style where they disagree; every dial defaults to Director's choice, which adds nothing. The proof sheet is always ONE image, and it renders in the run. Running the Director renders the sheet right after the plan (the whole film as a single contact sheet, at the price on the bar) and opens the review: the sheet large, the frame chips, and your call — Take this sheet (the run goes on; a later run whose sheet is unchanged never asks again), ↻ New take (a fresh render of the same plan, paying again), ✎ Reinvent the ✗ frames (the sheet re-renders for the new plan, the review stays open), or Stop (nothing downstream runs, nothing more is spent). An unchanged plan replays its sheet, free; a render that fails offers to go on without a sheet. The sheet's shape follows its grid: ten 16:9 frames render as two columns of five on a 3:4 sheet, so every frame keeps the film's shape instead of stretching wide (an aspect you set on the bar wins). 🎬 Proof on the face still renders by hand, ⤢ Review reopens the review, 🕘 opens every sheet the film ever rendered, from the project ledger, and 📌 pins one — a pinned sheet stays the film's validated sheet (and keyframe reference) through plan edits and new takes, until unpinned, and a run never asks about a pinned sheet. Inside a closed card (the Stills → Film workflow) the same review opens over the canvas, the card carries a 🎬 Proof sheet button to reopen it and a 📖 Plan button that opens this same document review for the Director inside; the image model of the sheet and of the keyframes is pinned on the card (GPT Image 2.5 Flare, xhigh at 2K) and changed by opening it. The node's Setup, plan and Proof sheet sections all collapse to keep the card compact. Your own brief and style are wires, not notes. The node has two labeled text inlets — brief (optional) and style (optional) — made for a Prompt node (whose text is saveable as a preset, or refined through a Refine). A wired brief composes with the select: the canned entry sets the genre, your wire carries the project's specifics, and where they conflict the wire wins — the node says "⇄ wired in" under the select so the precedence is never invisible. For a fully custom film, set the select to None and let the wire direct alone. The Notes box is just notes: extra guidance, always honored, never secretly the brief. The proof sheet — see the whole film for cents. Below the plan, the Director carries the sheet's bar (pick the image model, size and quality; cheap settings are fine, this is for your eyes): ONE image generation renders the entire film as a numbered contact sheet — every frame, one shared grade — from your stills and the plan's prompts. Judge it, then ✗ the frames that fail (the chips match the sheet's number badges) and hit ✎ Reinvent — one planning call rewrites only the rejected clips with genuinely new compositions; every kept clip stays exactly as it was. The sheet re-renders for cents; loop until the film reads right. The spend ladder is the point: ~1¢ of plan → ~6¢ of proof → keyframes → clips, and you never pay the next tier until the previous one convinced you — which is why the run itself stops on the sheet and waits for your call. The validated sheet then guides the keyframes. When a Storyboard downstream generates an invented shot's keyframe, that shot's frame on the sheet guides it, while your stills keep the building true. A new sheet means the unpinned keyframes render again: what you validated is what gets produced. Frames generated separately read as one film, sheet or no sheet. (The sheet itself is never cropped into a frame: its resolution is for your eyes only.) It emits the exact same plan document as the legacy DoP chain, so everything downstream is identical: the Storyboard, keyframes, end frames, Film Shots, Review and Revise.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor

Legacy since 1.1.1. The Director plans better films than the four-agent chain. The crew nodes are therefore hidden from the node browser — but they remain fully functional: every saved graph that uses them keeps loading and running, Review/Revise included. New films should start from the Director (or the Cinema Director library template).
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Scenarist

Writes the treatment — the story and beat structure — from your stills. You pick a brief (or Custom, where your notes are the brief). Each shot stays on one still, so every shot stays anchored to a real still. It may also invent shots — compositions no still contains (detail close-ups, reveals, human presence, pull-back endings; the Cinematic Reel (flourish) brief leans into this). An invented shot names the stills that anchor it and carries a written keyframe prompt; Brut generates that missing frame from your stills on the Storyboard before any video runs, so the identity never drifts. No still is overused, and the "Invent every shot" switch goes all the way: stills become references only, every start frame generated.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Artistic Director

Sets the look: a style bible and per-shot art direction — palette, lighting, mood. Choose a style (or Custom). It builds on the Scenarist's treatment. On invented shots it also styles the keyframe prompt (palette, light, lens character) — composing the frame is exactly its job.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › DoP (Director of Photography)
Turns the treatment into an executable shot plan — the camera language, motion, and which still grounds each shot, as a concrete list of clips with durations. This is the plan Film Shots executes.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Script Supervisor
The continuity pass: harmonizes speed, light and palette across all the clips so the sequence feels like one film, not a pile of clips. It never changes which still a shot stands on.

Not an agent but the crew's review surface. The Storyboard turns the plan into an editable board of shot cards: per-clip start/end frame swaps with thumbnails, editable and lockable prompts, add/reorder shots, dynamic position badges. It passes the actual frames along with the plan, so Film Shots needs only one wire. ✕ mutes, it never deletes. A muted card stays on the board, greyed and badged muted, out of the film: its keyframes, pins and prompts are kept, the position badges renumber around it, and ↺ on the card (or ↺ N muted in the header) brings it back in place. Only a hand-added shot can be deleted for good: 🗑 on its card, muted or not (it asks first when a keyframe was rendered for it). Hand-added shots carry names of their own (x1, x2…), so a plan that grows to more shots never takes a hand-added shot's name; a shot added before this rule is renamed the moment the plan claims its name, and stays muted if it was. The same discipline as the Shot Board's ✗: a clip you cut is a clip you can still see. Wrong still numbers never pass silently. When Brut can fix a plan's still numbers, it does and says so in the Activity panel; any other number the board can't serve stops with a clear message on its card. Invented shots arrive frameless with a 🎨 Generate keyframe button: a render from the shot's anchor stills at the film's aspect (cents, priced on the board next to the image-model picker). A keyframe is kept as long as its prompt and anchor stills don't change, ↻ re-rolls, 📌 pins, 🕘 opens the card's history — every keyframe it ever generated, from the project ledger, any past take re-pinnable as the start frame for free — a wired image overrides, and the start selector can still ground the shot on a real still instead (🎨 generate in the same selector brings the keyframe back). The 🎨 entry is on every card: a grounded shot, or a shot you added with +, switches to a generated keyframe of its own. Write its keyframe prompt (✏, the 🎨 line), check its anchor stills (the still the card was on, by default; empty = every still on the board), 🎨. An invented shot with no keyframe blocks that clip in Film Shots — it is never silently sent as text-to-video; a card whose keyframe prompt is still to write says so and stays blocked the same way. Swap a start frame, generate a keyframe for an invented shot, drag a frame out to keep it The board also owns the film's aspect ratio: a dropdown (defaulting to the plan's format) that conforms every keyframe and travels in the emitted plan. Changing it re-crops the kept raw renders for free — no regeneration. ▶ on the board batch-renders every pending keyframe behind one itemized confirmation (count, per-frame price, total); the per-card 🎨 stays for one-offs. Its companion ↻ New takes re-rolls every generated keyframe at once — fresh takes on the current model, each paying again, one itemized confirm — for a model switch or a general do-over; 📌 pinned, wired and grounded cards are kept, and old takes stay pinnable in each card's 🕘 history. A prompts on/off switch declutters the cards, and the whole pre-wired chain ships as the Cinema Crew library template (File ▾ → Browse library…). End frames, on demand. Each card's end selector is none · a still · 🎨 generate. Pick 🎨 and the card grows a second frame block to the right — same image box, own in-socket and out-plug, own tools — for a generated end frame that continues the start frame, at the film's aspect. Its prompt is drafted for you, with up to three reference stills picked to show what the move reveals (one text call on the planning model of the node feeding the plan); ✎ / 🎨 open a review — start frame beside the editable draft, ✎ re-drafts, the still picks as toggleable thumbnails, Generate renders — so nothing renders from a prompt you haven't read. ↻ re-rolls, 📌 pins (surviving prompt edits and a re-rolled start; otherwise a new start frame needs a new end frame), 🕘 = the end frame's history. ▶ on the board reviews every armed card in one modal after the start keyframes. An armed end frame still pending blocks its clip downstream; a video model without an end-frame input runs the clip from the start alone and the Film Shots table says so on that row. Every frame block is also a source: the plug on its image edge carries that frame — the start frame (keyframe, wired image or grounded still) or the end frame — and a pending frame delivers nothing; the labeled plug bar at the card's bottom carries the clip's final prompt (overrides and wired prompts applied; in on the left, out on the right), an invented shot's keyframe prompt (its own in pin on the left too: wire a Refine output or a Text Board tile and it becomes the generated frame's prompt, a new keyframe) and the validated end prompt, for reuse or refinement anywhere. Card images can be dragged straight onto the canvas to detach into a ready-filled Image In.
📖 Review — read it like a document, direct it like a director

The plan text on the node is written for the next node, not for reading. Every crew node has a 📖 Review button that opens the document as a document: the title as a headline, the analysis as prose, the style bible as labeled sections, every shot a numbered card with its prompt, camera, duration and grounding badges. Two verbs live in that modal, with two costs: Edit — free. Every text field is editable in place. Save writes each field back into the same place in the document, so the structure the downstream chain depends on can never drift; it behaves exactly like hand-editing the node's text, just humane. Anchors are editable too. An invented shot's card shows its anchor stills (their numbers on the Reference Board) as a small list you can rewrite: 0, 3. The field knows how many stills the node is wired to and flags any number the board can't serve, so a stray anchor is a two-second fix instead of a re-plan. 💬 Comment → Revise — one planning call (cents, in the ledger). Every section and shot card takes a margin note ("shot 4 slower", "the whole film should feel like dusk"), plus an overall-notes box. Revise with comments hands the agent its own document and your notes; it returns the same document revised — same shot ids, same structure, only what your notes require changed — and the comments clear once addressed. A revision that would break the document's structure is rejected and your document stays untouched. Comments survive closing the modal, and the node's Review button shows how many are waiting. The plan as a document; a margin note on one shot, Revise, and only that changes They compose: fix wording directly, comment the conceptual asks, revise — the revision starts from your edited text.

Agent output is editable text. Hand-edit a plan and your changes flow downstream while inputs are unchanged; change an input or roll again (🎲) and the agent regenerates over your edits — deliberately. The planner sees your stills (downscaled for the model's request cap; generation always gets full resolution), and its analysis shows in the Activity panel. The plan you approve is the film you get. Every clip starts from a frame you have seen (a still of yours, or a keyframe generated from your stills), a shot without its frame never rolls, and every clip asks for a steady camera.
→ Video — shoot the plan, review the clips, cut the sequence.
Where stills become motion. Brut treats video like the expensive thing it is — every clip is quoted and confirmed before a cent is spent.

The footer of every video node reads the clip's size, duration and frame rate (1920 × 1080 · 5.0 s · 24 fps) at the bottom left, on the output pin's row. Animate a single image into a clip. Wire an image into the node, pick a provider and model, set duration/resolution and (where supported) audio and an end frame, and run. Pick the model and duration, read the estimate, run, and the clip plays on the node Providers: Kling (REST and subscription), Gemini Omni, and Seedance — see Providers. Some models do text-to-video too. The node shows a cost estimate before you run, from each model's published prices. Which picture is which. Under the inlets, the node lists the start frame, the end frame and every reference with its thumbnail, the @name it answers to and its role. Write those names in the prompt (@woman walks in from the left, the people of @cast stay seated), by hand or through the Prompt node's @ list: Brut tells the model which picture you mean, on Kling and Seedance alike. Names come from the Image In (a picture is named after its file or the node that made it until you type a name). Clip length follows the model: Kling offers a few fixed durations, Gemini Omni 3–10 s, Seedance 2.5 anything from 4 to 30 s (or smart, where the model picks). Where a model ties the two selects together (a resolution that renders at one length only, reference images that need a set length), the picks that cannot go together grey out in place with the reason, and a ⚠ line under the selects says what to change; where the provider's endpoint takes no audio switch, the audio box shows ticked and greyed. On models whose clip must keep the start frame's aspect ratio (Seedance 2.5), the aspect select disappears while a start frame is wired and the node says so. With nothing on the image inlet the run is text-to-video, the node says so under the model, and the aspect select is back, since that run takes a ratio of your choice; the Text → Video node is the same thing without the picture inlets. Ratio: follow the input. The aspect menu's first entry follows the start frame: the clip runs at the provider's ratio nearest to the wired image's (a 2048 × 1143 still runs at 16:9, a portrait one at 9:16), so the clip keeps the frame you composed instead of being stretched or banded to a fixed ratio. Steady camera asks the model for one smooth, stabilized move, as Film Shots does for every clip: the prompt says what stays still, and on models whose maker takes a negative prompt (Kling's API) the camera faults to avoid go there, beside your own negative prompt, never into the prompt itself. The switch cannot steady a model that trembles on every move: on Kling 3.0 (standard) a moving shot from a still shakes as much as it moves in our measurements, with the switch on or off, while a locked-off shot is clean; Kling 3.0 Omni and Seedance 2.5 held the same moves smoothly on the same frames. Running a finished node again replays its clip, free. Want another take of the same shot? The title bar's ↻ re-roll generates a fresh one (billed again, at the same estimate); the previous clip stays in the node's 🕘 history, pinnable.

Tick Draft take and the node renders a 480p draft, billed like any 480p clip. When the draft is the shot you want, ⬆ Render final 1080p re-renders the same shot at 1080p from the draft: BytePlus reuses the prompt, the frames, the references, the duration, the seed and the audio, nothing is re-sent, and the final is billed like any 1080p clip, after the usual confirm with its price. The final then replaces the draft on the node and on every wire (the footer line reads 1920 × 1080), while the draft stays in the node's 🕘 history. A re-roll or a changed prompt starts a new draft, and the old final stays in the ledger like every paid file. A draft can be finalized for seven days; the node's line says until when. Explore at 480p, pay 1080p only for keepers. Draft mode needs your own BytePlus key: a node running through another service such as OpenRouter shows no Draft box. The same box sits on Text → Video and on Video → Video with Seedance 2.5: a 3D preview or an edit drafted at 480p, the final at 1080p from the same run. Last frame (Seedance). Seedance returns every clip's final frame as an image, at the clip's exact size, and Brut keeps it beside the clip. ⏭ Last frame → Image In under the result drops it on the canvas as an Image In: wire it into the next Image → Video's start frame and the shot continues where this one ended. When a final was rendered from a draft, the button gives the final's last frame. The trust line (Seedance). BytePlus refuses a wired picture that looks like a real person unless one of its own models made it on your key. Brut checks where each wired picture came from, the start frame, the end frame and each reference, and says in green which ones carry that trust, with the day the 30-day window closes: made on your BytePlus key: start frame, references 1, 2. A picture counts when it is a Seedream text-to-image result or a Seedance clip's last frame. When the same set also holds pictures Seedance will refuse a face in (a Seedream edit, a picture from another model), an amber line names them, so a refusal is visible before the run. A picture with no line either way is one Brut cannot trace (an upload, a Conform cut): that is no verdict. A node fed only by other makers' pictures shows no line at all. When a video model runs through another service (the "⇄ runs via …" chip — e.g. Kling v3 on your OpenRouter key), the node shows only the knobs that service actually accepts: settings it doesn't carry (like the aspect-ratio select or the negative prompt on OpenRouter's Kling) disappear rather than fail the run. The clip's aspect still follows the start frame you wire in. Add the native key to get the full control set back.

Some models accept extra reference images alongside the start frame — a character, a product, a style plate — and keep them consistent in the clip. When the selected model supports them, the node grows a references inlet and its info line says so ("✓ takes reference images (up to N)"); models that don't say that too, so you never guess. A Reference Board plugs straight in — its numbered tiles (or the whole curated pool) wire onto the inlet. Current support: Seedance 2.5 (up to 30, addressed as @Image1… in the prompt), Gemini Omni Flash, Kling o1 / 3.0 Omni (subscription, up to 6), Kling 4.0 (subscription, up to 9), Seedance 2.0. Wiring references into a model that can't take them fails with a clear message — Brut never silently drops an image you wired. Kling 4.0 with references runs as Omni-Ref. Kling's 4.0 image-to-video takes a first frame and a last frame, no reference; its Omni-Ref takes pictures alone. So when references are wired, the node sends the clip as Omni-Ref: it opens on your start picture, and the references carry their people and things into the shot (a character sheet, a product, a piece of furniture). The node says so under the model. Omni-Ref has no end frame, so an end frame wired beside references shows a ⚠ line naming the two ways out (unwire the end frame to keep the references, or the references to keep the first and last frame), and the run refuses before anything is sent. At 720p it costs the same as a plain Kling 4.0 clip (measured); at 1080p with references the price line reads $? until that price is measured. A start frame, an end frame or a reference that comes from an element of your vault is named in the prompt with the element's line (start, end, then references, in that order); the ✦ line on the face says which, untick to send the pictures bare.

Give the person in the start picture a voice. On Seedance 2.5 the node shows a Voice row: Pick an audio file… takes a recording (a line you recorded, a voice-over from a text-to-speech tool), and the clip has that person speaking those words in that voice, lips on the words, with the rest of the shot as the prompt says. The row reads the file's name and its length; ✕ takes it off again. One sentence under the row says what it does; the prompt describes the shot as usual (where the person stands, what the camera does), not the words, which come from the recording.
