Two ways to use it: with no spoken line in the prompt, the person says the recording itself; with a line in quotes in the prompt, the recording gives the voice and the person says your line in it (the way to have a character say new things in a voice you already have). What a recording must be: 2 to 30 seconds, 15 MB at most, mp3 or wav best (an m4a, aac, ogg or flac file is converted before it leaves). A file outside that is refused before anything is sent, by name, with the fix. The recording travels to Seedance the way a Video → Video clip does, as a link from your own BytePlus storage: the row shows the ⚠ Add your BytePlus storage key button until that key is in ⚙ Settings, and Brut deletes the file from your bucket when the job ends. With a recording wired the start frame is no longer pixel-exact, as with reference images on this model: the clip opens on your picture, framing close, the aspect measured from it; an end frame rides the same way. Draft mode works with a recording (the final re-renders the same shot from the draft). A node running Seedance through another service shows no Voice row; the same row sits on Text → Video, where the person speaking in the clip gets the voice.

A clip from a prompt alone. Wire or type the prompt, pick the provider and model, the aspect ratio, the length, the resolution and (where the model has a switch) audio, and run. The node is the Image → Video node without its picture inlets: the same models that make a clip from words (every Kling tier on your plan, Gemini Omni, Seedance 2.5 and 2.0), the same estimate before the run, the same Steady camera switch, draft mode and the Voice row on Seedance 2.5 (a recording alone is enough there: the person speaking in the clip says its words in its voice), ↻ re-roll and 🕘 history. With no picture to follow, the aspect ratio is yours to pick (the menu opens on the provider's first). Nothing in the shot is anchored to a frame of yours, so expect more variation between takes than from a still: it is the node for a quick mood clip, a plate to cut against, or a first look at a model.

A clip in, a new clip out. Wire a clip on the clip inlet (a Video In, an Image → Video, a Sequence, any node that makes a clip), say what you want on the prompt inlet, pick a Task, and run. Four tasks: Edit the clip. Keeps the clip's camera, motion and timing and changes what your prompt names: replace an object, restyle the scene, change the season or the time of day. Wire up to 4 pictures to show what to use (the chair that should replace the sofa, the look to match). The new clip keeps the clip's framing and length. Borrow the camera. A new shot that follows the clip's camera move and motion: film a move on your phone, get it back on another scene. The prompt and the wired pictures say what the shot shows; you pick its aspect ratio (it starts on the clip's own) and its length. 3D preview to real shot. A clay, untextured or viewport playblast becomes a finished shot with the same geometry, camera path and timing. The look comes from the wired pictures. The surest one is a render of the same view: take a frame of the playblast with Extract frame (free), render it with Image → Image using your pictures as references, and wire that frame as the look. A portrait or a picture of the place also works, as a reference for appearance, when the prompt says what maps to what (@man is the small seated figure of the clip, with the picture named on its Image In) and describes the shot as the playblast frames it: the shot size, where the horizon sits, how small the figure is. A close-up wired alone, with a prompt that describes the close-up, pulls the result toward the picture: you get the portrait animated and the wide shot is gone. The prompt is optional when the look is a render of the same view. Drive a character. A picture of a person or an animal performs the motion of the clip. Wire exactly one picture. Facing sets which way the character faces: as in the clip, or as in the picture (the clip then has to be 3 to 10 s). One clip, edited into a winter dusk: the camera and the people stay where they were Which picture is which. Under the inlets, the node lists every wired picture: its thumbnail, the @name it answers to and its role. Write those names in the prompt (replace the sofa with @chair, @woman sits in the left armchair), by hand or through the Prompt node's @ list: Brut tells the model which picture you mean, whatever the order of the wires. A picture is named after its file or the node that made it until you type a name on the Image In; one nothing names reads unnamed · @picture2, and @picture2 works too. An Image In's own name covering several pictures is listed below them, with the pictures it covers. The legend follows a rename at once. The Task menu comes first; the Model menu then lists the models that do that task (Kling 3.0 Omni and Kling 4.0 edit, borrow a camera and render a 3D preview; Kling 3.0 and 2.6 Motion Control drive a character). On your Kling plan, or on Seedance 2.5 with your own BytePlus key: Seedance borrows a camera, edits a clip with up to 5 pictures of what to use, and renders a 3D preview; it takes the clip and the pictures only through your own storage on BytePlus, set up once, and the node says when that key is missing. The clip. Kling takes a clip of 3 to 10 seconds (up to 30 s on Kling 4.0, or to drive a character as the clip faces), between 720 and 2160 pixels on both sides, at 24 to 60 frames a second. On Kling 4.0 an edit is billed on the output's length alone, at a higher rate than its image-to-video (measured). The node reads the wired clip and says it under the selects (Clip: 4.0 s · 1076 × 1926 · 24 fps). A clip outside the size or frame-rate range is resized or resampled on your machine before it is sent, and the line says so (→ sent at 960 × 720); a clip outside the length range is never cut for you: the node says to trim it first (the Sequence's in and out points do that, free). What blocks a run is said before it. No clip, no prompt where the task needs one, too many pictures, no character for Drive a character, a clip too long or too short: a ⚠ line under the selects names it, and the run stops there without calling anyone. Cost. Every run asks first, like every video node, with the clip's length and your plan balance in the question. Edit the clip and 3D preview to real shot at 720p are measured: about 9 credits a second (36 credits for a 4-second clip, about $0.39 at the Pro rate). The other tasks and resolutions show no estimate until measured; compare your plan balance before and after. A finished node replays its clip for free; ↻ re-roll makes a new take, and the old one stays in 🕘 history. Time. A video-to-video render can take a while on Kling's side, well past the length of the clip, on a busy day. Brut waits up to an hour (the job survives an engine restart, like every video job). A run that still times out keeps its task id on the node and in the ledger, and the clip, once finished, can be fetched from your kling.ai gallery: the timeout itself bills nothing more.

Seedance refuses a picture with a face in it, generated or not, unless BytePlus made the picture or the picture is registered in your BytePlus asset library. This node registers. Wire pictures of your people into it (a Character Lab's outputs, an Image → Image, an Image In), name the Set (the node proposes your project's name) and click Register: each picture is copied into your asset library through your own storage, in about a second, free, and Seedance accepts the people in it from then on, as a start or end frame, a reference or a picture beside a clip, in every graph and every project. The pictures pass through. What flows out is what flows in, in wire order, registered or not, then the assets you picked from your library. Put the node anywhere between the pictures and the video node; nothing downstream changes and nothing re-runs. There is no ▶: Register is a click, and a whole-graph run passes the pictures on. Pick from your library… opens every asset on your BytePlus account in one grid, with pictures, each card naming its set and the day it was registered. Tick the ones you want and click Use: their pictures are downloaded into this project's inputs and flow out of the node, already accepted by Seedance; a picked tile carries a ✕ on the picture that takes it off the node only. Tick and Delete from library removes assets from BytePlus after a confirmation. The tiles say the state. Each picture shows full width with either its asset id (✓ registered) or not registered, with a field to paste an id you registered by hand in the BytePlus console. The Register button counts what is left to register; a picture BytePlus refuses as an asset is named on the node. The Set field is the name of the group new registrations are filed under, never a place for an asset id; the long explanation of the node sits on hover of its first line. It remembers by content. A registration follows the picture's pixels, not its path: the same file under another name, or in another project, is the same asset. A re-export or a crop is another picture and needs its own registration. The quota. The free BytePlus plan holds 50 assets; the line under the buttons says how many your account holds. ⚙ Settings → BytePlus storage shows the same library and deletes an asset on request. Nothing is registered or removed on its own. The key. It needs the same BytePlus storage key as Video → Video, with the Ark rights beside the storage ones. The node says when the key is missing; the paste field works without it. On Image → Video, a registered picture reads green in the trust line (registered as a BytePlus asset), and the ledger row of a clip lists the asset ids it went out on. The details and the rules on whose faces may be registered are on the Seedance page. Three character pictures registered in one set, the Image → Video below reading them as accepted
Film Shots — the cinema batch executor

Film Shots takes a shot plan (from the Director / Storyboard) and shoots the whole sequence. Prompts written for the model you picked. Before a clip is shot, Film Shots adapts the Director's prompt to the video model you picked, automatically (one cheap text call per clip, cents, in the ledger). There is nothing to set: the table marks adapted rows with ✦ (hover one to read the Director's text), and the confirmation says how many were adapted. A clip whose adaptation fails is flagged on its row and in the confirmation, and goes out with the Director's text. Its defining feature is the cost guard: It prices every clip — model, duration, resolution, estimated cost — and shows an itemized confirmation before any spend. Cancel a line and the total updates. The table follows the plan, before and after a run. Add a shot on the Storyboard, re-plan the Director with more or fewer shots, change a clip's prompt: the rows change at once. A clip that already rendered keeps its result on its row as long as its request is the one that ran; a changed clip is queued again, a dropped one leaves the table, a new one appears priced. Tick boxes choose what gets sent. Every row has one, all ticked by default; untick a clip and it stays in the table, greyed, not sent, not priced, not in the output pool — generate three, judge them, then tick the rest. The Σ row's box ticks or unticks everything, and its N of M clips line always says what Generate would actually send. Ticks are saved with the graph (never in library items). Clips already made (unchanged) and pinned clips cost $0 and are never re-quoted. A ruled resolution snaps the plan's durations. On a model whose resolution renders at one length only, every clip in the table snaps to it, the line under the Resolution select says so, and the confirm lists the snapped rows. A row that still breaks a rule is blocked with the fix, like an invented shot without its keyframe. It shoots several clips at a time, with the same per-clip controls as Multi-Shot: free replay / ↻ re-roll / ✓✗ verdicts / 📌 pins. On Kling (subscription) without a subscription, kling.ai runs one clip at a time and watermarks it: clips refused for that reason wait and run one by one after the pool, the row saying so on hover, the Activity panel saying why once. Every clip asks for a steady camera, and a clip gets sound only when you switch audio on and the model makes sound. An invented shot whose keyframe hasn't been generated on the Storyboard is a per-clip error — that clip is blocked (and counted in the confirm), never silently downgraded to text-to-video. The rest of the batch rolls normally. A shot added on the Storyboard with no clip prompt yet is listed and blocked the same way, the row naming the fix, instead of vanishing from the table. Draft mode on Seedance 2.5: tick Draft takes and every clip rolls at 480p, billed like 480p. Once the drafts are in, each row grows a final 1080p tick; ⬆ Render N finals re-renders exactly those shots at 1080p from their drafts, after its own itemized confirm. A finalized row's output becomes the final, on the Clip Board and in the Sequence downstream, while the draft stays in 🕘. Seven days to finalize a draft; your own BytePlus key only. Every clip priced in the table, one itemized confirmation, nothing spends before your OK Nothing is generated until you confirm the total. Other branches keep running while it waits. Like Image → Video, a model reached through another service (the "⇄ runs via …" chip) shows only the knobs that service accepts — the quote table and the clips both use exactly what will be sent, and the film's aspect rides each clip's start frame.

The review board for Film Shots — video tiles, ✓ / ✗ / ↻ per clip, and a plug per tile to route one clip onward. The video equivalent of the Shot Board. Tiles show a still poster of each clip (in the clip's own aspect ratio) and stay feather-light — press ▶ on a tile to play it; one clip plays at a time, and 🔍 opens it full-screen — ←/→ screens the whole board clip by clip. The /row select goes up to 15, so a whole reel can sit in one row.

Takes one still out of each clip wired into it, at the clip's own size, on your machine. Free. Last frame (the default) is the continuity move: wire it into the next shot's Image → Video as the start frame, and the next clip begins exactly where this one ended. Kling and Gemini Omni give back no last frame of their own; this works with every video model. First frame, or at a time: a slider runs through the clip one frame at a time, with the time and the frame number under it, and you can type the time in seconds. While you drag, the clip itself shows that moment; the frame is taken when you let go. Several clips wired in give one frame each, in the order of the wires. A time past the end of a shorter clip takes that clip's last frame, and the node says how many clips it happened to. The frames flow out as pictures: into an Upscale Image for a delivery still, an Image → Image, a Storyboard card's socket, a Preview. Right-click a frame for Reveal and Export, like any picture. There is no ▶: the node takes its frames as soon as the clips, the choice or the time change, and a frame it already took comes back at once. The last frame of a clip, wired as the start frame of the next shot

Wire your curated clips into a Sequence node and it assembles them into one mp4 on your machine — cuts or chained crossfades, scaled and padded to a common size. It's free, and an unchanged assembly replays at once. Two clips cut together with a crossfade and played in Preview: local ffmpeg on your machine, no cost Nothing to install: the video tool ships inside Brut. The film follows the first clip's orientation — a pool of vertical 9:16 clips assembles into a vertical reel, not a pillarboxed landscape frame. The Quality select sets the short side (1080p vertical = 1080 wide). Clip audio is kept. Clips with native sound (Gemini Omni, Seedance, Kling with audio on) carry it into the film, in sync even beside silent clips; crossfades fade the audio too. A pool with no sound anywhere produces a clean video-only file. Trim each clip. Every clip in the list has an in and an out point in seconds, with its length beside them: cut the first second of a clip that starts on a shaky frame, or the last one where a clip morphs at its end. ↺ puts the clip back whole. The film's length under the list follows the trims and the crossfades. A trimmed clip keeps at least 0.1 s, and more than the fade when you crossfade; the row says so before you run. A trim stays with its clip wherever you move it in the list, and the sound is cut with the picture. Every wired clip is in the list, wire after wire, in the order the film plays them: wire two clip nodes into the Sequence and both show, each with its own in and out. ↑ and ↓ move a clip anywhere in the film, across wires. A clip's last second trimmed off before assembly, the film's length updating under the list
The video nodes are the back half of the Cinema Sessions: Storyboard → Film Shots → Clip Board → Sequence → Preview. Read that walkthrough to see them working together.

Upscalers grow an image to delivery resolution — the finishing step after you've generated and curated. They are paid nodes: the source image goes to the upscaling provider with your own key, and cost scales with output pixels, not input.

Wire one image in (from Image In, any generator, a Shot Board tile…), pick a model, run. The upscaled image flows out the bottom port like any other image — into a Preview, a Conform, and so on. Batch: wire several images (an Image In folder, a curated Shot Board pool) and each one upscales as its own job, and each image is remembered separately, so a re-run only pays for what changed and a partial failure retries just the failures. The estimate line sums the whole set, and each output's 🔍 compares against its input. Never pay twice, as everywhere: unchanged input + unchanged dials = free replay; the 🕘 history lets you re-pin any past result. The node shows a live estimate — input size → output size, megapixels, and the approximate cost — before you spend anything. A preset, a live estimate, run, then the before/after wipe zoomed into the brickwork

Model What it does Gigapixel Standard 2 / High Fidelity 2 / Low Resolution 2 Faithful precision upscaling — no invention, tuned respectively for everyday use, maximum preservation, and tiny sources. Gigapixel Art & CGI Precision upscaling for renders, illustrations and graphics — keeps clean edges and flat color, avoids photographic texture artifacts. The archviz workhorse. Redefine / Standard MAX / Recover 3 Generative enhancement (photoreal, true-to-input, or restoration) with an optional guidance prompt and a 1–9 creativity dial. Wonder 3.5 / Wonder 3 Topaz's newest generative upscalers, priced lower. One Enhancement setting (auto, low, medium, high: how much detail Topaz rebuilds; auto lets Topaz pick from the picture). Wonder 3 adds the guidance prompt and the creativity dial; Wonder 3.5 has nothing else to tune. Output up to 100 MP. Topaz bills credits (see the provider page); the node shows your live balance and a per-run credit estimate, and the ledger records the credits each job actually billed.

Model What it does Upscaler Creative The famous "reimagining" upscaler: 2x/4x/8x/16x with a guidance prompt and the creativity / HDR / resemblance / fractality dials, plus an engine choice (Illusio = smooth, Sharpy = crisp, Sparkle = detailed). It invents plausible detail — great for stylized finishes, wrong for strict fidelity. Input capped at 25.3M pixels. Upscaler Precision V2 Faithful, detail-preserving upscale from 2x to 16x with sharpen / smart grain / ultra detail knobs and a flavor per image type: Photo, Sublime (illustration), Photo denoiser (grainy or low-light sources). The archviz default.

The 🔍 on the node's result opens straight into a full-screen before/after comparison of the input against the upscaled output: drag the divider to sweep between them (the input is shown at the same size, so you're comparing detail, not scale). The mouse wheel zooms — the fast display copy is shown until you zoom, then the original files load so you're judging real pixels — drag pans when zoomed in, double-click resets, Esc or a click outside closes. The same wheel-zoom works in every magnified preview across Brut.

Your favorite dial combinations can be saved as named upscaling presets — the 💾 button next to the preset select stores the current model + dials in Brut's global library (all projects). Picking a preset applies it; editing any dial detaches it (your settings win); ✕ deletes it from the library.

The clip finisher: wire one clip in (a Clip Board tile, an Image → Video output, a whole Sequence), pick a provider and model, choose a scale — plain 2x / 4x or a standard target: → HD, → 4K, → 8K (the target sizes the clip's short side, so a portrait 9:16 reel "at 4K" comes out 2160 wide) — and run. The upscaled clip flows out — audio is kept. Two providers, same models: Topaz Labs (cloud) — bills credits per job, works anywhere. Topaz Video AI (local) — free: if you own the Topaz Video desktop app, Brut runs the upscale on your GPU. No key, no credits, no confirm dialog, and the clip never leaves your machine. See the provider page. Nothing bills without your OK — every cloud run opens an itemized confirmation with the credit estimate first (free replays and pinned results never ask; free local runs don't either). Topaz quotes a range; you're billed the lower figure, as shown in the ledger. Cloud jobs can take a while on real clips; they keep going if you close Brut and pick up again when you reopen it. Local jobs simply re-run if interrupted — nothing was billed. Output caps at 8K per side; cloud uploads at 500MB. Target 4K on the short side, read the itemized confirmation, keep the clip's sound Model When Proteus 4 the general-purpose default — upscale, denoise, sharpen in one pass Rhea natural-texture enhancement, higher scales Gaia CG rendered/CG clips — archviz animations, clean edges

Upscales are priced by output image area (and for video, × duration). Magnific's doc rates work out to roughly €0.025 per output megapixel with a €0.10 minimum — Brut shows this as an approximate $ figure before the run, and the ledger records the estimate from the actual output pixels after it. Rough feel: a 1080p still → 4K is ~€0.20; pushing a 640×480 crop to 16x lands near €2. As everywhere in Brut: your key, your bill, zero markup.
Small, local, free — the glue between generation steps.

Brings stills to one aspect ratio before generation, so a set of mixed-ratio renders becomes a clean, consistent batch (video models in particular want a single ratio). Choose a target aspect ratio and a method: crop trims each still to the ratio. The edges outside the frame are lost; what stays keeps its full resolution. Free. extend takes the still to the new ratio by having a painter paint what the frame adds. A render that must grow from 4:3 to 16:9 without losing the building is the case. The frame is free and applies itself; the paint is the paid step, one call per still: ✦ Paint this still in the ✂ editor paints that one, ✦ Paint N stills on the node paints every pending one, and Run prices them first. Each tile says to paint until it is, then ✦ painted. Per tile, ↻ paints that still again (a fresh take), 🕘 opens every paint of that still from the ledger and 📌 pins a past take, which flows until unpinned or until the frame changes. What flows out of the node is the painted set, never a still that is not painted yet. pad keeps the whole still on blurred, darkened bars of itself, the letterbox look. Free. The node's height follows its tiles: each still shows at its conformed aspect and the node grows or shrinks with them (a 9:16 set makes a tall node, a 21:9 set a flat one); the n / row selector and the width grip are the size controls, there is no inner scrollbar. Per-image ✂ crop editor: drag an aspect-locked rectangle to choose which part of each still survives the conform (the default is a center cut — architecture rarely sits dead-center). The crop is stored per image; Brut crops the original at full resolution. A hand crop always wins over the method for its still. An edge close to the picture's edge snaps to it, a frame close to centered snaps to centered, and Shift while dragging locks the move to one direction. On extend and pad, the same editor places the frame: the stage grows room around the picture and the frame may reach into it. Drag it across the picture to choose which side grows (all of the extension on the right, for instance, or a little above and below as well), the corner scales it, the readout says how many pixels are added. A frame that reaches outside the picture belongs to those two methods: switch back to crop and that still takes the automatic cut again, with the frame kept for the next switch. On extend, the editor also holds the painter: provider, model, output size and, for GPT Image, quality. It starts on FLUX Outpaint when you hold a Black Forest Labs key, on GPT Image 2.5 Flare at xhigh otherwise. The line beside it is the price of painting this one still at this frame. The picks are the node's (every still is painted the same way) and apply at once; the frame and the optional note for the still (what should appear in the added part: more lawn, no new buildings) go with Save frame or ✦ Paint this still. Reset frame puts the frame back on its automatic placement. Two kinds of painter, and they do not behave the same. An outpainting tool holds your picture. FLUX Outpaint (Black Forest Labs) takes the picture and the frame and generates only what the frame adds: the picture stays where you put it. It answers at the frame's size up to 4 megapixels (or up to 2 or 1, your pick: its price follows the size, about $0.10 per megapixel in High; a Fast mode paints in seconds for about $0.05, rougher in the added part); a larger frame is painted smaller (the line under the picture says at what size) and delivered at that size, never scaled back up. Use Upscale Image after it when you need more pixels. It needs no prompt; your note travels as a hint. An image model redraws the frame. GPT Image, Nano Banana, FLUX 3 and Seedream have no fill mode: they paint a new picture of your still at the frame's ratio. The result is one coherent image, but it is the model's version of your still: details inside it are re-rendered, and the model may shift or re-proportion the scene. Same as the picture asks for the frame's own size; pick a tier to render the frame's ratio at that size instead. You get the painter's picture, as it is. Brut does not paste your original back over a redraw (a model that moved the scene would leave doubled edges at the seam). When the original must stay pixel for pixel, the outpainting tool is the painter to pick. The prompt is written for each still automatically when the painter is an image model: one cheap text call per still, cents, listed in the ledger. Free ratio: pick free at the bottom of the Aspect menu when the stills don't need one shared ratio. Each still's ✂ editor then crops freely: drag any corner or edge to any shape, the size in pixels shows under the image. Stills you don't crop pass through as they are, and the Method menu greys out (there is nothing to pick). Crops remember the ratio they were drawn for, so switching back to 16:9 uses your 16:9 crops, never the free ones. No ▶ to press: Conform applies itself. Save a crop, change the ratio, the method or the fill, wire a new still in, and the tiles update on their own. Only the stills that changed are re-cut: the others keep their files, so nothing downstream of them runs again. The stills sit on a resizable board: pick 1 to 5 per row from the n / row selector (never more columns than stills, so a single still fills the node) and drag the node's width to size the tiles. Each image gets its own output plug, so you can route conformed stills individually. Each row's 🔍 opens the lightbox on the conformed result — ←/→ pages the whole set, so you can flip through the batch and check every cut. Extend to 4:3 with FLUX Outpaint: drag the frame where the picture should grow, a note for the new part, Paint: the picture stays as it was, only the added sky is painted Cropping, padding and placing the frame run entirely on your machine: free, never metered. Only Extend's painting is a paid call, and only when you press Paint.

Inspect any output at screen size. Wire an image or video into a Preview node and it shows inline on a resizable frame, live: whatever is plugged in appears the moment it exists — when you open a saved graph, when an upstream node finishes, when you pin a past take — with nothing to press. There is no ▶ on the node (nothing to run; it is a viewing surface, like Compare). The image inlet displays video too. Hover a tile and its 🔍 opens the lightbox — wheel-zoom, and ←/→ pages through everything on the node. When several images are shown, the ‹ › buttons on each tile reorder them. Preview is the "show me the result" node you'll drop at the end of most branches; the full-resolution files live in the project's output folder.

Two images, one verdict. Wire any two takes into the A and B inlets (a Gemini attempt against a GPT attempt, an original against an Adjust correction, yesterday's keeper against today's re-roll), and the node shows them side by side, live, without running anything. Hover it and the 🔍 opens the real thing: the before/after wipe slider, both layers sharing one zoom and pan, so you can drag the divider across a facade while zoomed into the brickwork. The slider labels pick up the source nodes' names, so it reads "Image → Image vs Adjust", not "before vs after". Two takes side by side, then the wipe slider with a shared zoom Each pane carries the same small line as the single-output nodes: the picture's pixel size (2048 × 1152), a clip's length and frame rate. Compare is a viewing surface, not a processor — free, local, no output port and no ▶ (there is nothing to run; the tiles follow the wires live — route the winner onward from its source node). It's the generalization of the Upscale node's built-in input-vs-result compare: same slider, any two wires you choose.

Every take a node ever made, on the canvas. Projects grow hundreds of generations and the good one from Tuesday is somewhere in the outputs folder. Wire any generation node's output into the History board (the image inlet takes video nodes too) and the board fills with every take that node ever produced, newest first, straight from the project's generation ledger. Wire several nodes in and the board shows one group per node, in wire order, each headed by the node's name and id, its take count and what it has cost so far. That is the point of the board: it reads as "what is inside this branch", not as a flat pile. Tiles carry the model, the date, the cost and, where it applies, the shot number of a Multi-Shot take, the card of a Storyboard keyframe or the Director's proof sheet. The prompt sits under the caption and in the tooltip. Every tile shows the take at its own aspect: a 9:16 take is a tall tile, a 16:9 take a wide one, never a crop, so a node that changed format mid-way reads truthfully. A tile's 🔍 opens the Magnifier, and ←/→ page through that node's whole history. Video takes play in place: a still poster at rest, click ▶ to play (one tile at a time, so a board of forty clips stays light). 📌 pins on the source node. The pin is exactly the 🕘 re-pin: the take becomes the source node's active output on every run, free, until you unpin it there or here. A pinned tile wears the amber ring. Multi-Shot tiles pin their own shot, Storyboard tiles their own keyframe. The board itself has no output and never runs anything: pins act on the source, so keep the downstream wires on the source node and use the board to choose. Drag an image tile onto the canvas to detach it as a ready-filled Image Input, the same gesture as dragging any preview out of a node. Right-click a tile for Reveal in Explorer, Copy, Export. This graph's takes. A node id is a counter per graph (most graphs of a project have a text_to_image-1), so the board shows the takes made on this graph alone. Tick every graph in the board's header to see what the same id produced in the project's other graphs, each tile badged with the graph that made it (unnamed canvas for a take made before the canvas was saved under a name). Filter by model when a node has run on several, pick the tiles per row, ↻ re-reads the ledger (it also refreshes on its own whenever a tracked node finishes a run). Wires through a composite card or a reroute dot resolve to the node that actually generated: the board always shows the generator's own history. Wire two generation nodes into a History board: every take, grouped per node, pin one Free, local, nothing leaves the machine: the ledger is a file in the project folder. The board shows the newest 200 takes per node.

A sticky note for the canvas — annotate your graph the way you'd annotate a whiteboard: intent for future-you, instructions for a teammate opening the project later, review remarks next to the branch they're about. Notes aren't nodes — they're placement tools, living in the rail's Organize section (with Stamp, Group and Composite). Click the rail's sticky-note icon and the note rides your cursor: click the canvas to place it at the default size, or click-and-drag to draw its size (Shift places several, Esc or right-click cancels). While you're placing, the nodes underneath freeze — you can drop a note on top of anything. Double-click to write, click elsewhere to finish. Notes support a light markdown: # heading, - bullet, **bold**, *italic*, `code`. Select a note for the toolbar: five sticky colors, four fonts (Sans / Display / Hand / Mono), text sizes from 11 to 256px, bold and italic, left / center / right alignment, plus resize handles. Display order is fixed so annotations always show: stamps over notes over nodes (selecting anything still brings it to the front). Notes have no ports and never execute — free, local, never sent to any provider as part of a run. Notes travel: they're saved in graphs, templates and composites, so a library template can ship its own usage notes. Tidy moves them with the graph — each note keeps its position relative to the node it sits next to. Marcel reads them. A note sitting next to a node is exactly the kind of intent he should see — ask him about the graph and the notes are part of his picture. He can write them too. Place a note from the rail, pick a paper and a font, drop a stamp next to it

A frameless emoji mark — the quickest possible annotation. Click the rail's stamp icon, pick your emoji from the flyout, and it rides your cursor; click to drop it — on empty canvas or right on a node (Shift-click for a trail of them). Drop a ⭐ on the keeper, a 🚧 on the branch under construction, a 💩 on what it deserves. Select a stamp to swap the emoji, resize it by the grip in its corner (like a sticky), or delete it. Free, local, no ports.

Draw on the canvas — made for Wacom people (mouse works too). The rail's Pen icon (or the ring's Pen slice) enters draw mode: sketch freely, pen pressure sets the stroke weight, pick a color (theme ink + the five sticky colors) and a width, Alt-click erases a stroke, and Esc or ✓ finishes — the whole session lands as one frameless drawing you can move, resize (it scales as a unit) and delete like any annotation. Free, local, never sent anywhere. Draw over the canvas; the session becomes one resizable ink node

A clean label — for those who prefer tidy organization over stickies: it works like a note, with the paper removed. No fill, no shadow, just typed words on the canvas — perfect for titling regions of a big graph. The label sizes to its content by default; select it and drag the knob on its left or right edge to set the width (the height always follows the text, so a title never clips; double-click a knob to fit the text again), and the font size is its scale control, up to a poster-sized 256px. It gets the full note toolbar (four fonts, sizes, bold, italic, alignment), and the colors apply to the text itself, with a theme-ink default.

Right-click any empty spot on the canvas and a radial menu opens under your hand — every organize tool one flick away. The center names the ring you're on and clicking it cycles three states: Organize (note · stamp · pen · text · group · composite · add node · tidy) → your most-used nodes (learned from your own placements) → your recent stamps. Nodes land where you right-clicked; the annotation tools (note, stamp, text) hop onto your cursor so you place — or click-drag-size — them exactly like from the rail. Power move: press the right button, drag onto a slice, release — picked, no clicking. The rail keeps every tool too; the ring is just the fast hand. Hold the right button on empty canvas: tools, then your most-used nodes, then stamps; release on a pick That's the whole palette. Back to Nodes & graphs for how they run together, or on to the Providers.

Bring a 3D model onto the canvas, walk around it, frame physical cameras, and take a clay screenshot of each view. The screenshot lands on a Camera node as an ordinary picture: wire it into Image → Image or the Clay → Photoreal workflow and a model renders the photograph, exactly as with a viewport grab from your 3D tool. Both nodes are free and local, and the model never leaves your machine.

What it takes: a GLB or glTF, an OBJ (with its MTL and textures), an FBX, an STL or a PLY. Drop the file on the node, or on an empty spot of the canvas (a Scene node appears there), or click Choose… and pick it on disk. Picking an OBJ with Choose… brings its MTL and the textures it names along (a texture name with spaces in it included), and picking an FBX brings the textures it names that sit in the same folder; when you drop a model, drop its MTL and textures with it. A file of another kind is refused with one line on the node, and so is a GLB that did not copy whole or one saved with mesh compression (export it again without compression). What it shows: the file's name, then the model itself: a picture of the last view the navigator showed, in the view you left it on: with the model's materials when you left the navigator on Textured (and the model carries materials), else in clay under the sun. Hover the name for its size and what it holds (meshes, materials, triangles; an FBX gets its counts the first time you open it). The picture is made when you take a screenshot, when you close the navigator, and the first time you open a Scene node that has none yet; until then the empty box says so, and a click on it opens the navigator. A click on the picture opens the navigator on the view it shows (through the camera it was taken from, when it was), and a right click gives the usual picture menu (Reveal in Explorer, Copy file path). There is no 3D view on the node itself: the canvas stays fast with many of them. Under it, on the plug's row, a short line gives the model's faces, its file size and its units. The cameras: one row of small pictures under the model, each camera's last screenshot with its name. Click one to look through that camera in the navigator. A line names any file the model asks for that was not found beside it (an MTL, a texture: the model then opens grey there). Choose… (or Replace… once a model is in) and Explore, one row of buttons. Replace… swaps the model and keeps the cameras, the sun and the view; the picture of the old model goes with it. Explore opens the navigator. There is no ▶: nothing runs, the screenshots are taken in the navigator. The plug: scene goes to the Camera nodes. It carries the model and its cameras, never a picture.

A full-screen view of the model on the left, the panel on the right. The view is framed exactly like the screenshot will be. The first time you open one in a session, the frame says Loading the viewer… while the viewer itself loads, then Reading the model…. Moving around, the 3ds Max way (Arc): Alt + middle drag orbits, middle drag pans, the wheel zooms toward the cursor, Ctrl + Alt + middle drag zooms smoothly. The left button orbits too (Shift + left drag pans), for a trackpad. The keys of Walk work here as well: W A S D, Q and E move the camera, the view keeping its direction; the point it orbits around moves with it, unless an object is picked (see below), which stays the center of the orbit. Orbit around an object: in Arc, a click (without dragging) on the model picks the object under the cursor, as the file names it (an object made of several materials is still one object). It is outlined, its name shows at the top left of the view, and the view does not move. Arc then orbits around the object's center, as 3ds Max does: the object stays in its place on the screen while the camera turns, even when it sits off the middle. The pick lasts while you look through a camera, walk, or come back to Arc; picking never changes a camera's framing. A click in the empty space or Escape clears it. The outline is only on screen: it never appears in a screenshot or the node's picture. Z frames the picked object, or the whole model when nothing is picked. Walk: from exactly where you stand and where you look, with nothing reset. W and S move along the direction you look (looking down and pressing W goes down), A and D sideways, E straight up and Q straight down, drag to look around, Shift to go faster; the arrow keys work as W A S D. A key held down keeps you moving for as long as you hold it; leaving the window (another app, another tab) stops you where you are. Arc goes back to orbiting. Speed: how fast the keys move, in both modes. It follows the distance to what is in front of you, as in a game editor: close to a wall you move slowly, with open space ahead you move fast, so a site model a kilometer wide still walks at a building's pace near the building. The model's size only sets the top speed: with the whole model in view you move as before, crossing it in about ten seconds at 1×. When nothing is in front of you (the horizon, the sky, a gap between buildings), the ground ahead of you sets it: a walking pace at eye height, faster from high up. The Speed slider multiplies that, from a tenth to ten times, and Shift goes faster still. Each Scene node keeps its own speed; it changes nothing in the cameras or the pictures. Cameras: Add camera makes a camera from the current view and looks through it: navigating now moves that camera. Click a camera in the list (or Look through) to look through it, Free view to leave it. Double-click a name to rename it (its Camera node takes the new name at once), the bin removes the camera (its Camera node keeps its picture, and a camera added later never takes its place on that node). Lock a camera: the lock on a camera's row (the same lock sits on its Camera node) keeps a saved camera from moving. You can still look through a locked camera and Take screenshot to take its picture again. The first move through it (a drag, the wheel, a key, Z) leaves it for the free view, which starts from the camera's own view and lens, and the line at the bottom says so; the camera itself never moves. While you look through it, its lens and frame settings stay in place, greyed. Click the lock again to free it. The lock is saved with the scene and changes nothing in the pictures or what they feed. Lens: Focal length, from 8 to 700 mm; Film back, a list of film formats (36 mm full frame, APS-C, Micro Four Thirds, medium format); and Film width, the same width set to any value (36 mm is full frame, so 35 mm on 36 mm gives a 54° horizontal view). The focal slider gives most of its travel to the short lenses where most views live and still reaches 700 mm. The lens edited is the camera you look through, or the free view's. Lock verticals: levels the camera and shifts the frame so vertical lines stay vertical, the two-point perspective of architectural photography. The panel shows the shift it applies; a view steeper than 60° cannot be leveled and says so. Shift ↕ and Shift ↔ add a manual lens shift on top. Frame: Portrait, Square and Landscape in one click, or any aspect from the list (16:9, 3:2, 4:3, 1:1, 4:5, 3:4, 2:3, 9:16), and the Size: 1K, 2K or 4K on the long side. The line below gives the screenshot's pixel size (2K at 16:9 = 2048 × 1152). Sun: Azimuth (0 north, 90 east, 180 south) and Elevation (low = long shadows) move the shadows of the clay. View: Fill light (flat even light, no shadows, to find your way around), Clay (grey under the sun, with shadows: what the screenshot renders), Wireframe (the edges of every triangle), Textured (the model's own materials under the same sun). Model: the Units the file was exported in (a GLB is in meters; an OBJ, STL or PLY is guessed from its size, an FBX says its own) and Z up for a model exported lying down. The keys' top speed follows the model's size in its units. Take screenshot, always at the foot of the panel, renders the clay at the frame's size, plus a second picture with the model's materials when the file carries some (Textured picture too). A screenshot of the free view makes a camera of it first. While it renders, the camera list waits; you can keep looking around and adjust the lens, nothing you change is undone when the picture lands. Sliders move the view live and save when you let go. Every slider of the navigator (Focal length, Film width, the two shifts, the sun's Azimuth and Elevation, Speed) works the same way: double-click the number to type a value (Enter applies, Escape cancels; a value past the range is held to it); while you drag, it snaps to its neutral value as you pass it (0 for the shifts, 35 mm for the focal length, 36 mm for the film width, 225° and 40° for the sun, 1× for Speed); a double-click on the slider or on its name puts it back there. The arrow keys still reach every value. The line at the bottom lists the keys of the current mode. Everything done in one visit of the navigator undoes as one step once it is closed (Ctrl+Z on the canvas); while it is open, undo waits. A visit that only looked around (the free view moved, nothing else) is no step at all, and an undo keeps where the free view looks from.

One camera of a Scene node and the screenshot taken through it. It appears beside the Scene node, wired to it, the first time you take a screenshot of that camera, below the Camera nodes already there. When the Scene node sits in a frame, the Camera node joins the frame; when it sits inside a closed card, the Camera node goes beside the card, and a card with no scene plug for it gets one, so the wire shows. A new screenshot of the same camera replaces its pictures (a new file, so whatever is wired downstream sees the change and runs again when you ask). What it shows: the camera's name, its lens (focal length, film back, the vertical shift, the aspect and the size), the clay and, when taken, the textured picture. Lock: the lock beside Rename is the camera's own lock, the same one as on its row in the navigator: a locked camera can be looked through and shot again, never moved. Greyed while the node holds no camera of the scene. Rename: double-click the node's title, or click Rename beside Look through. A camera has one name: the Camera node, the Scene node's camera row, the navigator's list and the lines that name the camera all follow. A Camera node that holds no camera yet has nothing to rename: Rename stays greyed until its first screenshot. Look through (greyed until the Scene node holds a model) opens the navigator on this camera, and a screenshot taken there lands on this node. A Camera node added by hand from the node list, or one whose camera was removed from the scene before you open it, opens the free view instead: frame a view and Take screenshot, the picture lands on that node (the line at the bottom of the navigator names it). A camera removed while the navigator is open never hands its node to another camera. A screenshot still rendering when you close the navigator lands on its own Scene node, even if you open another one meanwhile; if that Scene node was removed meanwhile, or now holds another model, the picture is not kept. A copy (Ctrl+D, or Ctrl+C then Ctrl+V) gets its own camera: the Scene node gains a new camera with the view, lens, frame and size the original's had at the moment of the copy, and the copy looks through it. Moving it, changing its lens or taking its screenshot leaves the original alone, and the other way round. Copied together with its Scene node, it belongs to the new Scene node; pasted where its Scene node is not wired, it holds no camera yet and its Look through opens the free view. The plugs: clay (the main one), textured (greyed while it holds no picture: the model carries no materials, or the screenshot was taken without Textured picture too) and draft, greyed and empty for now: renders inside the navigator come later. A greyed plug takes no wire. There is no ▶ on the Camera node: free, nothing to run. An empty plug: any node that generates and is fed by a plug carrying no picture (textured after a clay-only screenshot, a Camera node with no screenshot yet) stops when it runs, before anything is sent and at no cost, with one line naming the camera; a closed card says it once, under the card's own name. An Image → Video never makes its clip from the prompt alone, a Compose never takes its reference as the scene, no node runs on fewer pictures than you wired. What a stopped node feeds waits on it, and ▶ Run neither prices nor sends it. Wherever it is wired: straight in, through reroute dots, through a Reference Board (a board inside a board too) or a Seedance assets node, into a closed card, or into a Storyboard card whose frame it uses. One camera not shot yet on a board stops what the board feeds, even when the other cameras there have their pictures. A Storyboard card whose start or end frame is wired from such a camera shows that frame empty, with the camera's name, and never puts its plan still or a keyframe in the camera's place; a card with no wire keeps its still. A camera not shot yet among the Storyboard's stills stops what the cards and the plan feed: without its picture, every card after it would take the wrong still. The cards that use a still show that frame empty with the camera's name, and the board makes no keyframe until the camera has its picture. A card whose start frame waits on a camera holds its end frame too: the keyframe bar counts and prices only what a run makes, and says which end frames wait and on which camera. Hover an empty frame to read what to do. The board's status says which cards wait on which camera. What still runs: a Conform on crop or pad (free; on extend it stops like the others), and a node holding a pinned result (📌): the pin costs nothing and flows on. The way to a photograph today: wire clay into Image → Image with a prompt, or into the Clay → Photoreal workflow, as you would a viewport grab. Several cameras, one look: wire every Camera node's clay into the Clay → Photoreal card (or into one Image → Image with Each picture its own render ticked): each camera gets its own render, and the first render sets the materials, the light and the sky of the others, so the building is not reinvented from one view to the next. Wire a photo or a render into the card's reference instead, and that picture is the look of every camera: the step that writes the prompt reads it too, so the materials, the planting, the light and the sky come from the reference, not from the clay or the textured capture.

Free and local: opening, navigating, taking screenshots and the node's picture cost nothing and call no provider. A screenshot goes to a provider only when you wire it into a node that generates, priced like any picture there. The model is copied into your project, with the files it names, and stays on your machine. Save project as… moves it with those files. A model over 512 MB with its files is refused: reduce it in your 3D tool first. Renders inside the navigator, materials per object, color IDs, depth and the live link with 3ds Max come later.

Brut is bring-your-own-key. You add a key for each provider you want to use; Brut calls that provider directly, on your key, at their price. Brut never holds a key that bills anyone but you, and never marks up a token.

⚙ Settings on the left rail (or the setup wizard) shows every provider as a card — its role, and one status line — grouped by what it does (generation, aggregators, upscalers). Click a card to paste a key (validated on save); the switch on the card turns a provider off without deleting anything. Keys live in your OS keychain — never in a graph, never sent anywhere but the provider. Settings, Providers: one card per provider with its status; the switch turns a provider off without deleting its key, a click opens its key
The one rule that trips everyone up

Image and video models need a billing-enabled key. Free tiers usually have zero generation quota, so your very first call fails with a quota error (429) — that's billing not enabled, not throttling. Turn on billing in the provider's console and it clears.

Model routes — native first, aggregator fallback

Some models can also run through an aggregator — a third-party service (like an aggregator subscription or a multi-model API) that resells the same model under its own billing. Brut treats those as routes, with three hard rules: Your direct key always wins. If you hold the native provider's key, the generation goes straight to the provider, exactly as before. Routes only activate for a model when you have no native key but do hold the aggregator's credential. Routing is always visible. A routed model shows a ⇄ runs via … chip on the node, the run confirm says who bills, and the ledger records it. Nothing routes silently. The catalog stays curated. An aggregator credential never adds models to Brut — the model list is exactly the one Brut ships, whatever route serves it. Estimates for routed runs come from the route's own measured price, or are absent; aggregators typically charge a margin over the direct API, and the node says so. A routed node says so on its face: runs via OpenRouter, on your OpenRouter account Adding or removing a key takes effect at once. Three route providers ship today: OpenRouter, the main one (one key for text, images with Brut's native menus and the whole video set, with the billed cost recorded per job); fal.ai (API key, optional: with both keys, GPT Image 2 and its video models run through fal); and Replicate (API token: Nano Banana Pro/2, GPT Image 2, Kling Omni, Seedance with text→video), also available. Text models route too: with an OpenRouter key the planning models — Refine, the Multi-Shot planner, the cinema crew, Text→Text — run at pass-through token rates when no native text key exists. Marcel routes through OpenRouter too — chat, ambient narration and acting, with Anthropic prompt caching passing through, so one OpenRouter key is a complete text seat. Deciding between direct keys and an aggregator? The full pros/cons and a feature-by-feature capability matrix live on Keys vs aggregators.

Gemini, OpenAI and Anthropic double as planning models — they power the Refine node and the cinema crew, where you pick which LLM writes your treatment or shot plan. Text calls cost cents and are billed separately. Provider errors are surfaced verbatim on the node — Brut never masks them, so what the provider says is what you see.

Brut is bring-your-own-key at heart: the cheapest, highest-fidelity way to run it is a handful of native provider keys, and nothing Brut does ever adds a markup to them. But not everyone wants to open four provider consoles — so Brut also speaks to aggregators, as routes: your aggregator credential serves models you have no native key for, visibly, at the aggregator's own prices. This page is the honest comparison.

Native keys Aggregator key(s) Setup ~5 min per provider console (billing on) One key (OpenRouter covers nearly everything; fal/Replicate optional) Price Cheapest — provider list rates, zero middlemen List rates + the aggregator's margin or fee (Seedance via fal ≈2× native; OpenRouter ≈ list + ~5.5% credit fee) Fidelity Every knob every model has Most knobs; a missing one stops with a clear message, never silently Priority Always wins when the key exists Used only where no native key exists Whatever you pick, routing is never silent: routed nodes show ⇄ runs via …, the paid-run confirm says who bills, and the spend ledger records it per generation.

Three setups cover almost everyone. Pick by what you care about most:
Which path should you pick? › 1. Native keys — pick this if you care about price and control

Gemini + OpenAI + one video provider (+ Anthropic for Marcel's best brain). This is what Brut is built around, and it wins on every axis except setup time: Cheapest per generation, structurally. You pay each provider's list rate, full stop — no reseller margin, no credit fee. At studio volume (hundreds of images, dozens of clips a week) the difference is real money. Every knob of every model: native inpaint masks (OpenAI), Kling's 4K master tier, Seedance Smart Length, native 4K rates — none of which any aggregator carries. The cost: ~5 minutes per provider console, each with billing enabled.
Which path should you pick? › 2. One OpenRouter key — pick this if you care about simplicity

The 2-minute setup, and a genuinely complete studio: images with Brut's own size/aspect menus (all four Nano Bananas), GPT Image 2, 2.5 and 2.6 at about 1K, the video set (Kling 3.0 std/pro and O1, Seedance 2.0 and 2.5), every planning model, and Marcel — chat, ambient narration and acting, with Anthropic prompt caching passing through so long conversations cost the same as on a native key. A unique honesty bonus: OpenRouter reports the exact billed cost of every job, and Brut writes it straight onto your ledger. The two-minute setup: one OpenRouter card configured, every other card empty, most of Brut lit up What you give up: GPT Image sizing (about 1K only), Kling 4K and the Omni / Turbo / 2.6 tiers, Seedance 2.5's 1080p and reference images, Smart Length, Gemini Omni Flash, native inpaint masks (approximate ones work), and the upscalers. Prices are pass-through list rates for text and images; video carries a modest margin.
Which path should you pick? › 3. OpenRouter + fal.ai: a second door, for narrower cases

Two keys instead of one. OpenRouter stays the main door for text, Marcel and the Nano Banana images (its native menus win there). With a fal key as well, GPT Image 2 (with fal's own size presets), Kling 3.0 and Seedance 2.0 run through fal instead; the node's ⇄ chip always says which service runs it. Most people don't need it: start with OpenRouter alone.
Which path should you pick? › The pattern to remember

Keys you add later always take over their models automatically. Start with OpenRouter today, add native keys whenever one provider starts costing real money — nothing to reconfigure, the routes just step aside. Also supported, for narrower cases: a Replicate token (a redundancy door covering roughly what fal covers). It works, but it isn't where we'd start.

Google's Gemini powers Brut's images (the Nano Banana family) and doubles as a text/planning model for Refine and the cinema crew. It's the cheapest place to start — a Nano Banana 2.1 render is about $0.034.

Create an API key at aistudio.google.com/apikey, then paste it into ⚙ Settings → Google Gemini. Enable billing. The free tier has 0 image quota — a first-call 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED means billing isn't on, not that you're being throttled.

Model Notes Nano Banana 2.1 The Flash-tier workhorse since October 2026: 1K → 4K, edits, up to 14 reference pictures, stronger text and multi-character consistency, ~$0.034 at 1K, $0.05 at 2K, $0.076 at 4K Nano Banana 2 Lite Fastest & cheapest (~$0.034, 1K) — text-to-image only Nano Banana 2 Deprecated by Google (no shutdown date announced yet). Its successor is Nano Banana 2.1, at half the price; 512 was its tier alone Nano Banana Pro Studio-quality up to 4K, precise text Nano Banana (legacy) Kept for image edits only — still the cheapest edit (~$0.04) Nano Banana 2 Lite replaced the legacy model on the Text→Image menu: newer, faster, slightly cheaper. The legacy model can't be picked for new text-to-image runs but stays on the Image→Image / Adjust menus, because Lite cannot edit images. Set the aspect ratio and image size on the node. Nano Banana 2 is deprecated. Google released Nano Banana 2.1 on October 6, 2026 and named it the replacement: the same request, the same menus (minus the 512 size), half the price per image, and it is what the Adjust node and the Correction Loop workflow now start on. Google has announced no shutdown date for Nano Banana 2; it stays in the menus until one is named, and a saved graph keeps whatever model its nodes carry. When Google does shut it down, a node still on it fails with Google's own "model not found": pick 2.1 on it (the node generates again on its next run). The file names of past renders keep their NB2 code; new ones say NB21.

Gemini also serves planning (Refine presets, Multi-Shot's planner, and any cinema agent set to Gemini): Gemini 3.8 Flash is the default (the newest and most capable Flash, strong at long planning), Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite the fastest (2.5 Flash's successor at the same price), Gemini 3.6 Flash the previous code/agentic tier (3.6 and 3.8 Flash at Google's introductory $0.75/M in · $3.75/M out through the end of 2026, $1.50 / $7.50 after), with Gemini 2.5 Flash kept for continuity, plus preview tiers. Gemini 3.7 Flash left the menu in October 2026: Google answers every call to it from 3.8 Flash, so a saved graph that still names 3.7 is switched to 3.8 when it opens (the Activity panel says so, and the node plans again on its next run). Gemini 4 Argon is Google's flagship reasoning model: pick it for the hardest plans, long treatments and multi-image analysis that needs deep thought. It reads pictures like the Flash models and works as Marcel's brain (tools included). It is priced like a flagship: $2/M in · $10/M out through November 30, 2026, then $4 / $20, about three times 3.8 Flash today. It thinks before it answers (Google sets the depth; Brut does not change it), and that thinking is billed as output. It is not on Google's free tier. It is a pick in the menus, never a default: a seat with only a Google key gets Gemini 3.8 Flash as Marcel's brain. Dated prices switch by themselves. Google's introductory rates (Argon to the end of November, the 3.6 and 3.8 Flash line to the end of 2026) are shown and counted at today's rate; on the day the offer ends, the picker rows, the estimates and the spend ledger move to the later rate on their own. Repeated prompts cost less. Google reads a long prompt it has just seen (4,096 tokens or more, the same opening) from its cache: Marcel's chat turns, a crew re-plan on the same stills. Those tokens bill at a tenth of the input rate on the Flash models and a twentieth on Argon, and the spend ledger counts them at that rate.

Silent content refusals. An edit that Google silently refuses (no image, no clear error) is a content refusal, usually caused by an input image (a real person's name in facade text, a face, a logo), not the prompt. Deterministic — Brut won't auto-retry. Remove or crop the offending image. Cut-off plans. A plan that comes back cut off is never passed on half-written: you get the full plan or a clear message.

Gemini Omni (video) uses the same Google key by default — you only add a separate key for it to split billing. Google Veo 3.1 rode it too until October 2026: Google ends those video models on the Gemini API on October 22, 2026, and Brut removed them; Gemini Omni is Google's named replacement, and Kling and Seedance stay.
OpenAI provides GPT Image 2, the GPT Image 2.6 pair and the GPT Image 2.5 pair (a Flare and a Sunburst each) for images, and GPT text models for planning.
Create a key at platform.openai.com/api-keys and paste it into ⚙ Settings → OpenAI. Like Gemini, image generation needs a billing-enabled account — a first-call 429 means billing, not a rate limit.

GPT Image 2 — text-to-image and image-to-image. Set the aspect ratio and quality on the node. GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst: the detail tier of OpenAI's newest image generation. Dense compositions, text-heavy layouts and many objects that have to stay in their place, in text-to-image and in edits. Aspect, sizes up to 4K, the five-step quality menu (low · medium · high · xhigh · max) and a Complexity setting. GPT Image 2.6 Flare: the speed tier of the same generation, with the same settings. On release day a 1K picture at high came back in about 10 seconds on Flare and about 50 on Sunburst. Use Flare to explore, then render the keeper on Sunburst. GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst — the quality tier: higher image quality than GPT Image 2, stronger subject preservation, OpenAI's pick "where editing precision matters most". Same aspect and size knobs, and a longer quality menu: low · medium · high · xhigh · max. GPT Image 2.5 Flare — the speed tier: a small model with image quality comparable to GPT Image 2, much faster. Same knobs and the same five-step quality menu. Use it to explore, then render the keeper on Sunburst. GPT Image 2 stays first in the menu and the default for new nodes (and for the Director's proof sheet) for now. Without an OpenAI key, the 2.6 and 2.5 models also run through OpenRouter: the aspect ratio and the full quality menu come through (and Complexity on 2.6), the size stays at about 1K, and masks need the OpenAI key. On 2.6, OpenRouter delivers three shapes only (square, 3:2 and 2:3), so a routed node lists those. The 2.6 models can also output SVG and animated GIFs. Brut does not use those two yet.

GPT Image 2 is token-billed, so the real price depends on size × quality × aspect ratio. Brut ships a measured square-baseline table (from under a cent at 1K low up to ~$0.71 at 4K high) and shows the estimate before any paid run. GPT Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst bill at the same token rates ($8/M image input, $30/M image output, per OpenAI's model pages) but the quality tiers are shifted: 2.5 max bills exactly what GPT Image 2 bills at high (1K $0.21 · 2K $0.43 · 4K $0.71), 2.5 high bills about GPT Image 2's medium (1K $0.054), and low / medium / xhigh sit around them (1K: $0.007 / $0.015 / $0.095). Same output for less, or better output for the same money, your pick. Flare and Sunburst bill identically at every tier, so Brut ships the same fully measured table for both. GPT Image 2.6 has its own table, measured on the day it came out and again the same on Flare and Sunburst. From high up it bills what 2.5 bills (1K: $0.053 / $0.094 / $0.211 at high / xhigh / max; 4K max $0.71). Low and medium cost more than on 2.5: $0.025 and $0.044 at 1K (2.5: $0.007 and $0.015), $0.050 and $0.089 at 2K, $0.083 and $0.147 at 4K. So a quick draft is cheaper on 2.5, and the top tiers cost the same on both generations. Things to know: Non-square is often much cheaper. OpenAI's token accounting can bill a 16:9 4K image at a fraction of a square 4K one (we've measured ~$0.15 vs ~$0.71 on GPT Image 2 at high quality; on 2.5, 16:9 high billed 0.50× / 0.40× / 0.57× the square price at 1K / 2K / 4K, and at 4K a 5:4 image billed 0.82×, 3:2 0.65×), so treat the estimate as an upper ballpark when your aspect isn't square. On 2.6 a 16:9 4K picture billed $0.047 at low, $0.10 at high and $0.40 at max, against $0.083 / $0.178 / $0.71 for the square one; Brut's estimate uses those measured 16:9 and 9:16 prices. Edits add a little on top. Measured on 2.5 at 1K high: an input image adds about $0.007 (a 20 MP render about $0.013), a second input about $0.009, an inpaint mask about $0.0035. On 2.6: an input picture about $0.012 (a 2K-wide one), a second one the same again, and a mask nothing by itself. The ledger holds the truth. Every run records the exact usage-priced amount OpenAI reported, never the estimate — check the spend panel for what a generation really billed.

The 2.6 models can plan a picture before they draw it, and Brut shows that dial as a Complexity select (low · medium · high) on Text → Image, Image → Image, Adjust and Compose whenever a 2.6 model is picked. In the Adjust editor each step has its own Complexity next to its Model, Size and Quality, and a line under it says so when the step will be sent at another setting than the one shown (a reference picture). High is the model's own default and what an untouched node uses. It helps with dense text, complex layouts and pictures where many objects relate to each other. Low is quicker and changes less, which suits a focused edit: a background, a sign, one object. It is separate from Quality, which sets how finely the picture is rendered. It costs nothing by itself: the same picture billed the same at all three settings. Changing it is a new render, like any other setting. Set back to high, the node replays its earlier result for free. On a workflow card, Complexity can be shown as a knob like Quality, and a look saved from a 2.6 node keeps a low or medium setting. The other nodes that render pictures (Multi-Shot, the Storyboard, the Director's proof sheet, the Sketchpad, Conform) run a 2.6 model at its default, high.

GPT-5.4 Mini, GPT-5.5 for Refine and the cinema agents when you choose OpenAI as the planner. GPT-5.6 family — three text tiers with a reasoning dial: Sol ($4/M in · $20/M out — promotional through 2026-11-21, the deepest), Terra ($2/M in · $12/M out, balanced), Luna ($0.20/M in · $1.20/M out, cheap and fast). Available everywhere text models are picked: Text → Text, the cinema agents, and Marcel's model lanes. GPT-6.1 Sol — OpenAI's new middle tier, "near-Astra performance for complex work at a lower cost": $2/M in · $10/M out (cached input $0.10/M; prompts over 272K input tokens bill $4 in / $15 out, and Brut's estimates account for it), 1M-token context, image inputs, reasoning dial low → xhigh (default medium; no none on this one). On your own OpenAI key Marcel can advise on this model but not act on the canvas; through OpenRouter he can. GPT-6 Sol stays listed. GPT-6 Sol and Luna — the two GPT-6 tiers under Astra: Sol ($2/M in · $10/M out, strong reasoning at half of GPT-5.6 Sol's price) and Luna ($0.10/M in · $0.50/M out, the cheapest text model on the OpenAI key). 1M-token context, image inputs, reasoning dial none → xhigh (their default is medium). There is no GPT-6 Terra. Both also run via OpenRouter when you have no OpenAI key; on your own key Marcel runs them with reasoning set to none (see below). GPT-6 Astra — OpenAI's frontier planner: 1M-token context, reasoning dial low → xhigh, $10/M in · $50/M out (long-context prompts bill more). Excellent for the hardest treatments and as a brain for Marcel's advice. One honest limit: on your own OpenAI key Marcel can advise on this model but not act on the canvas; through OpenRouter he can (switch the OpenAI provider off in Settings). Full support on your own key is on the roadmap.

GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 models can think before answering, and Brut exposes the dial: none · low · medium · high · xhigh (leave it on default to let OpenAI pick). Higher settings give deeper answers and cost more — reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens, so an xhigh answer can spend several times the tokens of the visible text. The dial appears on the Text → Text node, on the Director (and the legacy crew agents), and — for Marcel's brain lane — in ⚙ Settings; always only when the selected model actually supports it. Changing it re-plans, like any input change. Marcel on GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Sol / Luna. With your own OpenAI key, Marcel runs these models with reasoning set to none, because OpenAI only lets them act on the canvas at that setting; Settings shows it fixed. Through OpenRouter the dial stays free. Text → Text and the Director keep the full dial. GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.4 Mini have no dial.

OpenAI calls it markup-guided editing: you draw on the picture where each change goes, and the model reads the drawing beside the picture. In Brut that is a marks step of the Adjust node: arrows, boxes, circles, lassos and numbered points, each with its note, an optional color and an optional reference picture. On GPT Image 2.5 and 2.6 (Flare and Sunburst) the marks now go to the model the way OpenAI designed for them. Measured the day 2.6 came out: one mark and two numbered marks landed where they were drawn on both 2.6 models and on 2.5, the rest of the picture stayed as it was, and nothing of the marks showed in the result. A print hung from a mark's reference picture came out closer to the reference than with the earlier technique. GPT Image 2 keeps the earlier technique, and so does any of these models when it runs through OpenRouter. Marks drawn before this build also keep it until you save them again in the editor; nothing you already rendered runs again. A mark, or a mask, with a reference picture on GPT Image 2.6 (Flare and Sunburst) runs at medium Complexity unless you picked low: at high the model sometimes returns the reference picture itself instead of your edited picture (most runs on Sunburst, about one in three on Flare in our use). On 2.5, which has no Complexity setting, it can still happen now and then: Brut keeps your original when it does and marks the take not used, and a new take usually comes out right. Marks or a mask, not both: a step is one or the other, as before.

A mask step of the Adjust node says where the change goes. What the model receives depends on the model: GPT Image 2.5 and 2.6 see the whole picture, with the edge of your mask drawn around the area. They can change what is there (recolor the beams, swap the sofa) as well as add something new. Measured on both 2.6 models and on 2.5: a sofa recolored with its shape kept, a new sky inside the masked area, nothing of the outline left in the result. GPT Image 2 takes OpenAI's own mask, and that mask hides the masked area from the model: it can only paint new content there, it never sees what was under it. So say what goes in the area (a sunset sky, a brass floor lamp), never a change to what is there (make the beams red gives a red shape the size of your stroke). For a recolor on GPT Image 2, use a marks step. Either way the mask steers the change and does not lock the rest: GPT Image redraws the whole image, so the area outside comes back close to the original, not pixel-identical. Adjust keeps the original outside the edit by default (how); by hand, stack the result over the original in a Layers node and mask it to the region you changed. Extending a picture (Conform) still uses OpenAI's own mask, which is the right tool there: the new area is empty. On GPT Image 2.6 that fill is less reliable than on 2.5 (the area can come back black), so Sunburst refuses it before anything is billed and Flare runs it at low Complexity. Edits can lose a few edge pixels. An edit can lose up to 15 pixels at its edges so its size matches what OpenAI renders; nothing is stretched. The output is the input's size. The result comes back at your input's size with a mask, or at the input's shape at the size you pick (1K / 2K / 4K).
A plan that comes back cut off is never passed on half-written: you get the full plan or a clear error.

Kling (by Kuaishou) is Brut's most extensive video provider — a dozen image-to-video models, including the 3.0 line. There are two ways to pay for it: this page covers the REST API (credit packs); see Kling (subscription) for the cheaper plan-billed route.

Kling offers two kinds of key, and Brut accepts both: New style — a key starting with api-key-kling-. Legacy — an AccessKey : SecretKey pair. Paste it into Brut as AccessKey:SecretKey, joined by a colon. Get credentials at app.klingai.com/global/dev and paste into ⚙ Settings → Kling. Heads up on billing: Kling API resource packs expire in 30 days with no rollover. For steady studio use, the subscription option is about 3× cheaper — keep the REST API for many clips in parallel (over 5 requests per second) or Team needs.

Five image-to-video models, the ones Kling's API still serves: Kling 2.5 Turbo, 2.6, 3.0, 3.0 Omni and O1. On the node you set duration, mode and, where the model supports it, audio and an end frame. 2.6 makes sound and takes an end frame in pro mode only; 2.5 Turbo takes an end frame in pro mode only. In standard mode Kling refuses the clip before it starts, nothing billed, and the node shows its message. 3.0 runs 3 to 15 seconds, up to 4k, with an end frame and sound in every mode. O1 runs 5 or 10 seconds. Kling stopped serving its 1.x, 2.0 and 2.1 models on the API, and 3.0 Turbo and 4.0 are not open there: they run on your Kling plan. A saved graph that still names a removed model says so when it runs. Prompts: Kling's API takes at most 2,500 characters for the prompt, and the same for the negative prompt. A longer one is refused on the node, with its length, before anything is sent. Your Kling plan (Kling subscription) takes much longer prompts. Camera moves tremble on Kling 3.0 (standard) image-to-video in our measurements, whatever the wording; a locked-off shot is clean, cleanest at 1080p. Kling 3.0 Omni held the same moves smoothly on the same frames (so did Seedance 2.5): pick it for a moving shot from a still.

Brut uses Kling's international server; mainland China accounts may need help. Aspect ratio and audio on these models aren't fully confirmed; if Kling refuses a setting, its message shows on the node.

The same Kling models, billed to your kling.ai subscription plan instead of API credit packs — measured at roughly 3× cheaper than the REST API, with no 30-day pack expiry. This is the recommended way to run Kling for steady studio work.
How it's authenticated (no key to paste)

There's no API key here. You sign in with a browser sign-in through Kling's official tool, and setup is two buttons on the ⚙ Settings → Kling (subscription) card (or in the setup wizard): Install Kling CLI — one click. Brut downloads Kling's official tool (about 1 MB). Nothing else to install, no admin rights. Log in to Kling — your browser opens on kling.ai; sign in there. Your sign-in stays with Kling's tool on your machine; Brut never stores it. Check login confirms the session any time, and Log out (shown while signed in) drops it — switch accounts by logging out, then logging back in with the other one. Finished generations stay on disk. If Kling ends your sign-in. Kling can end the sign-in saved on your machine from its side. A run then stops with "Your Kling sign-in has expired" before any clip is started, and nothing is billed. The card then reads as signed out and offers Log in to Kling: sign in again, with the same account or another one. Log out on such a sign-in says Kling had already ended it, and the card offers Log in to Kling after any failed Check login. Kept up to date by itself. When Brut installed Kling's tool for you, it checks the tool each time it starts. When Brut needs a newer version, it downloads it in the background a few seconds after start (about 1 MB, the same download as the Install button) and Marcel says so in his panel. Your Kling sign-in is kept. If the download can't happen (offline, for example), Brut keeps using the tool you have and tries again at the next start; until then the card shows Update Kling CLI, and one click does it right away. A Kling tool you installed yourself with npm is yours: Brut never changes it.
