The Kling (subscription) card: Install the CLI, Log in to Kling, and your plan balance once signed in Brut saves every clip to your project right away (watermark-free on a subscription plan).

Kling 2.5 to 4.0, including Omni, Turbo and O1; image-to-video and text-to-video. Kling 4.0 (Kling's newest, added the day its tool listed it): image-to-video and text-to-video from 3 to 30 seconds, at 720p or 1080p, with a first and a last frame, or with up to 9 reference images. Sound is always on (stereo, no switch on these two nodes). Kling announces 4K and 10-bit HDR for 4.0; its tool offers 720p and 1080p for now, so Brut does too. It also edits a clip and borrows its camera on Video → Video (below). It costs 9 credits a second at 720p and 13.5 at 1080p, sound included (measured). On this model the aspect you pick is honored: a 16:9 pick on a portrait start frame gives a 16:9 clip, reframed; leave the ratio on follow the input to keep the frame you composed (the other Kling tiers always follow the start frame). Prompts reach Kling whole, whatever their length: we sent 30,000 characters and the model followed the first and the last line. End frame (tail image): v2.5, v2.6, 3.0 and 4.0 (4.0 without references, below). The omni family (o1, 3.0 Omni) and 3.0 Turbo have no end-frame input. One shot per clip: Kling 3.0 can compose several shots inside one clip (its multi-shot mode, on by default on kling.ai). Brut asks for one continuous shot every time, so a clip is the single move you wrote. Camera moves tremble on Kling 3.0 (standard) from a still, and hold on 3.0 Omni. We measured every move we asked of 3.0 on one keyframe, at 720p and 1080p, with and without the steady-camera wording: the camera path shakes as much as it moves; a locked-off shot is clean, cleanest at 1080p. The same six shots on Kling 3.0 Omni came out smooth (a third of the tremor, real moves), as did Seedance 2.5 at about twice the price per clip. For a moving shot from a still, pick Omni. Reference images: o1 and 3.0 Omni take up to 6 extra references besides the start frame — the Image → Video node grows a references inlet when you pick them. Kling 4.0 takes up to 9: its image-to-video has no place for a reference, so with references wired the clip runs as Kling's Omni-Ref, which opens on your start picture and carries the people and things of the references into it. Omni-Ref has no end frame: with an end frame AND references wired on 4.0, the node says to unwire one, before anything is sent. The node says when a clip runs as Omni-Ref. It costs the same as a plain 4.0 clip at 720p: 9 credits a second, sound included (measured); at 1080p with references the price line reads $? until measured. Video to video: 3.0 Omni and 4.0 edit a clip, borrow its camera for a new shot, or turn a 3D preview into a finished shot (4.0 takes a clip up to 30 s and up to 10 pictures beside it and keeps the clip's length on an edit); 3.0 and 2.6 Motion Control make a picture of a person or animal perform a clip's motion. See Video → Video. It needs the current Kling tool, which Brut keeps up to date by itself; if your card still shows Update Kling CLI, click it once (your sign-in is kept).

Three tiers carry a measured price: v2.5 (3 credits a second at 720p without audio, ~3× cheaper than API list), 3.0 Omni (6 credits a second at 720p, 8 at 1080p, without audio, measured on sixteen clips) and 4.0 (9 credits a second at 720p and 13.5 at 1080p, sound included, measured on seven clips). On 3.0 Omni, editing a clip costs about 9 credits a second at 720p (measured); on 4.0 about 10.8 credits a second of output (measured on two edits; the source clip's length is not added). Their audio surcharge, their other resolutions and the other tiers show no estimate until measured — Brut never invents a price it hasn't confirmed. When this provider is selected on an Image → Video or Film Shots node, the node shows your live plan balance ("🎟 Plan balance: 5,786 credits · Pro") — refreshed after every run — and Film Shots repeats it in the paid-run confirmation, so you always know where your credits stand before and after a batch.
No Kling sign-in? The menu still works

If you pick a Kling (subscription) model without the Kling sign-in, Brut falls back to an aggregator you do hold: Kling 3.0 and O1 route through your OpenRouter key, visibly marked ⇄ runs via … on the node (the provider and model pickers say so before you pick). (O1 via OpenRouter takes 5 or 10 s at 720p, no reference images.) Models OpenRouter doesn't carry (2.5, 2.6, 3.0 Omni, 3.0 Turbo, 4.0) say exactly that: they need the Kling sign-in (4.0: the sign-in alone for now).

Up to 5 requests per second, Personal workspace only, and tasks can't be cancelled provider-side. A plan without a subscription runs one clip at a time (even with credits on it: kling.ai treats it as a trial, and the clip carries a watermark). On Film Shots, the clips Kling refuses for running beside another wait and run after the others, one by one, and their row says so on hover. Subscribe on kling.ai for parallel clips and the watermark-free master. Sign in once on each computer. For higher throughput or Team workspaces, use the REST API instead.
Google's Gemini Omni Flash is a fast natively-multimodal video model: picture and sound generated together, a clip in under a minute, about $1 per clip.
The key: it rides your Gemini key

Omni uses the same Google key as Gemini by default. If you've added a Gemini key, Omni just works; Settings shows it uses your Gemini key. Add a dedicated key in ⚙ Settings → Gemini Omni only to split the billing.

Image-to-video from a start frame, optionally with an end frame (the two-image interpolation), and text-to-video. 3 to 10 seconds, 16:9 or 9:16, output at 360p, 720p, 1080p or 4k. Note that 1080p and 4k are upscales of the 720p render, not a sharper generation; if you plan a Topaz pass anyway, generate at 720p. Reference images on the references inlet: extra images of a subject (a product, a character, a facade) the clip should stay faithful to. Name them in the prompt. Audio is always on. There is no switch; describe the sound you want, or say "no dialogue, no music, natural ambience only". Every clip carries Google's invisible SynthID watermark. Omni has no negative prompt of its own: what you type in the node's negative prompt still reaches the model, as part of the prompt. The Gemini Omni video prompt preset in Refine writes the flowing-prose prompt style Omni reads best.
Pricing: flat per clip, so ask for 10 seconds

Google's page says "about $0.10 per second at 720p", but Google bills every clip the same, about $1.01, whatever its length or resolution (360p and 720p measured; 1080p and 4K show $?). The practical rule: ask for 10 seconds (the node defaults to it) and trim in the Sequence node if you want less. Your spend panel shows the amount Google billed; if Google's billing page shows you something different, tell us. Google keeps the interaction (your prompt, inputs and the clip) on its side for a while after it completes; that is what lets Omni edit its own earlier clips. Brut doesn't use that yet: editing and extending clips arrive with the Video → Video node later, together with the region note that matters for European users (Google doesn't allow editing or extending uploaded videos from the EEA, Switzerland or the UK; editing clips Omni generated itself is allowed).

Anthropic's Claude joins Brut as a planning model — text only. It generates no images or video; it's there to be your director: writing the concept, look and shot plan on the Director node, and powering the Refine node.

Sonnet 5.5 is Anthropic's newest Sonnet: faster and sharper than Sonnet 5, at the same price. Marcel's default brain. With an Anthropic key, Marcel's Auto brain is now Sonnet 5.5 (it was Sonnet 5). A brain you picked yourself in ⚙ Settings → Marcel stays picked. In every model picker: the Director, the crew agents, Text→Text, Refine and Marcel. It runs on your Anthropic key, or through OpenRouter at the same rates. Price: $2 in / $10 out per million tokens, the same as Sonnet 5. Marcel's long system context is cached, so after the first message of a session each turn costs cents. Reasoning goes from low to max (default high). Thinking off means no thinking before acting on this model, and works at low, medium or high effort only. Details under Reasoning dial & thinking switch. Marcel keeps talking while he works. Marcel keeps writing short notes between his actions, so you can follow what he does.

Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic's new small model: a tenth of Haiku 4.5's price, a 1M-token context, and the same two knobs as the big Claudes. The narrator's new default. With an Anthropic key, Marcel's Auto narrator lane (failure diagnoses, run commentary, recaps, the quiet taste passes) now runs on Haiku 5.5. A narrator you picked yourself stays picked. It is also in every text picker: the Director, the crew agents, Text→Text, Refine and Marcel's brain. Price: $0.10 in / $0.50 out per million tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens. Over 100,000 tokens a prompt pays five times that ($0.50 / $2.50): the one current Claude priced by prompt length. Brut's estimates account for it. A long chat on Marcel's full knowledge can pass the line; the narrator's few hundred tokens never do. Reasoning goes from low to max; thinking is adaptive by default and switches off cleanly (a plain off, unlike Sonnet 5.5's "no thinking before acting"). Runs on your Anthropic key, or through OpenRouter at the same base rates.
Create a key in the Anthropic Console and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Anthropic (Claude). Brut checks it when you save.

Anywhere Brut asks "which LLM should plan this?" — the Director (and the legacy crew agents), Text→Text and the Refine presets — you can pick Claude, Gemini or GPT. Claude reads your stills and writes the plan.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic's newest Sonnet), Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 carry the knobs Brut exposes wherever these models run — the Text→Text node, the cinema agents, and Marcel's brain lane: Reasoning effort (low to max): how deeply the model reasons before answering. Deeper = better on hard treatments, more output tokens billed. Claude's own default is high on every model but Opus 5.5, whose default is medium: on 5.5, set the dial when you want the deep end. Thinking switch (Marcel's brain, ⚙ Settings): Claude Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 5 think adaptively by default, and those thinking tokens bill as output tokens — so if Marcel feels slow or a chat turn costs more than expected, switching thinking off is the lever: faster, cheaper, a little shallower. The switch needs your own Anthropic key; it isn't available through OpenRouter. Opus 5.5 has no switch: its thinking is always on (Anthropic rejects "off"), so the row reads not supported and the cost lever there is a low effort. On Sonnet 5.5, off means "no thinking before acting": Anthropic's lowest setting on that model still lets it write short progress notes between actions, and it works at low, medium or high effort only (with the dial at xhigh or max, Brut asks you to lower it or turn thinking back on). Haiku 5.5 carries both knobs too (thinking adaptive by default, a plain off). Haiku 4.5 supports neither.

Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / $10 per million tokens in / out): Marcel's default brain and the everyday planner, faster and sharper than Sonnet 5 at the same price. Sonnet 5 ($2 / $10): the previous Sonnet, still listed for graphs and lanes that picked it. Opus 5.5 ($4 / $20): the powerhouse brain, Opus-tier reasoning below Opus 5's price. On this model, repeated context in long Marcel sessions costs half the usual. Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 ($5 / $25): still listed for graphs and lanes that picked them. Haiku 5.5 ($0.10 / $0.50 up to 100K tokens of prompt, $0.50 / $2.50 above): the narrator lane, and the cheapest Claude for Refine and Multi-Shot plans. Haiku 4.5 ($1 / $5): the previous narrator, still listed for lanes that picked it. List prices as of October 2026; the spend panel shows what you were actually billed.

A plan that comes back cut off is never passed on half-written: you get the full plan or a clear error. For available model names and pricing, see Anthropic's console; Brut's catalog lists the ones it exposes.

Seedance (BytePlus ModelArk) is ByteDance's video family with native audio: a clip comes with sound in one pass. Brut carries Seedance 2.5 (the current flagship), Seedance 2.0, and the 2.0 family's two cheaper tiers, Fast and Mini.

Create a ModelArk key in the BytePlus console and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Seedance. The same key serves Seedream images. Activate the model first. ModelArk models are switched on per account: open the console's Model activation page and activate each model you will run (Seedance 2.5, 2.0, and the Seedream models) before the first call. It is a one-time switch. Until then every request fails with "Your account … has not activated the model dreamina-seedance-2-5-260628"; Brut shows that message verbatim on the node. How BytePlus bills you. Everything is pay-as-you-go, and resource packs are optional: Credits (recommended): prepaid by card from Billing → Billing overview in the console, minimum USD 5 per top-up, they never expire, and the balance is a hard ceiling on spend. A balance of USD 30 unlocks the Seedance family (Seedream needs no minimum). Automatic billing: a bound card charged when consumption reaches a threshold (USD 50 by default) and on the 2nd of each month. No ceiling on BytePlus's side, so Brut's project budget caps are the ceiling. Resource packs are optional: one model each, 90 days, priced at the list rate, outside promotions. An activated model keeps running on the card or the credits after any pack is used up. A Savings Plan exists too; you do not need one. PayPal-only accounts cannot run pay-as-you-go ModelArk: add a card, or buy a pack.

Seedance 2.5 (first in the menu): Image-to-video from a start frame, or start + end frame, and text-to-video. 4 to 30 seconds in one clip, or smart length (the model picks). Long single takes are its headline. 480p, 720p, 1080p (1080p is 10-bit HEVC: it plays in VLC/mpv and modern browsers; older players may refuse it). Up to 30 reference images on the references inlet (a Reference Board plugs in). Address them in the prompt as @Image1, @Image2… in wiring order and say what each supplies ("@Image1 is the building, copy its materials exactly"). The clip's aspect ratio follows the start frame. Seedance 2.5 refuses a ratio on frame-to-video runs, so the node hides the aspect select and says so. Text-to-video keeps the full menu (16:9, 9:16, 4:3, 3:4, 21:9, 1:1). Draft mode: a 480p draft take costs exactly what a 480p clip costs, and for seven days it can be re-rendered as the same shot at 1080p, billed like a 1080p clip. Explore at 480p, pay 1080p only for keepers. In Brut: the Draft take box on Image → Video, Text → Video and Video → Video (and Draft takes on Film Shots), then ⬆ Render final. Your own BytePlus key only. Native audio on by default (it costs nothing extra). Prompt grammar: integer-second beats (0-3s: …, 3-8s: …), () for music, <> for sound effects, {} for dialogue, "no BGM" / "no audio" when you want silence. The Seedance 2.5 video prompt preset in Refine writes this structure for you; Seedance 2.5 shot plan rewrites a whole cinema plan in it. A voice. The Voice row on Image → Video and Text → Video takes a recording (2 to 30 s, 15 MB at most, mp3 or wav best; other audio files are converted first) and the person in the start picture speaks its words in its voice, lips on the words. The recording reaches Seedance as a link from your own storage, like a Video → Video clip (the next section), and is deleted from your bucket when the job ends. With a recording the start frame is approximate, as with reference images. Your own BytePlus key only. Seedance 2.0: 4 to 15 seconds (or smart length), up to 4K, first/last frame, reference images, and it accepts an explicit aspect ratio on frame-to-video runs. Still the choice when you need 4K straight out of the model. Its grammar is different (shot labels rather than timestamps, full-width audio symbols): use the Seedance 2.0 video prompt and Seedance 2.0 shot plan presets for it. Both generations stay in the menu; pick per job. Seedance 2.0 Fast and Seedance 2.0 Mini are the same family at a lower rate: 4 to 15 seconds (or smart length), 480p and 720p only, first and last frame, text-to-video, up to 9 reference images, native audio, the 2.0 prompt grammar (so the Seedance 2.0 video prompt preset). No draft mode: that is 2.5's. Mini is the cheapest video in Brut, about $0.18 for a 5-second 480p clip at list price; use it to test a move before paying for the 2.5 or 2.0 render. Both also run through OpenRouter. Watermark is always off. Video editing and video references are the Video → Video node; a voice reference is the Voice row above; video extension is still to come. No BytePlus key? Both generations also run through an OpenRouter key, marked ⇄ runs via OpenRouter on the node. Seedance 2.5 there is 480p/720p only, 4 to 30 s, first and last frame, no reference images, no smart length and no draft mode, billed per video token at the same rate as BytePlus (the ledger records the exact billed amount). The 1080p tier, the 30-reference workflow and draft mode need your own BytePlus key.
Video to video: your own storage

Seedance 2.5 runs on the Video → Video node: Borrow the camera (a new shot that follows a clip's move and timing, rebuilt from your prompt and up to 30 pictures), Edit the clip (the clip kept, what you name changed, with 1 to 5 pictures of what to use; a 4 to 30 s clip), and 3D preview to real shot (a playblast rendered as a finished shot; the look comes from the wired pictures, best a render of the same view, and when a picture is framed differently the prompt says which figure of the clip it is and describes the shot as the clip frames it). Seedance makes its own sound: the node's box reads Generate audio. Seedance takes a clip only as a link, never as a file in the request, so it needs a place to fetch it from: your own storage on BytePlus, set up once. In the BytePlus console, create an IAM user with programmatic access and the TOS (object storage) rights, plus the Ark rights if you want to register pictures as assets (below), and note its access key and secret key. Create a private TOS bucket in the ap-southeast-1 region (the one ModelArk runs in). Add a lifecycle rule on the bucket that deletes objects under brut/ after one day: a safety net, since Brut deletes each clip itself. In ⚙ Settings → BytePlus storage, paste ACCESS_KEY:SECRET_KEY:bucket (add :region at the end if your bucket is elsewhere). Brut checks that the key reaches the bucket before saving it. For each run, the clip and the pictures go from your machine to your bucket, BytePlus fetches them through links that expire after a few hours, and Brut deletes them when the job ends (a request BytePlus never answers leaves them to the one-day rule). A recording on the Voice row of Image → Video or Text → Video takes the same road: your bucket, an expiring link, deleted when the job ends; the pictures of that run stay in the request as they always do. Before it leaves, the clip is fitted to what Seedance accepts: a 720-pixel short side (larger clips go down, smaller ones up) and 24 to 60 frames a second; the node shows the size it goes out at. A clip outside 2 to 30 seconds, or narrower than 0.4 or wider than 2.5 (width over height), is refused before anything is sent. People. Seedance refuses real-looking faces in the pictures you wire unless BytePlus made them or you registered them as assets (the next section); the same goes for faces in the clip itself. Architecture, products and places need nothing. Cost. BytePlus bills a run with a clip in tokens at its with-video rate ($6.40 per million at 480p and 720p, $7.00 at 1080p, list), counting the clip you send and the clip you get. The node asks first and the ledger row shows what BytePlus reports.
People: register your pictures as BytePlus assets

Seedance refuses a picture that looks like it contains a real person, a generated face included, in every role: a start frame, an end frame, a reference, a picture beside a clip. Two kinds of pictures pass: the ones BytePlus's own models made on your account (a Seedream picture made from text, a frame of a Seedance clip, see the gotcha below) and the ones you registered in your BytePlus asset library. The Seedance assets node does the registering: Wire the pictures into it: a Character Lab output, an Image → Image, an Image In, anything that makes or holds a picture. The same pictures flow out of the node, so it sits anywhere on the way to an Image → Video, a Storyboard or a Video → Video. Name the Set (the name of the group the pictures are filed under: a character's name, a project's; the node proposes your project's name) and click Register. Each picture goes to your own bucket, BytePlus copies it into your asset library, and the bucket copy is deleted at once. It takes a second a picture; the node's rows say which pictures are registered and under which id. Run the video node as usual. Brut remembers a registration by the picture's content, so a registered picture is accepted wherever it is wired from, in every graph and every project, as long as the asset exists on your account. The Image → Video face's green line says so, and the ledger row of a clip lists the asset ids it went out on. Pick from Elements. To use a person you registered before, in another graph, another project or by hand in the BytePlus console, click Pick from Elements… on the node: your Elements vault opens, filtered to the pictures Seedance accepts (the first time, every asset of your BytePlus account is brought into the vault under Brut/Cast, so the list is the account's library; without the storage key it is what this machine registered). Tick the ones you want and click Use: each picture flows out of the node with the wired ones, already bound to its asset id, so Seedance accepts the person in it in every role. A picked picture shows on the node as a full-width tile with a ✕ on the picture that takes it off the node and nothing else; the asset stays in your library and in the vault. Untick the Seedance-approved chip to pick any picture of the vault and register it. Nothing is typed: the Set field is a name, never a place for an asset id. Registered pictures also appear in the vault on their own, with a ✓, so a character registered once is one drag away in every project. Registering is free: the free BytePlus plan holds 50 assets in 50 sets, about three registrations a minute. Nothing is registered without your click and nothing is removed on its own: tick assets in the library, or on ⚙ Settings → BytePlus storage (the same library, every asset of the account), and click Delete from library: they leave BytePlus after a confirmation and free their slots. It uses the same storage key as video to video (the access key needs the Ark rights beside the TOS ones). A picture registered by hand in the console's asset page binds the same way: paste its id (asset-…) in the field under the picture's row, or pick it from the library. With the storage key Brut checks the id first; without it the binding is taken as is and Seedance tells at the first run. A frame or a reference. Wired as a reference, a registered person lands in the scene the start frame shows (a photo of someone registered in one set, wired beside a warehouse picture, danced in that warehouse). Wired as the start frame with a prompt that describes another scene, Seedance kept the person and followed the prompt rather than the picture's framing in the one run we have. When the framing matters, make the frame with the person in it and wire the registered picture as a reference beside it. Whose faces. Registering is your statement that you hold the rights to the people in the picture: generated characters are yours; a client's real face needs their consent, and BytePlus asks for an authorization letter in the console once per account. Pictures of a person BytePlus's moderation refuses as an asset are reported on the node, and nothing is kept.

Every clip comes with its last frame. The clip's final frame arrives as an image (at the clip's exact size, no watermark, not billed), kept beside the clip. On Image → Video, ⏭ Last frame → Image In drops it on the canvas: wire it into the next clip's start frame to continue the shot. Because BytePlus made that frame, the people in it are accepted as a start frame (measured; see the faces gotcha below). References loosen the start frame. Seedance cannot take an exact start frame and reference images in the same clip. With references wired into Image → Video, the start (and end) frame guide the clip instead of fixing it: the framing is approximate rather than pixel-exact, and the clip's aspect follows the start frame. The node says so on its references line; wire no references to keep the exact first-frame behaviour. Photoreal faces are refused in start frames and reference images, generated or not. ModelArk's moderation blocks start frames, reference images and videos that look like they contain a real person, and it cannot tell an AI-generated face from a photograph (field-tested: a fully generated woman was refused as "may contain real person"). Only faces made by ModelArk's own models under your account, their preset digital characters, or authorized-person assets pass. Brut carries the first of those: people generated by Seedream 5.0 on your own key are trusted as Seedance start frames and references for 30 days, and the trust survives a resize or a re-export. The rule we measured: a Seedream picture made from text passes on Lite, Pro and Flash, and so does a frame of a Seedance clip; an edit (Image → Image) is refused like a picture from any other maker, on every Seedream model, and a crop of an accepted picture is refused too. The refusal message on the node names the refused picture (the start frame, reference 2) and the two ways past it. The general one is the Seedance assets node above: a picture from any model, edits and crops included, registered once and accepted from then on. A populated archviz render from another model can trip this too; register it, or wire a version without people and bring them in with the video prompt, or do character swaps on Gemini Omni or Kling Omni, whose gates accept generated people. Heavy pictures. BytePlus takes at most 64 MB in one request and 30 MB per picture. On Image → Video, Brut refuses a heavier set before anything is sent and names the picture to shrink: Export JPG from the picture's right-click menu makes a copy of a few MB that looks the same. On Video → Video the pictures travel through your bucket like the clip, so their size is no problem there. Three concurrent tasks per individual account. When Film Shots runs more clips than that, the extra ones queue on BytePlus's side and finish a little later; nothing fails. A draft can be finalized for seven days; at the very edge BytePlus may refuse, and the node says so.
Pricing, read this before you buy credits

Seedance's billing has two sharp edges (how to pay at all is under Get a key above): Credit packs are model-bound, and optional. A Seedance 2.5 pack does not cover 2.0 (or the fast/mini tiers), and vice versa. Buy the pack that matches the model you'll run, or stay pay-as-you-go on credits or your card. Rates are per token, and tokens depend on resolution and on whether the request contains video. BytePlus's list rates, as approximate prices per second: Seedance 2.5 ~ per second (16:9, no video input) 480p $0.10 720p $0.23 1080p $0.57 Seedance 2.0 ~ per second 480p $0.07 720p $0.15 1080p $0.37 4K $0.78 Seedance 2.0 Fast / Mini ~ per second (16:9, no video input, list price) Fast, 480p $0.056 Fast, 720p $0.12 Mini, 480p $0.035 Mini, 720p $0.076 The node shows the estimate before you run, and Film Shots itemizes it per clip. The ledger row is priced from BytePlus's own token count, not from the estimate, so what you see in the spend readout is what you were billed. Failed generations cost nothing. A draft take bills like a 480p clip and its final like a 1080p clip: no discount on either, the saving is that you render 1080p only for the shots you keep, and the final is the same shot, not a new roll of the dice.

Seedream (BytePlus ModelArk) is ByteDance's image family. Brut carries the Seedream 5.0 trio: Pro, Flash and Lite, for text-to-image and image-to-image, on the same BytePlus key as Seedance. It is the cheapest photoreal tier in Brut, and the one BytePlus trusts for people that Seedance will animate.

Nothing new to paste. Seedream rides your Seedance key automatically: ⚙ Settings → Seedream reads uses your Seedance (BytePlus) key. Set a key there only to split Seedream's billing from Seedance's. Activate the models first. Like every ModelArk model, each one is switched on once per account: open the console's Model activation page (console.byteplus.com/ark) and activate Seedream 5.0 Pro, Seedream 5.0 Flash and Seedream 5.0 Lite. No resource pack is needed: activation is a one-time switch and the images bill pay-as-you-go on the account's credits or card (see Seedance, pricing). Until then a call fails with "has not activated the model", shown verbatim on the node. Lite comes with a free quota of 50 images.

Model Sizes Price per image Inputs Seedream 5.0 Pro 1K · 1.5K · 2K $0.045 at 1K and 1.5K, $0.09 at 2K; from the second input image $0.003 each up to 10 reference images Seedream 5.0 Flash 1K · 1.5K · 2K $0.018, any size up to 10 reference images Seedream 5.0 Lite 2K · 3K · 4K $0.035, any size up to 14 reference images Pro is the quality tier (BytePlus's pick for "commercial visual production": precise editing, lifelike scenes). Flash is the same family at a third of the price, for exploration and high-volume passes. Lite is the older line with the biggest canvases and 50 free images. Typical speed: Flash about 15 s for a 1K image, Pro about 30 s, Lite about 75 s at 2K. 1.5K bills like 1K and BytePlus calls it the better quality pick, so Pro and Flash default to it; Lite defaults to 2K. All three appear wherever an image model is picked: Text → Image, Image → Image, Adjust, Compose, Multi-Shot, the Storyboard's keyframes, the Sketchpad's generation layers, the workflow cards' Model knobs. On a marks step of the Adjust node, Pro and Flash read the marks; Lite does not.

Exact sizes. A picture comes back at the size the menu names (a 16:9 image at 1K is 1424 × 800, at 2K 2816 × 1584). On an edit, aspect auto keeps the input's own proportions, and when the input already sits in the size you picked (a 2048 × 1143 render at 1.5K, say) it comes back at exactly its own dimensions. Pick a bigger or smaller size and the output moves to that size at the input's aspect, so the picture is resampled. Edits: Same as the picture. On Image → Image, Adjust and Compose, the Size menu opens with Same as the picture on all three Seedream models, and it is what the node takes when you switch it to Seedream. The result comes back at the input's pixel dimensions (the scene's, on Compose), so it lays over the original in a Layers or Compare node with nothing to scale. Each model's range sets the limit: Pro and Flash 0.9 to 4.6 MP, Lite 3.7 to 16.8 MP; below it the picture comes back at the model's smallest size, above it at its largest, the proportions kept. A node that already carries a picked size keeps it, and a stage hidden inside a workflow card keeps the size its card set: both have "Same as the picture" one pick away. PNG, lossless downstream (Layers, PSD export, Seedance frames), and watermark off: BytePlus stamps an "AI-generated" mark bottom right by default, Brut always turns it off. Input limits. Your pictures go in at full size and quality, within BytePlus's limits: 30 MB per image, 196 px² to 36 MP, both sides above 14 px, aspect between 1:16 and 16:1. A picture outside them stops the run before the call, with a clear message naming the fix. Masks are guidance. Seedream has no native mask input, so on a mask step of the Adjust node the mask steers the edit, as on Gemini. Strong steering, never a pixel lock; the step keeps the original outside the edit by default. Brut saves every image to your project as soon as it's ready.
People for Seedance: the trusted path

Several pictures on Image → Image blend. Seedream treats two or more wired pictures as references for a new composition (BytePlus calls it multi-image blending): no picture is the base, and the framing follows the richest one. A clay frame wired first with a portrait second came back as the portrait, reshaped to the frame's aspect, on Pro and on Flash; Nano Banana 2.1 rendered the frame. To keep one picture's framing and bring a subject in, use a marks step of the Adjust node on Seedream (a box on the place, the subject as the mark's reference), or an Image → Image on Nano Banana or GPT Image. ModelArk's moderation refuses Seedance start frames and references that look like they contain a real person, and it cannot tell a generated face from a photograph (see the Seedance gotchas). The exception BytePlus documents: face-containing images generated by Seedream on your own account are trusted as Seedance 2.x input for 30 days. Seedance's own clips and their frames are trusted the same way. We measured it with real requests and a clear face in frame, on Seedance 2.5, 2.0 Fast and 2.0 Mini, as a start frame and as a reference: The picture Seedance Seedream text-to-image, on Lite, Pro or Flash, the whole picture accepted One text-to-image character sheet (several views and expressions in one picture) accepted A frame of a Seedance clip (its last frame, or one taken from the middle) accepted Any Seedream edit (Image → Image), on Lite, Pro or Flash, even of a text-to-image picture refused A crop of an accepted picture refused The same portrait made by another maker refused A resize and a re-export (PNG, JPEG) keep the trust. A crop loses it, and so does anything that redraws the picture. What this means in practice: One populated picture: write it as a Text → Image prompt on any Seedream model and wire the result, uncropped, into Image → Video. A character: the picture Seedance accepts is the one made from text. The Character Lab makes the person as one picture, a 16:9 sheet with a bust and the full body from the front, both sides and the back: pick a Seedream model on its Model knob, wire nothing into character, and the sheet is a text-to-image picture Seedance accepts as a reference. With a picture wired into character, the sheet is an edit and Seedance refuses the face in it: register it as a BytePlus asset first (Seedance assets). Continuing a shot: the last frame of a Seedance clip is accepted as the next clip's start frame. People added to an existing render (an edit): refused when a face shows. Put the people in with the video prompt instead. When Seedance refuses a picture, the node's message says which wired picture it was (the start frame, reference 2) and repeats this rule. And before any run, the Image → Video node shows which wired pictures carry the trust: see the trust line.

Seedream 5.0 Pro and Flash can split one flat picture into a base (the scene with the elements lifted out and the gaps filled in) plus up to 16 layers with transparency, each with a name, a description and its place in the picture. In Brut: right-click any picture → Decompose into layers… (outputs, imports, board tiles, the magnifier), or Decompose result… under a Layers node's result. A small form asks for the model (Flash by default: the cheapest, and the one measured), the size and, if you want, what to separate ("the sky, the building, the trees in front, the people"). Leave that empty and the model picks the main elements itself. The price is shown before anything is spent. BytePlus bills every picture it returns, the base included: $0.018 each on Flash; on Pro $0.0225 each up to 2.61 MP and $0.045 above, each picture on its own pixels. How many layers come back is the model's call, so the dialog states the ceiling (16 layers and the base, 17 pictures: $0.31 on Flash) and the ledger row is priced from what actually came back. Measured on Flash: a 2752 × 1536 render split into a base and three layers (the sky, the building, the trees) in just under a minute for $0.072. The result lands as a new Sketchpad beside the picture: the base at the bottom, every layer above it in stacking order, scaled into its place and named by the model, and the original on top, hidden, one click on its eye away for a comparison. The node shows the recomposed picture at once. From there: move, scale, hide or mask a layer, paint between them, add a generation layer, or Export PSD and carry on in Photoshop. Right-click a render, Decompose into layers: the price, then a Sketchpad with the pergola, the bench, the building and each tree as its own layer The details: Size. Same as the picture (the default) brings the base back at the picture's own dimensions when it sits between 0.9 and 4.6 MP, so the stack lines up with the original pixel for pixel; a smaller picture comes back at 1K, a larger one at 2K. With this setting each layer also comes back at exactly its size in the picture, so nothing is rescaled. Or pick 1K, 1.5K or 2K yourself: the layers then come back near that resolution, usually larger than their place in the picture (detail to spare if you scale one up), and Brut scales them into place. One picture in, from 512 × 512 px to 36 MP, up to 30 MB, in any common format (PNG, JPEG, WEBP, TIFF), with no quality lost. The model lifts each element out whole. Trees that stood behind a hedge can come back with their full trunks, which then show in front of the base. The words you give it steer what comes back; and in the Sketchpad a layer mask hides the part that should stay behind (select the layer, add a mask, paint black over the trunks). All or nothing. If one layer fails on BytePlus's side the whole call fails, and the message is shown as it came. Nothing lands on the canvas. Your own BytePlus key. The ability is not sold through OpenRouter: on a seat without the key the menu item stays in place, greyed, and says why. Every file is kept in the project's outputs, named after the run (…_sketch-12-layers_seedream_SR5F_…, then -2, -3 in stacking order). Find in ledger on the Sketchpad's preview, or on any of the files, shows the run with its cost.

On Seedream 5.0 Pro and Flash, a marks step of the Adjust node places each edit where you marked it. Draw your marks as usual, pick Seedream for the step, generate: each mark lands where you drew it, and nothing of the markup shows in the result. An arrow points with its tip, a point marks a spot. A box, circle, lasso or polygon marks the area around it, not its exact outline: when an area holds several things, name the one you mean in the note. A mark's reference image and its color chip travel with that mark. Size: Same as the picture is the default on Adjust for Seedream: the result comes back at the picture's own dimensions (between 0.9 and 4.6 MP; a smaller picture comes back at 1K, a larger one at 2K), so the result and the original stack at the same size in a Layers node. Pick 1K, 1.5K or 2K to resample instead. The same size is not the same pixels: the model redraws the frame, and a result can sit a few pixels off its original (3 to 6 px on a 2752 × 1536 scene we measured). Adjust lays the result back over the original by itself and keeps only the edits: everything else is the original's own pixels (how it works). Five marks on a render, one of each kind, Seedream Flash on the node: each edit lands at its mark, for under two cents Measured on a 2048 × 1143 interior with five marks, one of each kind: both models applied all five at their marks and returned 2048 × 1143; Flash in 21 s for $0.018, Pro in 41 s for $0.045 (Pro matched the asked RAL green more closely). A second run placed an armchair from a reference image inside a box, turned the way the note asked, on both. The same marks on Nano Banana 2 were all applied too, with two of them placed loosely. The table is on the Adjust page.

The node shows the per-image price before the run (the output price: $0.045 / $0.018 / $0.035, Pro 2K $0.09). The ledger row is priced from what came back: the actual output pixels decide the tier (1K and 1.5K bill the same; above 2.61 MP is the 2K rate), and Pro's input-image surcharge is added from the count BytePlus reports ($0.003 per input after the first). A moderation refusal is not billed and the node says so. A decomposition bills per picture returned (the base and each layer), at its own rate: $0.018 on Flash, $0.0225 or $0.045 on Pro. The price dialog states the ceiling, the ledger the real amount. No BytePlus key? All three also run through an OpenRouter key, marked ⇄ runs via OpenRouter on the node, with OpenRouter's size menu (1K / 2K for Pro and Flash, 2K / 4K for Lite; no 1.5K or 3K there) at OpenRouter's listed pass-through prices. The ledger records the exact billed amount of every routed job.

Lite's smallest output is 2K (its pixel floor is 3.7 MP); Pro and Flash render between 0.9 and 4.6 MP. The size menus follow each model. Why Pro and Flash stop at 2K. It is BytePlus's limit, not Brut's: those two models render at most 4.62 MP, which is a 2K picture (2816 × 1584 at 16:9). 3K and 4K exist on Lite only. For a 4K Seedream picture, use Lite on Text → Image, Image → Image, Adjust (a mask step) or Compose; for a 4K result from a Pro or Flash edit, add an Upscale Image node after it. BytePlus recommends prompts under about 600 English words: longer prompts lose details rather than gain them. Sequential sets (Lite, up to 15 related images in one call) and transparent-background edits exist on the API and are planned for Brut. Layer decomposition and marked edits are in: see Decompose into layers and marks on Adjust.

Black Forest Labs makes the FLUX models. Brut calls their own API with your key, for three things: FLUX 3 Image, their flagship image model, in every image menu (Text → Image, Image → Image, Compose, Adjust, Multi-Shot, the Storyboard's keyframes, the Sketchpad's generation layers). FLUX 3 Image Klein, its small sibling, in the same menus: the same sizes, frames and pictures in, for about a fifth of the price at 1K. FLUX Outpaint, their outpainting tool, as a painter in Conform's extend. It is the one painter in Brut that holds your picture in place and generates only what the frame adds.

Create an account on the Black Forest Labs dashboard, add credits, make an API key and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Black Forest Labs. Billing is prepaid credits: 1 credit is $0.01, and a call on an empty balance answers "not enough credits". There is no subscription. Every answer says what the call cost, and that number is what Brut writes on the ledger row. No key? FLUX 3 Image and Klein also run through OpenRouter on an OpenRouter key (the node says "⇄ via OpenRouter"). FLUX Outpaint is on Black Forest Labs' own API only: no aggregator carries it.

Sizes 768, 1K, 1.5K, 2K, 4K. These are pixel budgets, the same at every ratio: about 0.6, 1, 2.4, 4 and 17 megapixels. Ratios Every ratio on Brut's menu, plus auto on an edit: the output keeps the first picture's framing. Pictures in Up to 10 per request, from 256 px a side. A picture over 16 megapixels is sent resized to 16 (the API's cap); above 4 megapixels Black Forest Labs scales a reference down to 4 before it works on it anyway. Price Per image, by size: $0.041 (768), $0.048 (1K), $0.07 (1.5K), $0.10 (2K), $0.607 (4K). Reference pictures and the prompt cost nothing extra; a refused request is not charged. Things worth knowing: It can look things up. By default FLUX 3 searches the web before it draws, which is how it gets a real building or a real product right. Brut leaves that on, except when Conform uses FLUX 3 to extend a picture (there is nothing to look up). It has no mask input. On a mask step of the Adjust node the mask steers the edit, as on Gemini. Like every mask in Brut it is guidance: the model redraws the frame. It is an edit model, not a fill model. Asked to extend a picture, it sometimes keeps your picture exactly where it was and sometimes recomposes the room. For an extension where the original must not move, use FLUX Outpaint. 4K is priced six times 2K. "Same as the picture" on a large frame lands on 4K; the frame editor shows the price before you paint, and 2K is one pick away.

The small FLUX 3, for many quick tries: drafts, variations, picking a direction before the final on FLUX 3 Image or another model. Sizes The same as FLUX 3 Image: 768, 1K, 1.5K, 2K, 4K. Ratios Every ratio on Brut's menu, plus auto on an edit: the output keeps the first picture's shape at the size you picked. Pictures in Up to 10 per request, as for FLUX 3 Image. Price Per image, by size: $0.008 (768), $0.009 (1K), $0.011 (1.5K), $0.014 (2K), $0.036 (4K). The cheapest image model in Brut. No web lookup. Klein draws from what it knows; for a real building or a real product it should look up, pick FLUX 3 Image. It redraws the frame on an edit, like FLUX 3 Image: on our first test edit (a summer lake house turned into a snowy evening) it kept the house and its window band but moved it in the frame. For a picture laid back over the original, use Reconcile with input after the edit. It renders text well: a sign asked for in the prompt came back spelled right on the first try. As on FLUX 3 Image, a mask on the Adjust node is guidance, not a hard boundary.

A tool, not a model you prompt: it takes a picture, the size of the frame around it and where the picture sits in that frame, and paints the rest. It appears in one place, the painter menu of Conform's ✂ frame editor, when the method is extend, and it is the painter Conform starts on once your key is in. Your picture is held. Where the frame covers the picture, the output is the picture; the tool generates only the added part. That is the difference with every image model on the same menu, which redraw the whole frame. 4 megapixels at most. The tool's frame cannot exceed 4 megapixels. A larger frame is painted smaller: a 2048 × 3641 frame comes back at 1520 × 2704 (a frame can also lose a few pixels at its edges). Brut delivers that picture as it is and never scales it back up; Upscale Image is the way to more pixels. The frame editor says so under the picture before you paint. A size menu to paint smaller on purpose. Up to 4 MP is the default; up to 2 MP and up to 1 MP lower the limit, and the price with it. No prompt needed. The tool reads the picture and continues it. The still's optional note ("more lawn", "no new buildings") is passed along as a hint; the tool may or may not follow it. High or Fast. High (the default) gives the best continuation of the picture. Fast answers in seconds for about a sixth of the price; your picture is held just as well, but the painted part is rougher: on an interior, a grittier floor and a wall that stops at the seam where High carries it on. Fast suits a first look, and scenes that extend easily (sky, lawn, water, a plain background). Price. Black Forest Labs publishes no rate for this tool. Measured through Brut, counted on the whole frame, your picture included: High, $0.10 per megapixel ($0.10 at 1 MP, $0.20 at 2 MP, $0.40 at 4 MP); Fast, about $0.05 ($0.045 at 1 MP, $0.051 at 2 MP, $0.063 at 4 MP). The frame editor shows the price for your frame, size and mode before the paint; the ledger row carries the billed amount after it.

Results are saved to your project as soon as they're ready. Their moderation can stop a request (the prompt or a picture) or a result. The node shows which, with their reason; a moderated call is not charged.

Calls go from your machine to Black Forest Labs' servers with your key, and nowhere else. With web lookup on, FLUX 3 itself sends search queries drawn from your prompt: that happens inside Black Forest Labs' service.

Ideogram makes the Ideogram image models, known for readable lettering and layout. Brut calls their own API with your key, for Ideogram 4.5 in two forms: Ideogram 4.5, in every image menu (Text → Image, Image → Image, Adjust, Compose, Multi-Shot, the Storyboard's keyframes, the Sketchpad's generation layers, the workflow cards' Model knobs): text-to-image at 1K or 2K, and an edit that re-renders the picture with your instruction. Ideogram 4.5 Precise Edit, on the edit menus (Image → Image, Adjust, Compose): the picture comes back at its exact size, and every pixel the edit does not touch is copied from it. It is the model's own claim, measured below, and the reason to try it on corrections: several passes on one picture without the drift every re-render adds. Ideogram 4.0 Transparent, in every text-to-image menu: a picture on a transparent background, a PNG with alpha, for cutouts, entourage and lettering to place on a layer.

Log in on ideogram.ai, open the API dashboard, create a key under API Keys (the full key is shown once, when it is created) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Ideogram. Billing is prepaid credits on that account: one-time amounts from $10, or an auto-recharge; a key pauses when the balance reaches $0, and if you hold an Ideogram subscription its monthly credits are spent first. There is no free tier. No aggregator carries Ideogram, so the key is the only way in.

Model Sizes Quality and price per picture Inputs Ideogram 4.5, text-to-image 1K · 2K low $0.03 · medium $0.06 · high $0.10 none Ideogram 4.5, edit Same as the picture · 1K · 2K very_low $0.008 · low $0.03 · medium $0.06 · high $0.22 the picture + up to 4 references (3 beside a mask) Ideogram 4.5 Precise Edit the picture's own, always very_low $0.008 · low $0.03 · medium $0.06 · high $0.22 the picture + up to 4 references (3 beside a mask) Ideogram 4.5 Replace Background the picture's own, always $0.22, one quality (the model's highest) the picture + a photo of the new setting; no prompt Ideogram 4.0 Transparent, text-to-image 1K · 2K · 4K · 8K turbo $0.03 · default $0.06 · quality $0.10 at 1K and 2K; 4K $0.19 / $0.22 / $0.26; 8K $0.35 / $0.38 / $0.42 none The prices are Ideogram's own: a quality costs the same at 1K and at 2K, at the picture's own size, with a mask and with reference pictures. Masks and references add nothing. The node shows the price before a run and the ledger row carries it after. Things worth knowing: Magic prompt, your call. Ideogram can rewrite and expand a prompt on its side before rendering (its "magic prompt"). On Text → Image, Image → Image, Adjust and Compose the node shows a Magic prompt box, off by default: unticked, your prompt is sent as written, so lettering and exact wording stay yours; ticked, Ideogram elaborates it (more detail, a fuller scene, a stronger style), which suits a short prompt and a first exploration. Same price either way. The Precise Edit has no such option, so its node shows no box. Sizes. On text-to-image, a 16:9 picture comes back at 1280 × 720 at 1K and 2560 × 1440 at 2K, a square at 1024 or 2048. 21:9 exists at 2K only (3072 × 1280): at 1K the ratio is greyed in the menu with the reason, and a node already set to it shows a line with the two ways out. On an edit, Same as the picture returns the picture at its own size (a picture too large for the model comes back scaled down, proportions kept); a picked size with aspect auto keeps the picture's proportions at that size, and a picked ratio reshapes it. Masks are real masks here. On a mask step of the Adjust node, Ideogram paints inside the mask and keeps the rest; the result is always the picture's own size, so the Size menu must stay on Same as the picture beside a mask (the run says so otherwise). On Precise Edit, the pixels outside the edit are copied from the original, mask or not. Measured on a 2048 × 1143 interior with one instruction, the sofa recolored to green velvet: the result came back at 2048 × 1143 with 95 percent of its pixels identical to the input, byte for byte, and every changed pixel inside the sofa's part of the frame. That is the behavior every other edit model only approximates, and the reason to try it first on a correction. References are references. On Compose and Image → Image, the pictures wired after the first guide the edit and are never edited themselves. The quality menu is the model's. Text-to-image offers low, medium and high; both edits add very_low, the fastest and cheapest, for a first look. In our runs a text-to-image took about 7 seconds, a precise edit about 9. On a marks step, one pass per mark. Pick Ideogram and the Precise Edit for a marks step of the Adjust node and Brut runs one precise edit per mark, in marker order, each on the previous pass's result: a box, circle or lasso keeps its edit inside the shape you drew; an arrow or a point aims the edit at the thing it marks. The picture outside each edit is copied as it is, so five marks leave a picture that differs from the original only where you marked, with no marker in the result. Five marks cost five passes at the quality you picked (5 × $0.03 at low). On the five-mark test interior (the same one as the Seedream comparison) all five edits landed, no marker anywhere, and 82 percent of the pixels came back identical to the input; five passes took about a minute and $0.15 at low. Replace Background takes two pictures and no prompt. Wire the picture to keep first and a photo of the setting you want behind it second (on Compose: scene and reference; on Image → Image: the first wire, then the second). The background is rebuilt as that setting, at the picture's own size; the people in your picture stay, the people in the setting photo are left out. The node reads no prompt (it says so under the model), so a prompt wired in costs nothing and changes nothing. Exactly two pictures: one or three stop with a message, and so does a mask (Precise Edit is the masked tool). The result takes longer than an edit (it runs at the model's highest quality, and Brut waits for it); the price is Ideogram's own $0.22 per picture, whatever the sizes. Pictures by Ideogram. Every picture these models make is generated by Ideogram's models, as their terms ask every app to say.

A text-to-image that comes back as a PNG with alpha: the subject alone, nothing behind it. It is the one for cutouts and entourage (a tree, a chair, a person, a car), logos and lettering to place on a layer. In every text-to-image menu. Sizes 1K · 2K · 4K · 8K. 4K and 8K are upscales of the render, priced accordingly. Ratios Every ratio on Brut's menu but 21:9, which this model has no size for: greyed in place with the reason. Quality turbo · default · quality, the model's own speeds. Price 1K and 2K: turbo $0.03, default $0.06, quality $0.10. 4K: $0.19 / $0.22 / $0.26. 8K: $0.35 / $0.38 / $0.42. Ideogram's own quotes. Measured: a potted olive tree at 1K came back as an 864 × 1152 PNG with alpha in 11 seconds, clean edges, nothing behind it. A cutout keeps its transparency wherever Brut composites it: on a Layers node it shows the stack below through its transparent pixels, with or without a mask, and in the Sketchpad's tray it places as an image layer with nothing around the subject.

Pictures in: JPEG, PNG or WEBP up to 25 MB each (other common formats work too, with no quality lost), with an aspect ratio between 1:6 and 6:1. Results are saved to your project as soon as they're ready. Ideogram's safety check can refuse a prompt (nothing is charged) or withhold a result; the node shows which. Ideogram runs ten requests at a time per account by default; past that, runs wait their turn instead of failing.
Calls go from your machine to Ideogram's servers with your key, and nowhere else. Ideogram's own terms govern what they keep of the pictures you send and receive.

Magnific is the reference AI image upscaler. Brut integrates its two upscalers — Upscaler Creative and Upscaler Precision V2 — in the Upscale Image node. Brut deliberately uses only the upscalers, not Magnific's other tools.
Generate an API key on your Magnific dashboard (API Keys page) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Magnific. You only need the API key, not the webhook secret the dashboard also shows.

The API bills credits from your Magnific subscription's allocation (for example, Premium+ includes 600K credits per year), consumed by output pixel area. Two things worth knowing: A credit's dollar value depends on your tier, so Brut doesn't pretend to convert: the ≈$ figure on the node is Magnific's published pay-as-you-go rate — a rough ceiling, not what your plan actually charges you. On a yearly plan, your effective cost is simply your plan price spread over your usage; at studio volume upscales barely dent the allocation (a few hundred credits each against hundreds of thousands per year). "Unlimited" plans are unlimited in the web app only — API calls always consume credits. Magnific doesn't share your balance with apps on individual plans; your dashboard is the truth.

Brut sends your original file, never re-compressed or downscaled. If an image exceeds Creative's 25.3M-pixel input cap, the run fails with a clear message instead of quietly shrinking your work (use Precision V2, or crop deliberately). An upscale in progress survives a restart of Brut. Provider errors are surfaced verbatim on the node.

Topaz Labs powers the precision side of the Upscale Image node — the Gigapixel-class faithful upscalers (including a model tuned for renders and CGI) and the Wonder-class generative ones — plus the Upscale Video node (Proteus / Rhea / Gaia CG, audio kept, itemized confirm before any spend). One key covers both. There are two ways to run Topaz video upscales in Brut: Topaz Labs (cloud) — the API below. Credits per job, works on any machine. Topaz Video AI (local) — if you own the Topaz Video desktop app and a capable GPU, Brut drives the app's own engine on your machine instead. No key, no credits, no cost per run — and the clip never leaves your computer. See local install below.
Create an API key on the Topaz developer portal and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Topaz Labs.

Model Class When Gigapixel Standard 2 precision the everyday default Gigapixel High Fidelity 2 precision maximum source preservation Gigapixel Art & CGI precision archviz renders, illustrations, game assets Gigapixel Low Resolution 2 precision tiny sources, thumbnails Redefine generative photoreal invented detail, prompt + creativity dial Standard MAX generative true-to-input generative restoration Recover 3 generative damaged / heavily compressed sources Wonder 3.5 generative Topaz's newest: rebuilds detail with one Enhancement setting (low, medium, high or auto) Wonder 3 generative the same family with a guidance prompt, a 1–9 creativity dial and the Enhancement setting Generative models cap input around 24–256 MP and cost more per pixel; the node stops with a clear message if your input × scale exceeds a model's cap — it never downscales your work silently.

Topaz bills credits by output megapixel: the standard class covers ~24 MP per credit, the generative class ~4 MP per credit, minimum one credit per job. Wonder 3.5 and Wonder 3 are cheaper and priced in steps: 1 credit up to 8 MP of output, 2 up to 16, 3 up to 24, 4 up to 32, 5 up to 40, 7 up to 50, 8 up to 64, 13 up to 100. A 2048-wide render upscaled 2× (about 9 MP) is 2 credits; Brut stops a Wonder job past 100 MP, where Topaz publishes no price. Credits come from one-off packs or a subscription's monthly allowance — the per-credit price depends on how you buy (packs run roughly $0.195 down to $0.158 per credit; subscriptions less). Brut shows a pre-run estimate in credits (with an approximate $ at a representative rate), the node displays your live credit balance, and the spend ledger records the actual credits Topaz reports for each job. Your Topaz account page is the billing truth. Credits are the billing truth: the live balance on the card and the quantized estimate on the node
An upscale in progress survives a restart of Brut. Results are saved to your project right away. Provider errors surface verbatim on the node; "not enough credits" says exactly that.

If Topaz Video (or the older Topaz Video AI) is installed and licensed on your machine, the Upscale Video node offers a second provider: Topaz Video AI (local). It runs the same models — Proteus, Rhea, Gaia CG — through the app's own engine on your GPU. No key and no account — Brut auto-detects the install (⚙ Settings shows "installed · free"); your app license covers it. If you install it mid-session, hit Check install. Free — no credits, no confirm dialog; the ledger records the run at $0. Private — the clip is processed entirely on your machine; nothing is uploaded. Missing model weights download automatically on first use (a one-time pause per model). Output is HEVC (H.265) with the clip's audio kept, like the cloud path. One run at a time — a second local upscale queues behind the first (one GPU). Closing Brut stops a local upscale (nothing was billed; run it again). If Brut doesn't find your install, contact us.

OpenRouter is the one aggregator key that can hold almost the whole of Brut: every text model (planning and Marcel — chat, ambient narration, acting), the full Nano Banana image family (incl. Nano Banana 2 Lite, the starter graph's model), GPT Image 2, GPT Image 2.5 and 2.6 (Flare and Sunburst), the Seedream 5.0 trio (Pro / Flash / Lite at 1K / 2K, Lite 2K / 4K), and the video models — Kling 3.0 and O1, Seedance 2.0 and 2.5. Outside it: the upscalers (they aren't resold anywhere, by design), Gemini Omni Flash and the other Kling tiers (4.0, 3.0 Omni / Turbo / 2.6 / 2.5 and older), which OpenRouter doesn't carry. Like every route, it adds no models to the menu and is always visible: routed nodes show ⇄ runs via OpenRouter, and Marcel's composer says so too. If you want the simplest possible seat: one OpenRouter key is a working studio. Native keys added later always take their models back automatically, usually at slightly better prices.

Every text model in Brut's catalog also runs here, at pass-through provider list rates — the same per-token prices as the native APIs (OpenRouter's revenue is a ~5.5% fee when you buy credits, not a token markup). Planning that reads your pictures works, the GPT reasoning dial rides along (including while Marcel acts on the canvas), and Anthropic prompt caching passes through — Marcel's long system context caches exactly as on a native Anthropic key, so routed conversations cost the same as native ones. New models usually arrive here too.

The Nano Banana family runs with Brut's own menus — the real 512/1K/2K/4K sizes and the full aspect list. Approximate inpaint masks work (the Gemini convention). Billing is pass-through: every routed image model bills the same as on the maker's own key, to the tenth of a cent. Nano Banana Pro costs $0.13 at 1K or 2K and $0.24 at 4K; Nano Banana 2 costs $0.07 / $0.10 / $0.15 at 1K / 2K / 4K; Lite $0.034 and the original Nano Banana $0.039. So the estimate before a run is the real price, and every image job records its exact billed amount on the ledger. Two OpenRouter-specific limits worth knowing: Very large pictures may be sent lightly compressed for that one request; your files are untouched. If even that can't fit, the run stops with a clear message; export the source smaller or use a native key. Heavy 4K image jobs can be slow. OpenRouter's queue sometimes stalls on large 4K multi-image jobs (a 4K edit that takes ~55 s on a native Gemini key can take much longer there). Brut gives up after about ten minutes. If that happens: retry, pick a smaller size, or use the native key, which takes over automatically the moment it's configured. The one exception is GPT Image, which OpenRouter renders at about 1K only: there's no size knob, so 2K and 4K need your OpenAI key. The aspect ratio and the quality do come through, on GPT Image 2 and on the GPT Image 2.5 pair alike: 2.5 keeps its full low to max quality menu, and image-to-image with aspect auto follows your input's shape. Masks don't: inpainting on GPT Image needs the OpenAI key. Measured: a 1:1 image costs $0.006 at low and $0.053 at high on 2.5 (the same on Flare and Sunburst), and 16:9 costs less ($0.004 at low). GPT Image 2.6 comes through with its full quality menu and its Complexity setting. One difference, measured the day the models came out: on 2.6 OpenRouter delivers three shapes only, square (1024 × 1024), 3:2 (1536 × 1024) and 2:3 (1024 × 1536), whatever ratio is asked, so a routed 2.6 node lists those three (16:9 and the other ratios need the OpenAI key). Image-to-image with aspect auto still follows your input's shape. Measured: a 1:1 image costs $0.025 at low, $0.044 at medium, $0.053 at high, $0.094 at xhigh and $0.211 at max, the same as on an OpenAI key at 1K; a 3:2 or 2:3 image $0.020 at low.
Video — the whole set, with billing truth

Kling 3.0 (std/pro) and Kling O1 (5 or 10 s, $0.112/s), Seedance 2.0 and Seedance 2.5 (480p/720p only, 4–30 s, first + last frame, no reference images there — the 30-reference and 1080p features need the BytePlus key) — image-to-video with end frames, text-to-video, reference images where OpenRouter offers them. Per-second rates, audio included in the estimate: Model Per second Audio Kling 3.0 std $0.084 · pro $0.112 +$0.042 · +$0.056 Seedance 2.5 $0.104 (480p) · $0.233 (720p) included Seedance 2.0 $0.071 (480p) · $0.15 (720p) · $0.38 (1080p) · $0.79 (4K) not measured The listed rates hold: Seedance comes out close to the BytePlus price. Kling O1 renders at 1924 × 1076. Kling 3.0 renders at 720p on OpenRouter, pro included, with no 4K: routed nodes offer only std and pro. And OpenRouter reports the exact billed cost on every job, which lands on the ledger row as is.
Create a key at openrouter.ai/keys (sk-or-…), buy a few dollars of credits, and paste it into ⚙ Settings → OpenRouter.

Your native key always wins. Add a Gemini/OpenAI/Kling/… key later and those models bill direct again automatically. Marcel works through OpenRouter only (among aggregators). Kling's 4K master tier, Seedance's Smart Length, Seedance 2.5's 1080p and reference images aren't on OpenRouter; Kling O1 takes only 5 or 10 s there. A missing setting always stops the run with a clear message, never silently. Every routed call — text, image, or video — lands in the spend ledger with provider-reported figures (token counts, cache activity, billed cost), marked "via openrouter".

fal.ai is an aggregator — a usage-billed API that resells many generation models under one key. Brut uses it as a route, not a provider in its own right: it never adds a single model to the menu, it just serves models Brut already carries when you hold no native key for them. OpenRouter is Brut's main aggregator, and fal.ai is optional. It serves the Nano Banana image family, GPT Image 2, Kling 3.0 and Seedance 2.0. When you hold both keys, GPT Image 2 and those video models run through fal, the Nano Banana models through OpenRouter. A node always says which: ⇄ runs via fal.ai.

Create a key on the fal.ai dashboard (two parts joined by a colon; paste it whole) into ⚙ Settings → fal.ai. fal has no free generation tier — add billing to the fal account before the first call, or the first run answers with a provider error (shown verbatim, as always).

Your direct key always wins. The moment you add a native key (Gemini, Kling, BytePlus, …), that model leaves the fal route and bills direct — usually cheaper. Routing is always visible. The node chip, the paid-run confirm, and the spend ledger all say "via fal.ai". Nothing routes silently. Honest prices only. Estimates for routed runs use fal's own list prices where known, and show none at all otherwise — never the native provider's numbers. Image prices are fal's list prices (Nano Banana about the same as on Google, GPT Image 2 by size and quality). Expect a margin over the direct API elsewhere (Seedance via fal is roughly 2× the native BytePlus rate; video rates aren't measured yet).
What the routes can and can't do

If a setting isn't available on fal, the run stops with a message instead of ignoring it. Current limits worth knowing: Adjust masks route APPROXIMATELY on the Nano Banana models: the same convention as Gemini native (the painted region is strong guidance, not a hard guarantee). GPT Image 2 masks don't route: masks on GPT Image need your OpenAI key. GPT Image 2 uses fal's own size presets (square, landscape 4:3/16:9, portrait, auto) — the node's Size menu shows exactly those instead of Brut's aspect + 1K/2K/4K pair. Nano Banana (original) renders 1K only via fal; pick 2K/4K models or add your Gemini key. Kling 3.0's 4K master tier isn't on fal — std/pro only. Audio on video models follows your node's switch (fal would otherwise turn it on and bill for it). Results are saved to your project, survive a restart, and appear in the spend ledger.

Replicate is the third aggregator route in Brut — a plain API-token, pay-per-use service that resells official builds of many models. Like every route, it never adds a model to the menu: it serves models Brut already carries when you hold no native key (and, for most models, no OpenRouter or fal.ai key), always visibly marked ⇄ runs via Replicate on the node. Current mirror set: Nano Banana Pro & 2 (text→image and image→image), GPT Image 2 (text→image and image→image), Kling 3.0 Omni, Seedance 2.0 (image→video and text→video).

Create a token at replicate.com/account/api-tokens (r8_…) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Replicate. Billing must be enabled on the Replicate account before the first run — errors come back verbatim, as always.

Your direct key always wins, and OpenRouter / fal.ai keys usually outrank Replicate when present. Replicate is the redundancy door. Routing is always visible — node chip, run confirm, spend ledger. No invented prices: image routes carry Replicate's list prices (Nano Banana 2 $0.067 · Pro $0.15/$0.30 at 4K · GPT Image 2 $0.012/$0.047/$0.128 by quality); video rates aren't measured yet, so those runs show no estimate rather than a wrong one. The ledger records every run.
What this route can do that fal's can't

Seedance text→video is available. GPT Image 2 sizes ride Replicate's aspect menu — ratios plus explicit sizes like 2048x1152 up to 3840x2160; the node's Aspect select shows exactly that menu (the entries above 2560x1440 are marked experimental by Replicate). Reference images ride on Seedance 2.0 and Kling 3.0 Omni.
And its own limits (each stops with a clear message, never silently)

Seedance tops out at 720p on Replicate — 1080p/4K need your BytePlus key. Smart Length isn't available either. Nano Banana 2 has no size knob — 1K only; pick Nano Banana Pro for 2K/4K. Kling 4K master tier doesn't exist on Replicate (std/pro only), and the Kling route is the Omni model. Adjust masks route approximately on the Nano Banana models (the Gemini convention: the painted region is strong guidance, not a hard guarantee). GPT Image 2 masks don't route: masks on GPT Image need your OpenAI key. Audio always follows your node toggle, never Replicate's default. Large pictures upload automatically; results are saved to your project and survive a restart.

Brut's most ambitious workflow: turn a handful of stills into a finished, cut sequence — planned by a crew of AI agents, shot on the video provider of your choice, and assembled on your machine, for exactly the bill it showed you. Stills → a crew that plans the film → a storyboard you edit → clips shot behind a confirm gate → a sequence cut on your machine. You stay in control at every step.

Conform → Reference Board → Director (plan + proof sheet) → Storyboard (keyframes) → Film Shots → Clip Board → Sequence → Preview Every arrow is a wire. The Director passes a plan document along; the boards are where you review and curate. Don't build this by hand the first time: the whole chain ships as the Stills → Film card (the library's From Brut shelf, or the home's Workflows row): one composite whose knobs are the Director's dials (brief, style, shots, runtime, people, audio), the film aspect and the clips' Quality (720p, 1080p or 4k). The card comes set up with models that work well together: GPT 5.6 Terra plans, GPT Image 2.5 Flare renders the proof sheet and the keyframes (xhigh, 2K), Kling 3.0 Omni on your kling.ai plan shoots the clips with audio (it holds a camera move where plain 3.0 trembles); open (⤢) the card to change any of them. Wire your stills in, set the knobs, run: the Director plans, its proof sheet renders right after and opens for your call (take it, a new take, or ✗ frames and reinvent them; stop, and nothing downstream runs), then the keyframe batch and the Film Shots table still ask before any spend. The card's 📖 Plan opens the Director's document to read, edit and annotate, its 🎬 Proof sheet reopens the sheet any time; open the card to judge the keyframes and the clips on their boards. Finish in 4K is the next card it offers. Let's walk what it does. The Stills → Film card: the whole chain from stills to the cut, one composite with its dials on the face

Start from your renders — an Image In node (or a Multi-Shot contact sheet you've curated). Run them through Conform to a single aspect ratio (video wants consistency), cropping each to keep the right part of the frame. Wire the conformed stills into a Reference Board. This makes the pool visible and numbered — and the tile number is the still number the crew will refer to. Reorder to taste; the plan refers to the stills by these numbers.

One Director node. It writes the concept, the look and the shot plan together, and the film comes out varied: an arc across the shots, lenses and framing changing shot to shot, no still used twice in a row. Pick a Brief and a Style, set shots and runtime, choose how much human presence you want, and wire it straight into the Storyboard. Every clip also gets a one-line ambient sound note for video models that produce audio. Before anything spends on keyframes, the Director's 🎬 proof sheet renders right after the plan, in the same run: one cheap image of the whole film as a numbered contact sheet, all frames in one grade. The run then stops on it and asks for your call. Select the frames that don't inspire you and ✎ Reinvent rewrites only those clips (the others stay exactly as they were) and re-renders the sheet for cents; ↻ New take re-rolls the same plan; Take this sheet lets the run go on (a later run with the same sheet never asks again); Stop runs nothing downstream. 📌 pin the sheet you validate to keep it through plan edits. The sheet you take guides every keyframe: what you approved is what gets produced. Run the Director: concept, look and the executable shot plan land in one call; the proof sheet renders the whole film for cents Pick the Director's LLM — Gemini, GPT or Claude — on your own key. The plan is editable text: tweak a line and it flows downstream. Don't read the raw plan text — the node's 📖 Review opens the plan as an actual document: edit it in place for free, or leave 💬 margin notes and let Revise apply them (details). The four-agent crew (Scenarist / Artistic Director / DoP / Script Supervisor) is legacy since 1.1.1: the Director plans better films, so the crew nodes are hidden from the node browser. Graphs that already use them keep loading and running exactly as before — details.
2 · The Director plans the film › Invented shots — the flourish

Your stills define the project's identity, not the shot list. The Director invents most compositions — a detail close-up, a reveal, subtle human presence, the pull-back ending — each anchored on the stills that carry its materials, with a written keyframe prompt already styled to the film's look. The rule never loosens, it moves one level: one clip = one keyframe. An invented shot's start frame is generated from its anchor stills, guided by the proof sheet you took, at the film's aspect, before any video runs. An invented shot is never quietly sent as text-to-video — without an approved keyframe it simply refuses to roll. Want the full reel behavior? The Director's "Invent every shot" switch makes the stills references only — no shot animates one directly, every start frame is generated. Off, the brief decides shot by shot.

The Storyboard turns the plan into shot cards: per-clip start/end frame swaps with thumbnails, editable and lockable prompts, add/reorder shots, and ✕ mutes a card (greyed, kept, ↺ to bring it back) rather than deleting it. Change a line here and only that shot re-renders. It passes the actual frames along with the plan, so Film Shots needs only one wire. The plan you see always matches the board's tiles. An anchor that points at a still the board doesn't have stops with a clear message on its card, never silently, and 📖 Review on the Director lets you rewrite a shot's anchors by hand. Invented shots arrive frameless. Each shows its keyframe prompt and a 🎨 Generate keyframe button — pick the image model, resolution and (on GPT Image) quality once at the top of the board (the pending count and per-frame price sit next to it and follow your picks; keyframes are cents, clips are dollars). A keyframe is kept as long as its prompt and anchor stills don't change (an unchanged card never re-pays), ↻ re-rolls a fresh take, 📌 pins one against later prompt edits, 🕘 opens the card's history — every take it ever generated, from the project ledger — so a re-roll never loses anything: pin any past keyframe back as the start frame, free. Wiring any image into the card's socket overrides everything. Prefer to ground an invented shot on a real still after all? Pick one in its start selector; 🎨 generate in the same selector brings its keyframe back. That 🎨 entry is on every card: a grounded shot, or a shot you added yourself (+ in the board's header), switches to a generated keyframe too. Write its keyframe prompt (✏ on the card, the 🎨 line), check the anchor stills beside it (the still the card was on, by default; empty = every still on the board), 🎨. Until the prompt is written the card says so and the clip stays blocked downstream, never sent as text-to-video. Swap a start frame, generate a keyframe for an invented shot, drag a frame out to keep it The film's aspect is your call. The board's aspect dropdown (default: the plan's format) conforms every keyframe to the format you choose and stamps it into the emitted plan. Switching aspect later doesn't re-bill: the raw render is kept and simply re-cropped, free. Batch it. ▶ on the Storyboard (or the 🎨 Generate N button) renders every pending keyframe behind one itemized confirmation — shot list, per-frame price, total. The per-card 🎨 stays for surgical re-work. Declining isn't an error: the plan flows on and Film Shots simply blocks the frameless clips.
3 · The storyboard — your edit bay › End frames, on demand

Every card's end selector offers three states: none, a still of the board, or 🎨 generate. Pick 🎨 and the card grows a second frame block to the right of the start frame — same image box, same in-socket and out-plug, same tools — for a generated end frame that continues the start frame (a still, a keyframe or a wired image), at the film's aspect. Where the camera arrives is now yours to direct, for grounded and invented shots alike. The prompt for that destination is drafted for you, and the draft also picks the reference stills that show what the move reveals (at most three), so the destination comes from your real project, not from invention.
