It uses the planning model of the node feeding the plan wire: one text call, cents, in the ledger like the plan's. Nothing renders from a prompt you haven't seen: ✎ or 🎨 on the end block opens a review — the start frame beside the drafted prompt, editable in place, ✎ re-drafts, and the writer's still picks as toggleable thumbnails (tick more, untick any) — and Generate renders. Cancel keeps the text and renders nothing. ↻ re-rolls a rendered end frame, 📌 pins it (it then survives prompt edits and a re-rolled start frame — otherwise a new start frame needs a new end frame, since the end continues it), 🕘 opens the card's end-frame history. Wiring any image into the end block's socket overrides everything, and the block's out-plug carries the resolved end frame wherever you want it. Every prompt a card owns has a plug, too, in a labeled plug bar at the card's bottom: prompt in / prompt out, 🎨 keyframe prompt on invented shots, ⇥ end prompt on armed cards — so any of them can feed a Refine or a Text Board, and you can read which is which. ▶ on the board covers end frames too: after the start keyframes, one review lists every armed card at once — drafts filled in, each editable — and one Generate renders them all. An armed end frame that isn't rendered yet blocks that clip in Film Shots, exactly like a missing start keyframe: it is never sent without it. And when the video model has no end-frame input (only some do — Kling 2.5+/3.0, Gemini Omni, Seedance among them), the clip still runs from its start frame, but the Film Shots table says so on that row — never silently. Budget-wise, an end frame is a second keyframe on that card (cents) plus one text call. Look at your frames. Click any card's image to magnify it full-screen, then browse the whole board like a gallery with ← / → (arrows or the on-screen ‹ ›); Esc closes. And every card has an output plug on its right edge carrying that clip's resolved start frame — the generated keyframe, the wired image, or the grounded still — so you can route a frame anywhere: into an Upscale Image for a delivery-res still, a Compose, a Preview. A card whose keyframe is still pending delivers nothing (never a wrong frame). The card's prompt has its own plug too, prompt out in the labeled plug bar at the card's bottom (the final clip prompt, overrides and wired prompts applied), so a line of the plan's wording can be reused or refined anywhere (a Refine, a Text Board, another card's prompt socket). And any card image can simply be dragged onto the canvas: it lands as a ready-filled Image In — detach a keyframe as the frozen base of a new exploration, safe from later re-plans.

Wire the Storyboard into Film Shots. It first adapts every clip prompt to the video model you picked (a cheap text call per clip, cents, in the ledger); the table marks those rows ✦. It then prices every clip — model, duration, resolution, cost — and shows an itemized confirmation. Nothing generates until you approve the total; cancel a line and it updates. A tick box per row chooses what gets sent (untick = kept in the table, greyed, not sent — render a few, judge, then the rest). Clips already made (unchanged) and pinned clips cost $0. Then it shoots several clips at a time, with per-clip re-roll / ✓✗ / pin. Every clip priced in the table, one itemized confirmation, nothing spends before your OK

The Clip Board plays every clip — keep the good, ✗ the misses, ↻ re-roll one. Route the keepers into a Sequence node, which assembles them into one mp4 on your machine — cuts or crossfades, clip audio kept, vertical reels stay vertical, free. Drop a Preview on the end. Two clips cut together with a crossfade and played in Preview: local ffmpeg on your machine, no cost Want it in 4K? Route a hero clip (or the assembled film) through Upscale Video — Topaz Proteus or Gaia CG, audio kept, itemized confirm before any spend. The shipped Finish in 4K card is this stage on its own (one Upscale Video, target and upscaler on the face, provider unset: the money choice stays yours); it is the next card the Stills → Film card and the clip workflows offer once they hold a result.

The Stills → Film card is the reusable starting point, and any tuned chain of yours (a Director with your house style and dials, a Storyboard with your keyframe model) can be selected and collapsed into a composite or saved as your own template: one library item, every film starts warm. Why it holds together: every clip starts from a frame you have seen (a still of yours, or a keyframe generated from your stills), a shot without its frame never rolls, and every clip asks for a steady camera. The plan you approve is the film you get.
How do I resize a node?

Hover it: a small ⌟ grip fades in at the node's bottom-right corner (the same mark a text box has, applied to the whole node). Drag it to set width and height together; it lights up while you drag and fades out when you leave. Every resizable node uses this one gesture, boards, Preview, the text nodes, stickies and stamps alike, and the size is saved with the graph. Nothing to select first, and no frame around the node.
How do I send one output to several nodes?

Either drag a second wire from the same output port (an output can feed any number of inputs), or split an existing wire where you are: Alt-click the wire and a small dot drops on it. Drag a new wire off the dot to another node, or onto empty canvas to pick one from the add menu, already wired. The dot is only a branch point: nothing re-runs or re-pays because of it, and deleting it heals the wire. Details in Nodes & graphs.
How do I move all the wires from one pin to another?

Alt-click the pin whose wires you want to move (every pin starts pulsing), then click the destination pin. Output to output (or input to input) moves every wire across and keeps their other ends; an input then an output makes that output feed the input instead. Esc cancels, Ctrl+Z undoes. Details in Nodes & graphs.
How do I turn the home screen off?

Untick Show this screen at launch at the bottom of the home screen. Brut then opens straight on the canvas; the house icon on the left rail (above Settings) and File ▾ → Home still open it whenever you want it. The choice is per machine.
Why does a graph card show results I don't see on the canvas?

The card shows what the graph's saved file (or its live canvas, when it has unsaved changes) holds: the most recent results of its most downstream nodes, up to five. Hover the cover to flip through them. If a node's result was never saved with the graph (a run that finished after the last Ctrl+S), the card shows the canvas' own results and marks the name with a •.

Yes. Brut ships a bank of pre-wired workflows for the recurring jobs: Clay → Photoreal, Clay to Client Set, Time of Day, Weather & Sky, Populate, Populate → Clip, Scene Dressing, Editorial Sheet, Look Transfer, Hero Still → Clip, the Character Lab, Stills → Film, Reel Script and Finish in 4K, plus the Correction Loop template. They sit on the Workflows row of the home screen and on the From Brut shelf of the library (the book icon on the rail). Everything adds to your canvas: a composite as one card with knobs, a template as a group of live nodes. The full list, with the models each one uses and what it takes in, is on the Workflows page.
Can I change the time of day or the weather of a picture in one move?

Yes, with a look. In the Elements panel, right-click the list → Add Brut's looks… (times of day, weathers, seasons, atmospheres, finishes, each with a picture), open Styles, and drag a look onto a picture on the canvas: an Image → Image node appears, wired from that picture and holding the look's words. Nothing runs until you press ▶, and the price shows first. Your own looks: right-click a picture you made → Save to Elements… → Save as a look.
Why does Marcel say there is nothing to recap?

Because nothing happened. At Narrator level Marcel recaps a project by himself the moment it opens, and the recap lands in his panel (the badge on the rail's Marcel button counts what you haven't read). Marcel only writes a new recap when something has happened since his last one. Run something, then open the panel again.

During the beta, yes. At launch, Brut itself will be a paid tool: we sell the orchestration (the canvas, the caching that never re-bills unchanged work, the ledgers, the catalog kept current as providers churn, Marcel), never the tokens. Expect tiers with different feature sets, probably a limited free tier to see how it looks and a short trial; the exact terms are announced before launch. What never changes: generation is paid to the providers directly, on your own keys, at their price. Brut takes no cut, ever.
Where do my API keys go?

Into your OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager). They're used only for direct calls from your machine to each provider, are never written into a graph, never sent to us, and never appear in a .brutpack.
Can I cap what a project spends?

Yes — File ▾ → Project budget… sets a per-project ceiling compared against the ledger. The toolbar readout shows $spent / $budget and changes color as you approach it; paid confirmations warn past the cap (or refuse, if you tick hard cap). It works from estimates; the ledger records what was actually billed.
Can I turn a key off without deleting it?

Yes — every configured provider in ⚙ Settings has an on/off switch. Off = the saved key (or your Kling sign-in) is ignored everywhere: the provider reads as unconfigured, and models with aggregator routes fall back to them — so you can test an OpenRouter-only setup, or bench a native key, without re-pasting anything. One tick brings it back.
Does Brut see my prompts, images or renders?

No. Everything you make stays on your disk (or your NAS). Brut has no server in the generation path. The only thing that ever leaves your machine is a tiny sign-in heartbeat — version/OS/install-id, no content.
Why do I have to sign in?

Today, to count seats during the beta. At launch, your account is also how you'll activate your plan on a machine. It's required, but it never bricks you: once you've signed in, a 30-day offline grace keeps you working through flights and outages, and if the sign-in server is unreachable a "continue for now" option appears. One exception, by design: a seat revoked for a breach of the beta license (a shared installer, a resold seat) signs out on that machine and paid generations stop until an active seat signs in. Nothing on disk is touched — your projects, outputs and keys stay yours.
Can I share Brut with a colleague?

Not the installer, please. Every beta seat is personal — that's the one rule of the beta license you accept in the app. Ask them to register on getbrut.app; applications are reviewed and approved seats get their own download link.
Windows says "Windows protected your PC" when I run the installer.

Expected during the beta: the installer isn't code-signed yet (a paid certificate we'll buy when the beta proves out), so SmartScreen flags it as unrecognized. Click More info → Run anyway. The installer runs per-user, without admin rights.
Where is my work on disk?

Everything Brut makes — projects, outputs, library, account state — lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut as plain files (keys are the exception: OS keychain). Brut's technical log is at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut\logs\engine.log. Uninstalling never touches this folder — your work survives uninstall and reinstall. Right-click → Reveal in Explorer on a result is the reliable way to locate it, because outputs are written to whichever project was active when the generation ran. File ▾ → Save project as… later moves the files the canvas uses into the new project (with their history rows), so the new folder is complete; a file another graph in the old project also uses stays there as a copy, and anything you generated there that the canvas no longer references stays where it was.
The project list is getting long.

It stays short on its own: the project selector lists the ten projects you opened most recently, newest first, and keeps the rest under N more… at the bottom. Hover a row and click its ✕ to take a project off the list; nothing is deleted, its folder, files and settings stay, and the row waits under N more… with a ↺ to come back. Opening a project, from there or from a graph card on the home screen, puts it back on the list as well. To forget a project on this computer for good (its folder stays on disk), use File ▾ → Forget “project”… while you are in it; that works for projects rooted at their own folder.

Text is ordinary text everywhere: select it and Ctrl+C copies it, in Marcel's messages, a node's result, a prompt. When nodes are selected on the canvas, Ctrl+C copies those nodes instead, unless you have text selected, in which case the text wins. Right-clicking selected text or a field offers the usual Copy, Cut, Paste and Select all.
Where do my references live? Can I put the vault on the NAS?

The Elements vault is made of folders on your disk: as many as you add (the 📁 button, or a right-click in the list), your references share included. Your folders are read as they are; what Brut saves goes under Brut/ in the one folder you mark for it (a studio marks its share, so the studio shares its elements). Each folder keeps one small index file inside it, so moving or sharing a folder keeps everything. Nothing in it leaves your machine.
What's in the right-click menu on an image?

For any single image or video, right-click its preview. The same menu appears on every picture Brut shows, outputs and imports alike, board tiles, the magnifier, history rows: Send to chat attaches the image to your next message to Marcel (stills only), Decompose into layers… splits a picture into a base and up to 16 layers on Seedream 5.0 and lands them as a new Sketchpad (the one paid item of the menu: the price is shown first, and it is greyed with the reason without a BytePlus key), Save to Elements… puts a copy into your Elements vault, named and shelved, or saves a picture you generated as a look that keeps its prompt and model (free), Frames to Elements… (on a clip) takes stills out of it into the vault, after every cut, every N seconds or at times you mark (free), Reveal in Explorer opens the containing folder with the file selected, Find in ledger shows the run that made the file (model, node, graph, prompt, parameters, cost, date) and can open that node's 🕘 history on the row, Copy file path copies where it lives, Copy image puts the pixels on the clipboard (a video gives its poster frame) to paste straight into Photoshop, a chat or a mail, Export JPG writes a full-resolution JPG (quality 92) and Export web JPG a 2048-pixel one (quality 85) into the project's outputs/exports folder, no dialog, and Explorer shows the file. A Sketchpad's preview also offers Export PSD (see the Sketchpad page). The right-click on an image never opens the ring menu: that is for empty canvas only.
What do the file names mean?

Every file Brut writes is named <project>_<graph>_<node>_<provider>_<model>_<date>_<job> — for example tournesol_facade-study_t2i-12_openai_GI25F_260923_a3f91c2e.png: the project, the graph, Text → Image node 12, made by OpenAI's GPT Image 2.5 Flare, on 23 Sept 2026, ledger job a3f91c2e…. The model codes (NB2, NBP, GI2, K30, SD25 …) are listed on the Projects page. Per-tile files say which tile (ms-4-s07, film-3-c02), files you drop in keep your own filename, and the free local tools name themselves (conform, layers, sketch, sequence). The last segment is the key: right-click → Find in ledger turns any file back into the run that made it. Files from before keep their old random names: renaming them would disconnect them from your saved graphs. The full key, and how to set your own pattern per project, is on the Projects & the ledger page.

Grab the latest installer from getbrut.app/download (log in with your beta email — the page always serves the newest build) and run it over the old install — no uninstall needed. Projects, keys and sign-in all carry over (see Where is my work on disk? above). There's no auto-update during the beta. You won't miss one, though: at every launch Brut compares the version you run with the latest installer (it uses the small daily check-in described in Privacy). If yours is behind, one line under the toolbar says Brut x.y.z is available with a Download button to that page; Later hides it for that version. Same version, no line at all. Offline, no line either. To check which version you're on: File ▾ → About Brut, at the bottom of the menu.
The download page says the sign-in link "is invalid or has expired".

Something opened the link before you did. Company mail systems (Microsoft 365's Safe Links, Mimecast and the like) fetch every link in an incoming email to scan it, and a sign-in link works once, so the scan used it up and your click came second. The timing gives it away: the link is valid for an hour, yet the message appears right after the email arrives. The emailed link now lands on the download page and signs you in only when you press Continue there, so a scanner cannot spend it. The same email also carries an 8-digit code: type it on the download page instead, from any browser, if a link ever misbehaves. Links and codes work once and expire after an hour, so request a fresh email if yours is older than that. The desktop app's own sign-in screen takes the same code (Brut 1.1.5 and later): after Email me a link, type the 8 digits from the email into the field that appears, no link needed.
The taskbar shows a blank document icon for Brut.
A bug in builds 1.0.95 to 1.1.2. Install the current build over it; if Brut was pinned to the taskbar, unpin it and pin it again.
My first generation returned a 429. Why?

Almost always billing isn't enabled on that provider's key — free tiers have zero generation quota, so the first call fails. Enable billing in the provider's console. A first-call 429 is billing, not throttling.
An image edit came back blank / refused.

Gemini sometimes returns no image without saying why (the error mentions OTHER). It is a content refusal, usually triggered by an input image (a real person's name in facade lettering, a face, a logo), not the prompt. Remove or crop the offending image. Brut never retries it for you: retrying won't help, the same input is refused the same way.
Where did Inpaint and Annotate & Correct go?

They are one node now: Adjust. Inpaint and Annotate & Correct nodes in older graphs open as Adjust nodes with one step: the mask or the marks become that step, the last result its picked take, and nothing runs again: a change you make to that step goes into its next take, made with ↻. A node changed after its last result and saved without running runs that step once, as it would have before. From there, + in the editor adds the next correction as a new step on that result, and the original is kept outside each edit.
Do I ever pay twice for the same thing?
No. Every node remembers what it was given: if nothing changed, the last result is reused for $0. See Never pay twice.
What does ▶ Run do exactly? Does it generate everything?

No. ▶ Run is reveal-then-ask. First it replays every cached, pinned and free step for $0 and marks the nodes whose inputs changed (or that never ran) with a needs a run badge, together with what they would bill. If nothing needs a run, that's it. Otherwise one dialog lists them with the estimate: Generate runs the graph (cached steps still replay free; Film Shots, Upscale Video and the Storyboard keyframes still show their own itemized confirm first), Keep cached only leaves the badges on so you can see which nodes are outdated. The ▶ on a node runs that node and its upstream directly.
I reopened a graph and some results are missing.

Every generation node shows its last result the moment the graph opens; the badge says whether it is current. If a node face is empty, it never produced a result in this graph. Hit ▶ Run: it replays what is already made, for free, and shows what, if anything, would need generating.
I changed the prompt and lost a result I liked. Is it gone?

No — nothing generated is ever discarded. Every paid node has a small 🕘 in its title bar, next to ▶: it opens that node's full history from the project ledger, every result it ever produced. Pin any of them and it becomes the node's output again, free, protected from later re-runs until you unpin (the button turns 📌). Multi-Shot tiles, Storyboard keyframes and Film Shots clips have the same 🕘 per tile. See Projects & the ledger.
The 🕘 history shows results I never made on this graph.

Node ids are counters per graph: most graphs of a project have a text_to_image-1. Older builds listed every take of that id in the project, whatever graph made it. The history now shows this graph's takes alone, on the 🕘 panel and on the History board. Tick Every graph in this project in the panel (or every graph on a History board) to see the others, each badged with the graph that made it, or unnamed canvas for a take made before the canvas was saved under a name. A take keeps the graph name it was made under: takes from before a rename stay under the old name, reachable through that switch.
How do I take an image out of a node to work on it separately?

Drag it. Grab the image on any node — a generation preview, a Multi-Shot or Shot Board tile, a Reference Board still, a Storyboard card frame — and drop it on empty canvas: a ready-filled Image In appears there, pointing at the same file (no re-upload). Drop it on an existing Image In to append instead. The detached copy is a frozen base: re-rolling or re-planning the source never touches it.
A shot failed with "Network error — connection dropped mid-request".

Your connection to the provider dropped while a request was in flight (Wi-Fi blip, VPN hop, a provider hiccup). Re-roll the failed items: the ones that already finished won't re-pay. One caveat, written in the message itself: if the connection dropped while the result was coming back, the provider may still have generated (and billed) it; check the provider's console if it matters.
Marcel or a node says "Could not reach api.anthropic.com" (or another address).

Your computer could not open a connection to that provider at all: usually it could not look up the address (no internet for a moment, a sleeping Wi-Fi), or something on the network stands in the way (a VPN, a proxy, a company network that filters AI services). The request never left your machine, so nothing was billed. Marcel tries once more by himself before showing the message; if it stays, check that you are online and that the address is not blocked on your network, then send again. Once a render has been sent to the provider, Brut is more patient: if the network drops while it waits for the result or fetches it, the node reads "waiting for the network" and Brut keeps trying for up to three minutes. If the network is still gone after that, the message names the task: the result may be waiting on the provider's side, so look for it on their site.
Can two people share a project?

Yes — put the project on a NAS and each seat opens the same folder, or pass a .brutpack file (with its results, so nothing re-bills). There's no cloud sync by design; collaboration is file/NAS exchange. On a shared NAS project the studio timeline is shared too — one diary everyone writes to, with each entry tagged by who was signed in.

Two ways today. Export the project that holds it as a .brutpack (File ▾ → Export as pack): the graph travels with its results, so nothing re-bills, and the other seat opens it as a project. Or hand over the item itself: every saved composite or template is one small file in the library folder beside your projects (library/composites/<name>.json, library/templates/<name>.json); copy it into the same folder on the other machine and it appears on their Yours shelf. Library items hold recipes only, prompts, models and wiring, never images or keys, so they are safe to pass around. A shared community shelf is planned for later.

The Marcel button opens your project's studio timeline — a chronological record of runs, results, plans and errors, saved with the project so it survives restarts and travels with a NAS share — and the chat with Marcel, Brut's built-in companion. He knows the whole model catalog (with real prices), every node, and these docs; he answers on your own text-model key and every call lands in your spend ledger. An Assist slider sets how present he is on his own — from Off (silent) through failure diagnosis and run commentary up to Partner-level 💡 suggestions. A header toggle switches between Raw events (everything) and Chat only. It all stays on your machine (see Marcel, the companion and Privacy).
What if Brut closes while a video renders?
Brut picks the job back up at the next launch and records it once, at its real price.
Will I lose my canvas if I close the app?

No — the canvas autosaves into the project folder moments after every change, along with which named graph it is. Relaunch (on this machine, or any machine sharing the project on a NAS) and you're back exactly where you were. A • next to the graph name means changes not yet saved to the named graph (Ctrl+S), and opening another graph over unsaved work asks first, saying how many nodes are at stake.
I replaced a canvas by mistake. Can I get it back?

Yes. Brut keeps the last five saves of every graph and the last five canvases another graph replaced (an open, a new graph, an import over work you had not saved under a name). File ▾ → Restore an earlier version… lists them with the graph, the number of nodes and the time; pick one and it lands on the canvas under its name, marked unsaved until you press Ctrl+S. Ctrl+Z brings back the canvas you restored over, and it is kept on the shelf as well, so nothing is lost by looking. A new graph is named when you create it (File ▾ → New graph and the home's New graph both ask), so a canvas never lives unnamed by accident.
Which video provider should I use?

For steady Kling use, the subscription is ~3× cheaper than API packs. Gemini Omni rides your Gemini key and is the fast lane (a 10-second clip with sound in under a minute, flat ≈$1 per clip whatever the length — so ask for 10 s). Seedance 2.5 does native audio and single takes up to 30 seconds. All quote the cost before you spend.
How do I pay BytePlus for Seedance and Seedream?

One ModelArk key covers both, and billing is pay-as-you-go: top up Credits by card in the console (minimum USD 5, they never expire, USD 30 unlocks the Seedance family), or run Automatic billing on a bound card. Resource packs are optional (one model, 90 days, list price), and activating a model is a one-time switch on the console's Model activation page, needed before the first call. PayPal-only accounts need a card or a pack. Details on the Seedance page; Seedream 5.0 Lite comes with 50 free images.
What does "⇄ runs via …" on a node mean?

You picked a model whose native provider has no key on this machine, but you hold a credential for an aggregator that resells the same model — so Brut routes the run there, on your account. Your direct key always wins when present (it's usually cheaper); routing only fills the gap, it's always shown on the node and in the run confirm, and the ledger records it. Adding the native key switches the model back to direct billing immediately. Details: model routes.
How do I see my Kling plan credits?

Pick the Kling (subscription) provider on an Image → Video or Film Shots node — the node shows your live plan balance ("🎟 Plan balance: 5,040 credits · Pro") read from your Kling account, and Film Shots repeats it in the paid-run confirmation.
How do I report a bug or ask for a feature?
The green speech-bubble button on the left rail — see Install & first run. Diagnostics are opt-in, and you see exactly what is sent first.
Why does Brut ask about my session when I quit?

It's the beta asking for your experience while it's fresh: after a session that actually ran something (a Run click, a generation, or an error), the desktop app shows "Before you go" with a one-line summary and the feedback form. Nothing is sent unless you press Send & quit; Quit without sending closes the app at once. An empty session (open, look, close) never asks.
No. getbrut.app and these docs load nothing from third parties — self-hosted fonts, no analytics, no trackers.
Brut is built local-first, and privacy isn't a policy bolted on afterward — it's the architecture. Here is, precisely, what stays on your machine and what (very little) leaves it.

Your prompts, images, renders and video. All of it is written to your disk (or your NAS), inside your project's outputs/ folder. Brut has no server in the generation path — your work is never uploaded to us, and we cannot see it. Your 3D models. A model on a Scene node is copied into your project and opened on your machine; it is never sent to a provider, nor to us. A screenshot taken in its navigator is a picture like any other: it goes to a provider only when you wire it into a node that generates. Your graphs and projects. Stored locally as files. A .brutpack or NAS share moves them between your machines; nothing routes through a cloud. Your exports. Exports made from the right-click menu (JPG, web JPG, PSD) are local files written into the active project's outputs/exports folder. Nothing is uploaded or shared by that menu. Your API keys. Stored in your OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager). Used only for direct calls from your machine to each provider. Never written into a graph, never sent to us, never in a .brutpack. The engine log. The desktop app writes a technical log to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut\logs so problems can be diagnosed. It stays on your disk: a feedback report never includes it unless you attach it yourself. Updates. Brut never updates itself: a new version is a new installer you download. At launch, while you're signed in, Brut checks whether a newer version exists, through the same small daily check-in (the heartbeat) described below; nothing else is sent for it. Generation calls go from your machine straight to the provider (Google, OpenAI, Kling, Magnific, Topaz, …) on your key. Those providers see the requests you send them, under their own privacy terms — Brut is never in the middle. One path goes through storage, and it is yours: Seedance video to video takes a clip only as a link, so the clip is put in your own BytePlus bucket, fetched by BytePlus through a link that expires within hours, and deleted by Brut when the job ends; a voice recording on the Voice row of Image → Video or Text → Video goes the same way (your bucket, an expiring link, deleted when the job ends). The Seedance assets node uses the same bucket the same way, for a different end: a picture you register is copied by BytePlus into your account's asset library, where it stays until you delete it (the bucket copy goes at once), so that Seedance accepts the people in it. Which of your pictures are registered, and under which asset id, is a small file beside your library on your disk; a clip's ledger row lists the asset ids it went out on. Opening your library in Brut reads the list from BytePlus and keeps small thumbnails of your assets beside that file; picking an asset downloads its picture from BytePlus into your Elements vault. The Elements vault itself is a folder on your disk with one small index file inside it; its palettes are computed locally; nothing in it calls a provider on its own. Its Describe… button, when you click it, sends up to six pictures of that element to the text model on your own key (Gemini by default), like any Refine call, and the answer is yours to keep or drop. Picture names by looking: with the switch on the Gemini card in Settings (on by default), a small copy of each new picture on an Image In, or wired into a node that takes pictures, goes once to Google (Gemini Flash) on your key so it can name the picture in a few words; the names are kept beside your library on your disk, by the picture's content, every call is a ledger row, and with the switch off nothing is sent (pictures keep their file names). Its Import from the web fetches only the addresses you paste, from your machine to those sites, one page deep, and never follows a page's links. A lifestyle Multi-Shot sends your place pictures and the cast's character sheets to its planner (Claude Sonnet 5.5 by default, on your own key or route), on Fresh and Crazy your place pictures and the cast in words once more for the angles, and each shot's people's sheets to the image model with that shot only. Nothing of this reaches us. One provider-side detail worth knowing: Gemini Omni: Google keeps each Omni request (the prompt, the input images, the clip) on its side for a while, which is what lets the model edit its earlier clips. Same key, same Google terms as Gemini. To be precise about that promise: there is no aggregator that Brut operates in the call path — no server of ours, ever. If you choose to run a model through a route (an aggregator you subscribe to yourself, when you hold no direct key), your requests go from your machine straight to that service, on your credential, under its privacy terms — and the node, the confirm dialog and the ledger always say so. The wand of the Adjust node runs on your machine: the picture never leaves it for that. The first time you pick the wand, Brut downloads its small model once from Hugging Face (about 156 MB, checked against a known fingerprint) and keeps it in your library folder, with its reading of the last pictures you used it on (so a picture is read once; never more than about half a gigabyte, the oldest readings go first, and nothing of it lands in your project folders); only the download request is sent, nothing of yours. One provider sends nothing at all: video upscales through Topaz Video AI (local) run entirely on your own GPU via the Topaz desktop app you installed — the clip never leaves your machine. One setup step downloads a tool rather than talking to a provider: clicking Install Kling CLI (for the Kling subscription provider) fetches Kling's official command-line client from the npm public registry (registry.npmjs.org), a download of about 1 MB, integrity-checked. Once Brut installed it that way, Brut keeps it current: when it starts and finds the tool older than the version it needs, it sends the same download request to registry.npmjs.org in the background. Nothing of yours is sent, only the download request itself. A machine that never installed the tool never downloads it, and a Kling tool you installed yourself with npm is never touched.

Brut keeps a studio timeline per project — the running record of runs, results, and your conversations with Marcel, the built-in companion. It lives in a plain text file in the project's ledger folder, on your disk or your NAS, and is never uploaded — it travels only where the project itself travels. When you export a project to a folder it's included by default (it's a backup); when you make a .brutpack to hand off, it's left out by default — a checkbox lets you decide either way each time. Chatting with Marcel works like every generation: the conversation goes from your machine straight to the text-model provider you picked (Google, OpenAI or Anthropic), on your own key, under that provider's terms. Brut is never in the middle, and every call is written to your local spend ledger with its token counts and cost. Images you attach to a chat message (the 📎 button, Send to chat, a pasted or dropped file, or the stills of a node you name in the message) are sent to that same provider as part of that one message — never re-sent on later turns, and only files inside your project's outputs can be attached at all (a file you paste or drop from elsewhere is imported into the project first, like any image you bring in). The composer tells you before sending when naming a node will attach its stills. When Marcel acts on your canvas, what he reads to do the job — your graph's structure, node prompts and parameters, output file names, lines from the studio timeline — becomes part of that same conversation, so it reaches the text provider you picked, and nothing else. The actions themselves (placing nodes, wiring, running) happen entirely on your machine, and anything that would bill a key stops at an itemized confirm first. When Marcel speaks up on his own (the Assist slider at Reactive and above — failure diagnoses, run commentary, the recap when you open a project), the material he reasons over is the same local record: recent timeline lines, the error text, what's still running. That goes to your chosen text provider on your key, exactly like a chat message, and each remark is a ledgered call you can see. Set the slider to Off and nothing is ever sent unprompted. What Marcel remembers also stays on your disk. He keeps a taste profile — a plain-text note about how you like your images — tied to your account and stored beside your library. It is per-account, private, and never synced or exported: it does not travel in a folder export or a .brutpack. Project notes (a small memory for each project) live inside the project and travel with it, like the timeline. Both are plain text you can open and edit; Marcel proposes additions from your recent work and applies nothing to the profile until you approve it. Marcel's notebook (your taste as short notes) is a folder of markdown files inside your Elements folder, written only when you agree to keep a note, never synced. When Marcel searches your Elements vault or your notebook, the search runs on your machine; what he then says about the result goes to your text provider as part of that conversation, like every other line of a chat. Two exceptions, both on your own key and both in the ledger: describing the library sends a small copy of each picture once to Google (Gemini) so it can write what the picture shows, and, once you have described the library, each picture you add to your folders as it arrives (the switch beside the count turns that off); the descriptions stay in your folders' index files. On a folder shared by several of your machines, one of them is its describer (its key pays): the folder's index records that machine's name and when it last ran Brut, and while it describes it leaves a small file in the folder naming it, so the others wait; that file goes when the work ends. And a search by meaning sends the stored descriptions' text once to Google or OpenAI to be turned into vectors, and each new query once (rewritten by Gemini, then turned into a vector); the ranking itself runs on your machine, and the quiet pass that proposes notebook notes sends the pictures you kept and rejected on a node to your text model with one question, at most a few pictures per pass, once per set, and never when the Assist slider is Off.
The local engine is locked to the app
Only the Brut app can make Brut spend money or change your files. Other programs and web pages on your computer can't.
The only thing Brut ever sends

When you're signed in, Brut sends a small heartbeat (a daily check-in) at startup and once a day, so we can count active seats during the beta. That's it. Here is everything it contains, verbatim: { "install_id": "a uuid minted once on this machine", "app_version": "…", "engine_version": "…", "os": "Windows", "os_version": "…", "arch": "…", "ts": "…", "eula_version": "the date of the beta license you accepted" } No content. No prompts, no images, no filenames, no graph data, ever. Brut sends those eight fields and nothing else. The license version you accepted. The date stamp of the beta license you clicked I accept on in the app — so we can show, if ever asked, that a seat took the terms. A date, nothing more. Nothing while signed out. If you're not signed in, no heartbeat is sent at all. The answer carries three things back: whether your beta seat is still active, the version number of the latest installer, and the version number of the latest recipes (Brut's own presets, workflows and model list). When newer recipes exist, Brut downloads that one small file from getbrut.app in the background, checks that it was signed by us, and uses it from its next start: a model retired or a preset improved reaches you without a new installer. That download sends the same sign-in and a version number, nothing of yours. If a seat is revoked for a breach of the beta license, Brut signs you out and stops paid generations on that machine; your projects, outputs and keys stay exactly where they are. If the latest installer is newer than the one you run, a single line under the toolbar says so with a link to the download page; same version, no line. Nothing extra leaves your machine for that check: the version you run was already in the heartbeat. You can see this exact list any time in ⚙ Settings → Account.
Feedback — only what you type, only when you click send

The 💬 Send feedback button is the one other thing that can send data, and it's entirely user-initiated: nothing is ever sent until you press Send. A report carries your message, your account email (so we can reply), and — only if you leave the checkbox on — a diagnostics block: the same eight heartbeat fields plus the last few error messages from the Activity panel. The modal shows that block byte for byte before you send it ("Show exactly what will be sent"). Never your graphs, images, prompts or keys. The desktop app's quit-time prompt ("Before you go") is the same form under the same rule: it appears only after a session that actually ran something, and nothing leaves your machine unless you press Send & quit. Quit without sending is always one click.

Identity runs through Supabase (magic link or Google/GitHub). It's used only to know who's using a seat — never to store your work. Your sign-in is stored in your OS keychain and checked on your machine, so it works offline. This is identity only.

getbrut.app and this documentation load nothing from third parties — fonts are self-hosted, and there are no analytics scripts or trackers. The site has its own short notice covering the beta form, sign-in and emails: getbrut.app/privacy. The beta sign-up form is the one place you hand us an email, and only if you choose to. When your seat is approved we send one approval email to that address, and the download page asks you to sign in with the same account the app uses — that sign-in is checked against the approved list to serve the installer, and nothing else is recorded.
Your keys, your work, your machine. The only thing we ever learn is that a version of Brut is running on an install of yours, on some OS — and only while you're signed in.
